en: Preface to the Original Narrative of the Water Repentance at the Compassion Maṇḍala:
Generally speaking, regarding the composition of the sacred teachings, there has never been one produced without some profound inspiration.
Formerly, during the reign of Emperor Yizong of the Tang dynasty, there was the National Teacher Wudao Zhixuan, who encountered the Venerable Kanaka in a monastery in the capital.

The Venerable One manifested a transformation body, displaying the symptoms of *kāmalā* disease. The assembly all felt aversion toward him, yet only the Master Xuan consulted him with earnest inquiry, showing not the slightest sign of weariness.
When he wished to part company, the Venerable One was moved by his integrity and exhorted him, saying:

"In the future, when you encounter difficulties, you may go to Mount Jiulong in Pengzhou, Western Shu, to seek me out. There is a pine tree on that mountain which serves as my marker. Not long after, [the Master departed].
Master Zhixuan was renowned for his profound virtue and realization; Emperor Yizong personally attended his dharma assembly and honored him as National Teacher (Guoshi).

Furthermore, the Emperor bestowed upon him a seat made of agarwood, an act of exceptional grace. Thereafter, a human-faced sore suddenly appeared on his knee, complete with eyebrows, eyes, a mouth, and teeth.
Whenever he was fed with food and drink, it would open its mouth and swallow, no different from a human being. [He] spread [the word] everywhere...
He summoned renowned physicians, but none were able to cure him. Consequently, he recalled the words of the Venerable One from days past and entered the mountains to seek him out.

There, amidst mist and clouds, he indeed beheld two pine trees; he immediately hastened to their location. There stood a lofty pavilion and a vast hall, shimmering with the interplay of gold and lapis lazuli.
The Venerable One received him with great joy. He then informed the Venerable One of his ailment. The Venerable One said, "It is no cause for concern. Below the cliff..."

“There is a spring; if you wash [the wound] there, it shall be healed. He ordered a youth to lead him to the source of the spring. Just as he was cupping water in his hands, the ulcerated area cried out loudly, “Stop!
Do not wash yet! Have you ever read the biographies of Yuan Ang and Chao Cuo in the *Hanshu*? The Master replied, “I have read them.”
Since you have already read this, surely you know that Dou Ang executed Han Chuo in the eastern market; how grievous was his injustice!

For generations, [Han Chuo] sought retribution from the Master, yet the Master was a high monk of ten generations whose precepts were so refined and strict that the retribution could find no opportunity.
"Now my teacher has received the sovereign's favor and patronage to such an excess that his mind has given rise to a craving for fame and profit;
this causes a decline in his virtue, and thus it is possible to harm him. My teacher is Yuan Ang, and I am Chao Cuo.

Having just been cleansed by Venerable Kanaka with the Dharma-water of samādhi, from this point forward I shall no longer be an enemy to my teacher. At these words, the National Preceptor was struck with awe, his soul leaving his body.
The pain pierced to the very marrow of his bones; he fainted and then revived, yet the wound was no longer visible. Looking back at the palace halls, they suddenly seemed as if lost.
The Master then established a hermitage at that site and composed three fascicles of a text for repentance (*chánwén*).

Because the causes and effects across kalpas are never obscured and the retribution received by all under heaven has manifest signs, he took the meaning of washing away karmic offenses through the water of *samādhi*; thus, it was named "Water" (*Shuǐ*).
Confession.

Having reverently heard the words of the Sangha Jewel regarding the *Water Confession* (Shuilu Chan), it is said that the Venerable Kanaka poured forth the stream of Dharma from within samādhi and attained awakening.
Upon reaching the National Preceptor, he washed away the defilements of ten lifetimes. As he contemplated the emptiness of the mind, the shadows of his karmic transgressions were entirely eliminated.

When he cupped water to pour over himself, his agonizing, retributive sores vanished instantly. Thus, the grudges that had remained unresolved throughout successive births were released, and the offenses that no Buddha could pardon were surely atoned for.
It is like taking the medicine "Good Vision" among all remedies: every illness is healed. Within the illumination...

He illuminates his divine radiance; there is no hidden darkness that it does not enlighten. Having encountered the Holy Teacher, Master Xuán felt moved and wished to bestow benevolence upon this degenerate age.
Consequently, he recorded the great names of all Buddhas and gathered the profound meanings of the various sutras, so that those who expound them may transform their enemies into kinsmen.
I pay homage. By transforming this thicket of transgressions into a field of merit, I offer this earnest prayer that the waves of karmic activity may be stilled.
Looking up and knocking upon the Buddha, the King of Awakening, I shall surely receive his compassionate protection.
Preface:

It has long been the case that the Six Classics possess commentaries and sub-commentaries (*zhùshū*), and the Buddhist scriptures (*neidiǎn*) possess translations and exegeses. Yet, while commentaries on the classics abound, commentaries on penitential rites (*chàn*) are few.
What can be said of this? I humbly consider that since the establishment of the teachings by the sages of India, a specific gateway for repentance (*chànhuǐ*) was opened.

If that is so, from what does repentance (*chan*) arise? From what does remorse (*hui*) arise? You must ensure that the great meaning of the repentance text has its main pillars raised and its details spread out, dissecting and analyzing it down to the very marrow.
Only then, when the fourfold assembly hears it, will their minds be suddenly opened and every word find its resonance.

In undertaking the task of this commentary, you, Master, truly desire what has been stated above; do not decline to shoulder this responsibility. As for the hardships of cold and heat—[there is no need to worry].

In the interim, I have exhausted my diligent efforts; as for the citations from various sutras and the thorough investigations conducted, even those instances in the Tripitaka where there were no annotations or where it was noted that further examination was required were all cases of "suspending judgment" (*queyi*) due to uncertainty, rather than any negligence.

As for what has been explained and then explained again, flaws therein are certainly not worth concern. As for the vulgarity of redundant fabrications and arbitrary conjectures, I have never dared to commit such.
My own supplement:
Regarding the texts of repentance (*chanwen*), their lengths vary; likewise, the commentaries (*zhù*) differ in their degree of detail.

Now, in this annotated edition, since the long sections have already been divided into paragraphs according to the general outline, I fear that for the short sections, the method of annotation might require one to flip back and forth through the text before suddenly being able to grasp the meaning.
I have followed the Tibetan edition in general; as for the various chapters and scriptures, there are few points that require further elaboration, which readers may discover at their own leisure.

If one were to say that this approach "hangs on to one thing while omitting ten thousand others," I would not dare refuse such criticism. However, to claim that it is intended to "adorn one's wisdom or dazzle others with the extraordinary" would be far from the truth.
Recalling that his teacher had studied Confucianism and taught the Classics, he immediately set his mind upon the Inner Canon (Buddhist scriptures).
Later, due to successive family calamities, he cast aside worldly ties and received the transmission from Master Chao Fan at Jinge Mountain, becoming a Dharma heir of the Xianshou school.
Although he frequently followed the Master’s requests to serve as a lecturer and administrative official at places such as Chenbodu, Jiangxin Dingqiao, and the present-day Long...

He always personally ascended the seat for these dwellings. Regarding the completion of this annotated commentary: while it was indeed the Master’s long-held vow, the fact that it began in the [specific] year and month had not been heard of previously;

nor was it known that it was concluded in the twelfth lunar month of the *dingmao* year due to the Master’s grave illness, resulting in his penning the final annotations for the *Chanyao* (Repentance Essentials) and leaving it unopened for public lecture—a source of no small sorrow. However, as for my own humble sentiments...

His efforts were largely successful, and he ensured that the Dharma-treasure was circulated, continuing the past and opening the way for the future; thus, one may already catch a glimpse of his achievements.

Regarding the three volumes of the *Sūtra of Repentance*, there are four-line verses in praise of the Buddha at the beginning of each fascicle. Currently, the first two volumes are not annotated, while only the final volume is annotated.

The Master followed the ancient original text in providing these annotations, yet he still chose to annotate only the final volume. That he did not annotate the others was due to the severity of his illness.
Let it rest here. May those who understand this not join in the chorus of those who harbor envy toward our Master.

Do not, on the basis of the previous case regarding the omissions in the printed Heart Sutra, engage in reckless criticism. You must possess the "double pupils" of wisdom yourself; do not, for ten thousand reasons, allow yourself to be disturbed by such demonic influences.

The difficult characters in this Buddhist scripture have been provided with phonetic annotations for all of them, making them extremely easy to examine and verify. Nevertheless, errors such as those of "boar and pig" or "Lu and fish" cannot be entirely avoided.
Now, these annotated sections are based entirely upon the *Zi-hui* (Lexicon of Characters), having been meticulously collated and verified.

They have been transcribed and carved into printing blocks so that they may be convenient for recitation and also conform to the rules of calligraphy. All phonetics and strokes have been rendered with elegance and refinement, and no vulgar or colloquial expressions have been permitted.
To provide the funds for carving the woodblocks is to solidify the radiance of the Buddhas and Patriarchs; to give according to one's capacity is likewise the merit and wisdom of a *dānapati*.
Within this volume, the youth Xinlian Tang was the first to offer his contribution, setting an example for the fourfold assembly; even those with only two coins each were counted among the donors.
All contributions have been cataloged and engraved at the beginning of this volume; this truly constitutes a magnificent undertaking for those who received the offerings.

As for the Master’s eminent disciples, they alone crawled forward in prostration, ensuring that not even a grain of merit was lost from the gateway of goodness, fulfilling their collective aspiration without fail.
May the dragon-elephants shine forever, and may the palm leaves flourish eternally. Your labor must not be forgotten; your name should likewise be appended here.

In the heavens above and on the earth below, none is equal to the Buddha; throughout the worlds of the ten directions, there is likewise no peer.
Having seen all that exists within the world, I find that none at all can compare with the Buddha.
—From the *Qiyun Cibei Daochang Chanfa* (The Ritual of Repentance at the Compassionate Way-Place for the Commencement of the Fortunate Era).

"Initiating the practice" means that at the time of beginning the repentance, one must immediately focus the mind with single-minded visualization. A "Dharma hall" (do-ch'ang) is the place for cultivating the Way.
Only through this *Compassionate Dharma Hall Repentance Method* can sentient beings truly be benefited;

for it is by establishing this Compassionate Dharma Hall that the compassionate repentance method exists. Furthermore, the two characters for "Dharma hall" possess both a phenomenal (factual) and a noumenal (principle) dimension.
Regarding the practice (*vastu*), it refers to those who arrange and adorn the site with incense, flowers, lamps, candles, and other such offerings at an araṇya.
Regarding the principle (*nyāya*), it refers to that which exists within a mind that is reverent, sincere, and pure. As for "repentance" (*chān*):
In Sanskrit, *kṣamā* means "to repent" (*huìguò*). "Repentance" (*chàn*) refers to ceasing and cutting off future transgressions;

"remorse" (*huì*) refers to feeling shame for past offenses. Thus, it is said: "I pray that you may eliminate the sins already committed, and that I shall not dare to create further evil that has not yet arisen.
This is why it is called *chàn*. As for "Dharma" (*fǎ*), its meaning is "guiding and maintaining. "Guiding" (*guǐ*) means providing a standard that gives rise to understanding.
To uphold means to sustain one's own nature; furthermore, it does not go beyond the path of benefiting oneself and others, which is what is called "Dharma.
With single-minded devotion, I take refuge in all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
This refers to being pure and single-minded. Although a person may be able to repent on their own, they must also seek the Buddha’s deliverance;
therefore, one must single-heartedly take refuge in all Buddhas of the past, future, and present—these constitute the three periods of time.
The following eight Buddhas are the true Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Homage to the past Buddha Vipaśyin.
In the Sanskrit language, Vipaśyin is also called Vīra; this is translated as "Victorious Vision. Śākyamuni appeared during the era of this Buddha.
In this world, he was the first to plant the seeds of the marks and signs [of a Buddha]; thus, he is the foremost of the seven Buddhas. He spoke the verse of entrustment as follows:
"The body receives birth from within the signless, Just like illusory manifestations of various forms. The mind-consciousness of the one who creates the illusion is originally non-existent;
Both sin and merit are empty, having no place of abiding. He was the ninth hundred and ninety-eighth honored one of the past *Kṛta-yuga* (Adorned Eon).
Buddha. Homage to Śikhin Buddha.
In the Sanskrit language, Śikhin means "One with a Topknot. He spoke this verse of entrustment: "The arising of all wholesome dharmas is fundamentally..."
Illusion. The commission of various evil karmas is also illusion. The body is like a mass of foam; the mind is like the wind.
These illusions arise without root and without real nature. This was the ninth hundred and ninety-ninth Buddha of the past Adornment Kalpa.
Homage to Viśvabhū Buddha.
In the Sanskrit language, Viśvabhū means "Pervasive Sovereignty over All. The verse says: "The body is provisionally formed by borrowing the four great elements;

the mind is originally without birth, arising only because of objects. If the external object does not exist, the mind likewise does not exist. [The nature of] transgressions and blessings is like..."
Arising like an illusion, he has also ceased; he is the first of the thousand Buddhas of the past *Vibhūṣaṇakalpa*.
Homage to Kāśyapa Buddha.
In the Sanskrit language, *Kāśyapa* means "that which should be severed. A verse says: To see that the body is without reality is the Buddha-body.

To realize that the mind is like an illusion is the Buddha’s illusion. To realize that the fundamental nature of body and mind is empty—what difference is there between such a person and other beings?

He is the foremost honored Buddha of the present Bhadrakalpa. When the human lifespan was decreasing to sixty thousand years, he appeared and attained the Way of the Buddha, serving as the leader of the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa.
Homage to the Buddha Kanakamuni.
In the Sanskrit language, Kanakamuni means "Golden Silent Sage. A verse says: The Buddha does not perceive a body to know himself as the Buddha;
If there were truly a knowing subject, there would be no Buddha apart from it. The wise are able to know that the nature of sin is empty; Thus they remain serene and unperturbed.

Trembling with fear of birth and death, this second honored Buddha of the present Bhadrakalpa appeared and attained the path of Buddhahood when the human lifespan was decreasing to forty thousand years.
Homage to Kāśyapa Buddha!
In Sanskrit, Kāśyapa; here it is translated as "Drinking Light. A verse says: "The nature of all sentient beings is pure;
from the beginning, they are unborn and cannot be extinguished. This very body and mind are born of illusion; within this illusory transformation, there is neither sin nor merit."

This is the third honored Buddha of the present Bhadrakalpa. He appeared and attained perfect enlightenment when the human lifespan had decreased to ten thousand years, during the ninth minor kalpa of the Bhadrakalpa.
Homage to the Original Teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha.

In the Sanskrit language, he is called Śākyamuni; here [in Chinese], it is translated as “Able Benevolent One” (Nénrén) and “Silent Stillness” (Jīmò). “Benevolent and Compassionate Transformation and Guidance” is his title for benefiting others;
“Silent Stillness Realizing the Truth” is his name for benefiting oneself. Because he benefits both himself and others, he is called “Able,” and so forth.
The verse says: "The Dharma is originally without Dharma; the absence of Dharma is itself Dharma. Now, when the absence of Dharma is transmitted, how has any phenomenon ever been a phenomenon?
This is the fourth Buddha of the Bhadrakalpa. He appeared in the world when the human lifespan was one hundred years.
As for the term "kalpa," it refers to a time when the human lifespan is eighty-four thousand years, decreasing by one year for every passing century.
Furthermore, after another hundred years, the lifespan decreases by one year. This continues until it reaches ten years.

Then, after another hundred years, the lifespan increases by one year, continuing until it reaches eighty-four thousand years. One such period of increase and decrease constitutes a minor kalpa (antarakalpa).
Twenty periods of increase and decrease constitute one intermediate kalpa (*antarakalpa*). Eighty small kalpas constitute one great kalpa (*mahākalpa*).

There is also a tradition stating that eighty periods of increase and decrease constitute one intermediate kalpa; it is not known which is correct. One should know that one period of increase and one period of decrease amount to 1,680,000 years.
Regarding the abiding kalpa (*vivartakalpa*), from its beginning until the ninth kalpa, when the human lifespan is one hundred years—
This amounts to one hundred and fifty-one million nine hundred thousand years. When the lifespan has decreased to ten years, there will still be ten thousand years remaining thereafter.
Homage to the future Honored Buddha Maitreya.
In the Sanskrit language, Maitreya is translated as *Maitrī*, which means "The Kindly One" (*Cishi*); this is his clan name. He is also called Ajita, which means "The Invincible";
this is his personal name. He currently preaches the Dharma in the Tuṣita Heaven palace.
Later, he will descend to be born in the city of Ketumatī into the family of a great Brahmin; he will take conception and grow to full maturity, reaching a height of three... [chi] (cubits).
It is twelve *zhang* in height; the chest is ten *zhang* wide, and the face is five *zhang* long. The lifespan of the people is eighty thousand years, and they stand sixteen *zhang* tall.
Their appearances are dignified and handsome. They are born by transformation, requiring no toil or hardship.
Their treasuries are filled with the seven treasures, including gold and silver, yet no one looks upon them. There are no calamities, nor cold, heat, thieves, or any other misfortunes.
Auspicious Event △ The tenth minor kalpa within the *sthāyikappa* (abiding kalpa). It appears when the human lifespan decreases from eighty-four thousand years to eighty thousand years.
Opening verse of the sutra.
The unsurpassed, most profound, and subtle Dharma is the supreme among all Buddha-dharmas; there is not a single dharma that can equal it. The Buddha-dharma is the deepest;
there is not a single dharma that can fathom its bottom. Its principles and patterns are obscure and subtle, inconceivable; therefore, it is called "unsurpassed," and so forth.
It is difficult to encounter [such a teaching] even in hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas.
As the Sūtra says: "When the Buddhas appear in the world, it is rare to meet them; though they may appear in the world, it is even more difficult for them to preach this Dharma.
It further states: "For immeasurable and innumerable kalpas, time passes in vain without a Buddha. Since there is no Buddha, [it is difficult to hear this Dharma].
Furthermore, there is no dharma [that exists independently]. Thus it is said, "a hundred thousand," and so forth.
I have now seen, heard, and attained the power of upholding this.
It is because Śākyamuni Bhagavān has left behind his holy teachings in all directions that we are able to see, hear, and uphold them.

This is the ultimate of good fortune. "Seeing and hearing" can be understood as explained above. Regarding "receiving and upholding" (*śrutadhāraṇa*): "receiving" (*śruta*) refers to the internalizing of external objects;

"upholding" (*dhāraṇa*) refers to grasping firmly without relinquishing. This is what is meant by practicing in accordance with the meaning. For now, it may be provisionally acceptable to refer to ritual recitation as "receiving and upholding."
I vow to explain the true meaning of the Tathāgata.
Now, it is also acceptable for one to compose an explanation of the ritual for repentance before the Tathāgata based on the present text;

however, one need not alter it by relying on the ancient "Explanation of the True Meaning of the Tathāgata," for there is no reason to change what was established in antiquity. Furthermore, within this ritual of repentance, the majesty of the Buddhas—

These names originally issued from the golden mouth of the Tathāgata; moreover, since the text of this confession also cites Buddhist sūtras, they are none other than the true meaning of the Tathāgata.
Therefore, there is no need to alter them. These four lines constitute a praise of the Dharma and also express the sincerity and earnest devotion of one’s resolve.
The Buddha-Dharma is difficult to encounter; now that we have fortunately heard it, we only pray that we may understand it and practice according to what has been taught.
Cultivation of Practice:
The Ritual of Repentance for the Water of Compassion, Volume One.

Regarding this single section of repentance text, I shall provide only a brief explanation of its meaning and intent; were I to follow the ancient method of structural analysis, the text would be too voluminous to complete.

Regarding the meaning of "Dharma" as explained above, the term "scroll" (juan) is used in contrast to what is spread out. Generally, the Dharma-treasures of the Western Regions are neither written in the Sanskrit script nor bound in booklets;
rather, they are fashioned as a single roll. When one wishes to read them, they are unrolled; once the reading is finished, they are rolled back up.
It is indeterminate whether it is rolled up or spread out; therefore, it is called "rolled. This sutra consists of three fascicles; therefore, it is marked with a circle above.

Regarding the phrase "venerating and repenting with a sincere mind," one must first understand the meaning of the two characters for "repentance" (*chàn-huǐ*). "Repentance" (*chàn*) means to repent and eliminate what has occurred in the past. "Remorse" (*huǐ*) means to reform and repent from this moment forward.
Thus, only one who is capable of remorse can truly perform repentance. As for the term "compassion" (*cí-bēi*): "loving-kindness" (*cí*) is able to bestow happiness, while "compassion" (*bēi*)...
It is capable of uprooting suffering. The Patriarch established this method of repentance precisely to give rise to a mind of great compassion;
thus, it rescues sentient beings from suffering and bestows happiness upon them. Therefore, it is called the "Repentance Method of Compassion.
As for the "Water Repentance," it takes its name because it uses the water of samādhi to dissolve enmity, as detailed in the preceding section on the origin of the practice.
All Buddhas, out of compassion for sentient beings, have proclaimed the general dharmas of the Water Repentance Altar (the opening words).
This is because the defilements of sentient beings are heavy; who among them is without sin? Who is without fault? The conduct of ordinary people is foolish, shrouded by the darkness of ignorance.
Associating with evil friends, their minds are distracted by afflictions; being ignorant by nature, they indulge their own conceit.
Because their defilements are heavy, they commit many transgressions. As for "defilement," it refers to the impurity of body and mind, and the flowing filth of the three poisons.
Defilement stains the wondrous clarity, just as dust and grime defile a precious mirror, causing it to lose its brightness; therefore, it is called "dirt" (*mala*).
Ignorance (*avidyā*) shrouds in darkness until one becomes willful and self-reliant; this refers precisely to the state where the defilements are heavy.
"Ignorance" means a lack of clarity. To be stubbornly deluded and unaware of one's own faults and transgressions is what is meant by being "shrouded in darkness," which arises because of ignorance.
Therefore, they are deluded and obscured from their true nature. This applies equally to all ordinary persons, both here and there.
Regarding the terms "intimacy" (*pratyāsatti*) and so forth, there are two meanings: first, because they compete with one another to create [defilements], it is called "intimacy."
Second, those who lacked the seeds of faith and roots of goodness in past lives were unable to draw near to virtuous friends, but instead associated with evil people.
They were entirely deluded by greed, anger, ignorance, and the like; their afflictions threw their true mind into chaos, leading them to such a state as described in the text.
[The text itself clarifies this. Greed, anger, ignorance, pride, doubt, and false views—these six are the fundamental [afflictions], along with the twenty secondary [afflictions].
Regarding the passage on the afflictions and so forth: ignorance is none other than nescience (*avidyā*), and so on.
This refers to not believing in the Buddhas of the ten directions, not believing in the Honored Dharma and the Noble Sangha, and being unfilial toward one's parents, six relations, and kinsmen.
In the prime of their youth, they are heedless and self-conceited; they give rise to craving and affliction in their hearts toward all wealth, all music and song, and all female beauty.
They associate with those who are not noble and familiarize themselves with evil friends, showing no sign of reform.
Furthermore, they may kill and harm all living beings, or drink alcohol until they are stupefied, lacking any wisdom in their minds, and constantly [engaging in such ways].
Sentient beings have committed acts of rebellion and violated the precepts; all past transgressions and present evils, I now sincerely repent them all.
As for sins not yet committed, I dare not commit them again.
Lacking faith in the Buddhas, one reaches a state of stupor from drinking alcohol. To speak truly, the transgressions are many;
therefore, one must strip away all pretense and repent with sincerity, placing faith in the Triple Gem, which is the field of merit for transcending the world.

Regarding the "ten directions": these are east, west, south, north, the four intermediate points, above, and below. "Buddha" means awakening (*buddha*). Awakening is spoken of in contrast to delusion; it refers to awakening oneself and awakening others.
Enlightened practice is perfected. "Dharma" means correctness; it refers to the Tripitaka of Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma. "Saṃgha" means purity;
it refers to Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, as well as the successive patriarchs of the West and the East.

"Prime years" refers to the period of vigorous maturity; because of the boldness of one's blood and qi, "one" (*eka*) is used in the sense of universality, and "all" (*sarva*) carries the meaning of reaching the ultimate limit.
It encompasses and subsumes everything; therefore, it is called "all. *Greedy for wealth, one’s arrogance grows; greedy for pleasure, one’s lust is aided;

greedy for form, one’s rectitude is disturbed.* Regarding the phrase "the mind is equal" (*citta-samatā*), according to the teachings of the *Abhidharma* school (*Lakṣaṇa-yāna*), it is explained as follows: [The following is] a collection.
The "arising of mind" (*citta*) belongs to the *ālaya*, which is the eighth consciousness; the "deliberation" (*manas*) constitutes the seventh, the *manas* consciousness;

and the "discrimination" (*vijñāna*) constitutes the preceding six consciousnesses and so forth. Now, when it is said that "the mind gives rise to the arising of [mental] states," this generally emphasizes the preceding six consciousnesses and so forth.
Whether moving the body or initiating speech, even up to the arising of afflictions and the creation of karma, all proceed by means of these six consciousnesses.
Because it is supreme, it may be known as such; this is the meaning of being attached with longing. It is "not upright," for those who are wicked and debauched are therefore called "non-sages.
Furthermore, it extends even to harming human life and so forth. Wisdom (*jñāna*) is the essential nature of the person, while discernment (*prajñā*) is the person's illuminating function.
Regarding wisdom and discernment in contrast to the nature of consciousness (*vijñāna*): when consciousness is transformed, it becomes wisdom.
One is able to sever delusions and realize the Truth. Because of confusion and a lack of wisdom, one commits such offenses as these...
[and so forth] ...all of which are fully repented. This is precisely the intent of reforming the past and cultivating the future.

Therefore, one speaks before the Buddha: "As for offenses not yet committed, I dare not commit them again. This is what constitutes true repentance. In the third fascicle of the *Sūtra of Repentance*, these two phrases serve as...
In essence, this is ultimately so. For one who truly reforms evil and follows good, it can truly dissolve past transgressions;
for one who truly severs [afflictions] with a single prostration, not only will there be no portion of hell, but what difficulty could there be in attaining Buddhahood?

If, with an ordinary or selfish mind, you rely on the method of repentance and claim that it is no hindrance even to commit sins day after day, then this method of repentance will instead open the door for further transgressions rather than liberating people.
To prostrate and repent daily while simultaneously committing sins in hopes of extinguishing those very sins and generating merit—such a thing is impossible. It is like [drinking] wine...
It is like pouring water into a leaking cup; it can never be filled.

Therefore, today with a sincere heart, I take refuge in all the Buddhas throughout the entirety of space, all the great Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, Arhats, Brahma Kings, Śakra Devānām Indra, the Eight Classes of Devas, Nāgas, and all the assembly of holy ones. I pray that you will deign to...
Witnessing and reflecting upon the ten directions before one’s eyes, throughout the entirety of the realm of empty space— this means it is infinite and inexhaustible.

Those who practice the ten wholesome actions of the highest grade with purity, maintaining equanimity toward both enemies and kin, and even those who cultivate the four immeasurable minds, shall immediately attain Buddhahood.
The immeasurable Dharma gates do not transcend the ten wholesome actions; one must not fail to know this. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:

"The superior grade of the ten wholesome actions cultivates and purifies the mind, for it is vast and immeasurable. It is fully endowed with great compassion and extensively practices the six perfections."
Because their conduct and vows are vast, they become Bodhisattvas. As for the Pratyekabuddhas, they arise from the purity of the superior grade of the ten wholesome paths;

because they do not rely on the teachings of others, they lack great compassion and skillful means, yet through their own self-awakening, they understand the profound law of dependent origination, and thus they achieve the vehicle of the Solitary Realizers (Pratyekabuddhayāna).
As for the Arhats, the four fruits [of the śrāvaka path] arise from the superior grade of the ten wholesome paths.
They cultivate wisdom because their minds are narrow and inferior, because they fear the three realms, and because they lack great compassion.
Having understood the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths by following the voice of others, they belong to the Śrāvaka Vehicle. The *Dharmatā-śāstra* states:

"The 'toward' (向) refers to the direction [of practice], and the 'fruit' (果) refers to the realization of the fruit. There are eight types of *pudgala*—the four fruits and the four directions. This is translated here as "those who repeatedly advance" (數趨).
This refers to repeatedly coming and going through birth and death; that is, practicing the four paths and abiding in the four fruits. Regarding the Brahma King:
this is the Great Brahma Heavenly King, the lord of the Form Realm. Regarding Śakra: this is Śakradevendra, the lord of the Desire Realm.
As for the eight classes of beings, the *Chan-kao* (Meditation Manual) states: first, devas; second, nāgas; third, yakṣas; fourth... [text continues].
1. Gandharvas: These are the celestial musicians. 2. Asuras: These do not drink alcohol and constantly engage in combat with Śakra.
3. Garuḍas: These are the golden-winged bird deities. 4. Kiṃnaras: These resemble humans but have horns upon their heads.
The eighth are the mahoragas, which are the great serpent deities; they have human heads, snake bodies, and move by crawling on their bellies.
The *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā-sūtra* asks: "By what causes and conditions are the eight classes of spirits born into the evil realms, yet constantly hear the True Dharma?
The Buddha replied: "It is due to two kinds of karma: first, because of evil, they are born into the evil realms; second, because of goodness..."
Therefore, they experience happiness. He asked again, "May I hear the distinction between the two paths of good and evil? The Buddha said, "It may indeed be heard.
First, there was a celestial deity who previously provided vehicles, palanquins, dwellings, food, and drink as offerings to the Triple Gem, his parents, and worthy sages;
yet, he still harbored stinginess and envy. Second, there were dragon deities of the void who cultivated virtuous conduct and practiced generosity (*dāna*).
They do not rely on right mindfulness because they are impetuous and prone to anger. Third, the yakṣa deities are fond of great giving;
they may first cause harm and later bestow benefit, dwelling in the heavens, mid-air, or beneath the earth according to their merits and failings.
Fourth, the gandharvas are fond of giving but possess anger, as they offer music and dance. Fifth, the asura deities are... [of] intent.
They possess a forced joy and equanimity; they do not follow virtuous friends; and because they perform various false merits, they pursue only illusory and counterfeit deeds.
Sixth, as for the *garuḍa* deities: although they previously practiced great equanimity, they now harbor haughty minds that look down upon others. Seventh, as for the *kiṃnara* deities:
in the past, they were fond of exhorting others to resolve upon *bodhicitta*, yet they did not rectify their own wills and instead pursued various erroneous practices.
Therefore, as for the eight classes of mahoraga spirits, they protect the Dharma through their practice of giving, yet their natures are prone to anger.
Thus, all of them rely upon false teachers; by using the false to confound the correct, they each claim their own path to be the true Way and establish themselves therein.
As a verse says: "By performing two kinds of causes—wholesome and unwholesome—one becomes one of the eight classes of humans and non-humans."
Homage to Vairocana Buddha.
Vairocana Buddha is none other than the pure Dharmakāya. In the Sanskrit language, *Vairocana* means "pervading all places.
This refers to the ocean-like nature of Vairocana, whose essence is pure of afflictions and who is fully endowed with all virtues; his body and his land are mutually interpenetrating.
"Cheng" (Praise/Invocation) means pervading all places.
"Namo to our Original Teacher, Śākyamuni Buddha.
Śākyamuni Buddha is the teacher of the Sahā world and the Great Master of the three realms; therefore, he is called the "Original Teacher. That is to say, [of] hundreds and thousands...
This refers to the billions of transformation bodies. Śākyamuni means "Capable Benevolent One" (Nengren) and "Tranquil Silence" (Jimo).
This signifies that his virtue is benevolent and rescues all classes of beings, while his Way is tranquil, silent, and unconditioned.
Homage to Amitābha Buddha.
In the Sanskrit language, Amitābha means "Immeasurable. This refers to immeasurable life, immeasurable light, and all that is immeasurable.
He is the teacher of the Land of Bliss. Those who now seek rebirth in the Pure Land are precisely being born into that Buddha’s land.
Homage to Maitreya Buddha. When Maitreya descends to be born,
billions of Jambudvīpas shall all have ground made of pure gold, as level as the palm of a hand.
Non-glutinous rice grows spontaneously; food and clothing arrive of their own accord; there is immeasurable happiness. Men and women marry only at five hundred years of age.

According to the *Xiányújīng* (Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish), the Buddha said that Maitreya will hold three assemblies and deliver countless people—all those sentient beings who planted blessings through my bequeathed Dharma—and only thereafter will he transform his fellow practitioners of common affinity.
Namo to the Buddha Nāgottamarāja. Regarding "Nāgottamarāja":

*nāga* in the Sanskrit language means "dragon" (or "serpent"), which denotes one who is courageous and powerful. *Jāti* (translated here as "kind") carries the meaning of "lineage" or "clan," and must refer to his family name.
*Uttama-rāja* (translated as "Supreme Honored One") signifies that he is the most eminent within his lineage.
He is the most supreme and most honored; thus, his sacred title is manifested through this supreme honor. "King" (*rāja*) is a designation for one who possesses sovereignty.

The Buddha has exhausted the five stages of dwelling (*pañca-vihāra*) and eternally extinguished the two types of death (*dvividha-maraṇa*); he moves without obstruction, and is therefore called "sovereign," and so forth.
Homage to the Buddha Nāgeśvararāja.

"Nāgeśvararāja" means the king who is sovereign over the nāgas; the interpretation is the same as above. The name is designated according to his virtues, with slight variations in detail, and so forth.
Homage to the Buddha Ratnottama.
As for "Ratnottama" (Supreme Jewel): it is like a mani-jewel that excels and surpasses all other jewels;
the Tathāgata, the supreme jewel, transcends the jewels of all sages. Therefore, it is so called, and so forth.
Homage to the Buddha Awakening-Flower Samādhi Sovereign King.

Regarding "Awakening-Flower Samādhi," this must be the name of a samādhi. Speaking in terms of principle, "awakening" (jue) refers to the awakening of fruition, which signifies fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna).
The flower is the cause; it symbolizes primordial wisdom (*ādi-jñāna*). Since the beginning and the fundamental are non-dual, and principle and wisdom are of one suchness, they are inconceivable.
Therefore, it is called the "Awakening Flower Samādhi. Because he constantly abides in this samādhi, he takes this as his name, O Sovereign King.
The explanation is the same as above.
*Namo Kāśyapadhvaja Buddha*.
Regarding "Kāśyapa," the *Mahāvaipulya-mahāsannipāta-sūtra* states that "kāśa" means "removing impurities" (*qu yì*) in the Jin language. Furthermore, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* says:
It is called "Free from Defilement" (*viraja*). It may also be appropriate to use such terms as "Field of Merit" (*puṇyakṣetra*), "Free from Dust" (*vītarajas*), or "Lotus" (*padma*).

Furthermore, within the scriptures there is mention of a world-system named Kāśadhvaja; it remains uncertain whether this name was established based on the world itself. A "banner" (*dhvaja*) signifies correctness;
for the Buddha subdues the heterodox to manifest the correct, erecting the great banner of the Dharma and so forth. Moreover, the banner serves as a metaphor for the unsurpassed nature of the Dharma.
Therefore, he is called Kāśyapa-dhvaja (Kāśyapa Banner).
Homage to the Buddha Siṃhanāda (Lion’s Roar).
As for "Lion’s Roar": it is like a lion emerging from its cave, whereupon all other beasts hide their tracks; when the Buddha-lion emerges, the multitudes [of beings] likewise [flee].
Because Māra flees and cowers; furthermore, it is said that when a great lion lets out a single roar, the young lions become courageous and strong.
When the Buddha, the Teacher, lets out a single roar, all the bodhisattvas and others likewise become valiant and diligent; thus it is said.

However, the Buddhas of the ten directions do not exceed manifesting their names through their virtues; when explained according to their meaning, there is nothing else particularly marvelous or clever.
Homage to Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva.
Mañjuśrī means "Wondrous Virtue" (Miaode) in this language. As a sutra states: "He clearly perceives the Buddha-nature, just like Mañjuśrī and others.
Because he is the foremost among all bodhisattvas, Mañjuśrī is mentioned first. He is also titled Mañjuśrī.
This is called *Mañjuśrī*. He is also titled *Mañjuśiri*, which means "Wondrous Head.
Homage to Samantabhadra Bodhisattva. Samantabhadra Bodhisattva:
in Sanskrit, he is called *Viśvabhūta* or *Samantabhadra*; this means "Universal" (or "Pervasive").

"Worthy" (*xian*) means one whose conduct pervades the *dharmadhātu*; "Universal" (*pu*) means one whose rank is adjacent to the ultimate Sage. Because this Bodhisattva’s practice and vows are foremost among all, he is called Samantabhadra.
Furthermore, both the *Amitābha-sūtra* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* translate the name as "Pien-chi" (Ubiquitous Auspiciousness). Other details are omitted for brevity.
Homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta. Mahāsthāmaprāpta;
in the Sanskrit language, *Mahāsthāmaprāpta*, which is translated here as "Great Power Attained. The *Siddhārthamati-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states:
"Wherever I set my foot, it causes the trichiliocosm and the palaces of Māra to tremble. Hence, he is called "Great Power."
[He] arrives. The *Sūtra of Contemplation* states: "By means of the light of wisdom, he universally illumines all beings, causing them to leave the three miserable realms and attain supreme power.
It is for this reason that it is said thus.
Homage to Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva.
The Vow of Kṣitigarbha states: "If hell is not empty, I shall not become a Buddha. Thus, he serves as the Master of the Netherworld.
The *Kṣitigarbha Sūtra* states: "In future ages, if anyone hears the name of this Bodhisattva, or praises him, or gazes upon and pays homage to him..."
Whether by reciting the name, making offerings, or even by painting, carving, or sculpting images using lacquer,
such a person shall be reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three a hundred times.
Homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāvyūha.
As for the Bodhisattva Mahāvyūha, although it has not yet been definitively ascertained where he is recorded,
it can be known that his holy title was established because his Dharma-body is adorned with the various merits of the six perfections and the myriad practices.
Homage to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
As for Avalokiteśvara: when practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, he clearly perceived that the five aggregates are all empty.
"Clearly perceiving" (*āloka*) is precisely "contemplation" (*avaloka*); "all empty" is precisely "sovereignty" (*īśvara*). This leads to the subsequent passage: "Therefore, emptiness..."
Within it, there is no form, nor sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, up to and including the bodhisattva.
By relying on the *prajñāpāramitā*, one attains liberation from inverted dreams and delusions, reaching ultimate nirvāṇa.
How could one not be called Avalokiteśvara? Furthermore, the *Yongjia ji* says: "When no dharma can be apprehended, this is the Tathāgata; only then does one receive the name."
Having paid homage to all the Buddhas as Avalokiteśvara, one next performs repentance,
using words that acknowledge those above and address those below.

Now, one who wishes to perform rites of repentance (this also serves as the opening of the discourse) must first pay reverence to the Triple Gem. The reason for this is as follows (to explain the meaning of the preceding statement).
The Three Jewels are the true friends and fields of merit for all sentient beings. If one can take refuge in them, immeasurable sins will be extinguished and immeasurable blessings will increase.
This clarifies the evidence of the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).
It enables the practitioner to leave behind the suffering of birth and death and attain the bliss of liberation;
it is the proof of a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). The Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha constitute the Triple Gem (*triratna*). The Triple Gem can cause people to turn their backs on...
The dust of the senses is cleared away; one is shown, awakened to, and enters into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision—is this not indeed a true friend?
It is like a good and virtuous friend in the world, who leads people onto the path of goodness.
Not only this, but it can also serve as a vast field of merit for sentient beings. Regarding the fields of merit, there are three; first, once one knows the Triple Gem, one is then able to...
Reverent faith is called the "field of respect" (gongtián). Second, being able to repay the kindness of one's parents is called the "field of gratitude" (entián).

Third, being able to feel compassion for those in poverty and suffering is called the "field of pity" (beitián). Because one can plant all manner of merit within the Three Jewels, they are collectively termed the "field of merit" (futian).
From the words "If one is able... onwards, the text directly reveals the benefits; the meaning of the passage is clear.

Therefore, those who take refuge in all Buddhas throughout the ten directions and the entirety of the realm of empty space, and who perform rites of repentance, must necessarily take the Three Refuges as the cause for entering the Way. First is taking refuge in the Buddha. As for "Buddha":
It is awakening. It is great awakening. It is the Honored One. Taking refuge in the Buddha, one shall never fall into hell.

"Awakening" is spoken of in contrast to delusion; it is self-awakening and awakening others, wherein the practice of awakening is perfected. All of the ten directions and empty space appear before one's eyes.
I take refuge in all the Honored Dharmas throughout the ten directions and the entirety of the realm of empty space.
Second, I take refuge in the Dharma. "Dharma" means correctness; it refers to the Tripiṭaka of Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma.

By taking refuge in the Dharma, one shall never fall into the realm of hungry ghosts. Furthermore, "Dharma" carries the meaning of an upper standard or a principle to be upheld—that which is elucidated within the teachings. Fourth.
The Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, and the dharmas of the Six Perfections and Four Immeasurables—by practicing in reliance upon these, one attains Perfect Enlightenment;
therefore, they are called "Dharma.
I take refuge in all the holy Sangha throughout the ten directions, as far as the limits of empty space.
Third is taking refuge in the Sangha. "Sangha" means purity; it refers to the Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and the successive patriarchs of the West and the East.
By taking refuge in the Sangha, one will never fall into the animal realm. There are three Jewels.
These are the Three Jewels of the ten directions. Furthermore, there are the Three Jewels of the sustaining community (*dharmadhara*):
clay shrines and molded images, as well as those carved and gilded in gold, are the Buddha Jewel; yellow scrolls with red bindings, square volumes, and palm-leaf manuscripts are the Dharma Jewel;

those with shaven heads and square robes, who maintain the precepts with rigorous purity, are the Sangha Jewel. Moreover, there are the Three Jewels of the single essence, which are inherent in every person.
That which possesses these qualities is as follows: the self-nature of constant awakening and non-obscuration is the Buddha Jewel;
the self-nature of maintaining the track and not losing it is the Dharma Jewel; and the self-nature of purity and harmony is the Sangha Jewel.

That they are all collectively termed "Jewels" is because they are uniquely honored and uniquely precious, peerless and without equal, and are certainly not like the rare treasures or exotic objects of the mundane world.
...and therefore they are called "Treasures. Regarding the Three Jewels, one must always perform a full prostration; it is incorrect for people today to prefer brevity and fail to prostrate.
This is why we, [Name] and others, now perform this repentance.
Whenever the phrase "such-and-such and others" is used, one must invariably state one's own name;

all subsequent instances follow this pattern. This is precisely because, since beginningless time, while remaining on the level of ordinary beings, regardless of status high or low, the manifestations of transgression have been immeasurable.
These may arise from the three karmas, or originate as faults through the six sense faculties, or stem from one’s own internal, perverse reflections.

Or, by relying on external objects, various defiled attachments arise. In this way, even up to the point where the ten non-virtues increase, eighty-four thousand gates of worldly affliction (*kleśa*) flourish.
From time immemorial, throughout past lives and lifetimes—stretching back directly to before heaven and earth existed—there has been none.
The karmic offenses accumulated over immeasurable kalpas, as described in the following text, are all fundamentally rooted in this body.
Regarding the three types of karma—body, speech, and mind: the body involves the karmas of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct;

speech involves the karmas of lying, frivolous talk, divisive speech, and harsh abuse; and the mind involves the karmas of greed, anger, and delusion. Taken together, these are termed the "three karmas," which are further divided [into ten].
These constitute the ten non-virtues. Not committing the ten non-virtues is precisely the ten virtues. Since good and evil karma arise from these, they are called the three types of karma.
Regarding the six sense faculties: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. These six serve as the roots for deluded conditions.
Internal mental deliberation belongs to the objects of conceptual thought; external sensory attachment belongs to the objects of contact.
The *Dongjing* (Scripture on Movement) says: "Because the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise; because phenomena arise, all manner of minds arise.

This refers to the internal perversions and external defilements. Regarding the eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*), as stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, sentient beings [engage] with the objects of form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch;
that is to say, the five sense organs correspond to the five sensory objects.

There are five hundred internal afflictions and five hundred external afflictions, totaling one thousand. This is discussed in terms of the ten fetters (*daśa-anuśaya*) of the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*).

The ten fetters of the delusions of view are: greed, hatred, delusion, pride, doubt, the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), false views (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*), clinging to views (*dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*), and clinging to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
Furthermore, if one calculates based on the seven branches—the three of body and four of speech—each having one thousand, the total becomes seven thousand.
One thousand [factors], further categorized by the three periods of time, become twenty-one thousand.

Furthermore, classifying those with a predominance of greed, those with a predominance of hatred, those with a predominance of delusion, and those with equal proportions of these three, each group consists of twenty-one thousand;
thus, they collectively total eighty-four thousand. By means of these eighty-four thousand rules...
By applying the appropriate remedies, these become the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates.
Although the manifestations of such offenses are indeed immeasurable, when summarized broadly, they do not exceed three types: first, afflictions (*kleśa*).
The second is karma; the third is the retribution thereof. These three types of phenomena can obstruct the Noble Path as well as the superior and wondrous blessings of humans and devas.
For this reason, they are designated as the "three obstructions" in the sutras.

Although the transgressions and karmic deeds of human beings may number in the thousands or tens of thousands, they are rendered particularly grave when defiled by the three obstacles (*trividha-āvaraṇa*).
Thus, one should know that body, speech, and mind constitute the root of sinful obstructions; these three obstacles are, in fact, the primary leaders of the host of worldly afflictions (*kleśa*).
As for "obstacle" (*āvaraṇa*), it means to hinder or to conceal. When these three types exist, they obstruct and veil [the true nature].
It obstructs all the noble paths and the superior states of humans and devas. For example, it is like a person of the present day who ordinarily possesses extremely wholesome intentions;

yet, upon encountering a single stimulus, they immediately give rise to afflictions and initiate the causes and conditions for unwholesome karma. This results in the hindering and retreating of many virtuous thoughts—how could this not be an obstruction?
How much more so when it leads to the retribution of the three evil realms! Furthermore, how can one know that the noble paths and [the higher realms] even exist?
How excellent are the matters of humans and devas! One must know that where there is karma, there must be obstacles;

since all human life is necessarily accompanied by karma, one knows that repentance, the [Four] Truths, the [Twelve] Links of Dependent Origination, and the Six Perfections constitute the Path of the Sages, while the Ten Wholesome Actions and the Five Precepts are the good matters of humans and devas.
Therefore, when the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas teach the application of skillful means to repent and eliminate these three obstacles,
then the six sense faculties, the ten unwholesome actions, and even the eighty-four thousand gates of affliction will all become completely pure.

"Method" (fang) refers to the technique; "expediency" (bian) refers to seizing the opportune moment. What is later called "arousing the seven kinds of mind" as the method and expedient path for repentance and the eradication of karmic obstacles corresponds precisely to this.
Throughout the *Shuilu Chanyi* (Water Repentance Ritual), only the three obstacles are discussed from beginning to end;
in the middle section, greed, anger, and ignorance are assigned to the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), while the three [actions] of the body...
The offenses committed through the four [actions] of the mouth, the six sense organs, and the three jewels are classified as karmic obstructions (*karmāvaraṇa*).
The remaining retributions from the hells, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and devas are classified as retributive obstructions (*vipākāvaraṇa*).

These are expounded as a three-fascicle text of repentance because all worldly people are burdened by these three heavy obstructions, which prevent them from escaping the suffering and affliction of birth and death; therefore, one must practice repentance. Now, regarding repentance...
One must certainly repent with the mind. Therefore, one should arouse seven kinds of mental states to perform repentance;
only then can [the obstacles] be eliminated. For this reason, O assembly, today you should employ this superior and excellent mind to repent of the three obstacles.

Those who wish to extinguish the three obstacles, what kind of mind should they use to cause these obstacles to be eradicated? (This is the formal commencement; the following sets forth the intent. First, one should arouse the seven kinds [of mental states].
By taking the mind as the means, these hindrances can then be extinguished. What are the seven? (The following list their names):
First, shame and remorse; second, fear and dread; third, weary detachment; fourth, generating the bodhicitta; fifth, equanimity toward enemies and kin;
sixth, mindfulness of repaying the Buddha’s kindness; seventh, contemplating the emptiness of the nature of offenses.
In the Abhidharma, there are originally seven kinds of methods for repentance (*pratideśanā*). These are based upon the cultivation of seven types of mental states as the fundamental means.
This precisely accords with the "sentences on the cultivation of means" taught by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas above. Regarding "shame" (*hrī*):

as the *lakṣaṇa*-school (Dharmalakṣaṇa) says, shame has the nature of revering and honoring the virtuous and good based on the power of one's own [wholesome] qualities. As for... [the text continues].
Its function is to counteract shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and to cause the cessation of unwholesome conduct. "Self" refers to one's own person; "dharma" refers to the teaching. It means:
"I, with such a body, understand such a dharma, and thus I dare not commit various evils. As for "shame" (*apatrāpya*), its nature is to reject violence and evil by relying on the power of the world.
Its function is to counteract lack of shame (*anapatrāpya*) and to cause the cessation of unwholesome conduct. That is to say, it is the censure of worldly people.
"Hā" refers to worldly power. It means to treat those with evil lightly and not associate with them, and to reject evil dharmas and karmic actions and not perform them;
hence the terms "lightning," "rejecting," and so forth. The rest is clarified below in the section on repentance (*pratikramaṇa*).
First, regarding shame and remorse: I reflect that I and the Śākya Tathāgata were once fellow ordinary beings.
Yet, since the World-Honored One attained the Way, countless eons as numerous as the sands of the Ganges have already passed.

Meanwhile, we have remained immersed in the six sense-objects, transmigrating through birth and death with no prospect of escape. This is truly something for which one should feel shame, remorse, and humiliation before the world.
It is shameful.
First, it is shameful not to attain Buddhahood. For the sage and the ordinary person share the same essence; if one does not accomplish the Way of the Sage, one will ultimately fall into saṃsāra.
To harbor such thoughts would be a cause for dying of shame, leaving no ground for concealment. "Reflecting upon oneself" means one should contemplate within oneself.
Reflecting upon eons past, long ago, even before the World-Honored One had attained the Way, he was likewise an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
It may seem that since the World-Honored One attained Buddhahood in this present life, not much time has passed; yet, when tracing back his prior causes, it is as follows:
he encountered and served seventy-five thousand Buddhas, such as the ancient Śākyamuni and others, thereby completing the first *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*. Then...
He served seventy-seven thousand Buddhas, beginning with Dīpaṃkara Tathāgata, thereby completing the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa.
He continued until he served Vipaśyin Tathāgata, thereby completing the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa.
After this, he spent another ninety-one kalpas cultivating the karma for the marks of excellence, until finally, upon meeting Kāśyapa Buddha, he attained perfection.
He filled [all realms]. During this time, he was born above as a Heavenly Emperor thirty-six times and below as a Wheel-Turning Sage King thirty-six times.
Furthermore, he occasionally became a rishi, a bhikṣu, a minor king, or a brāhmaṇa in incalculable numbers, delivering immeasurable beings.
Therefore it is said that since his attainment of the Way, through kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges... yet.
Such matters as the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* and so forth are merely expedient means within the "Life Span" chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*;

they are not the ultimate reality. In truth, since the World-Honored One attained Buddhahood, immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable numbers of kalpas—as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—have passed;
this is why it is said thus. As clarified in the sutra, there is no need for further elaboration here. The six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*).
These are form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and mental objects; they defile the wondrous clarity and act as dust.
As explained above regarding the eighty thousand afflictions (*kleśa*), one should merely reflect with a sense of shame and remorse.

One must exhaustively repent with sincerity, reform the past and cultivate the future, and with courageous diligence, strive to achieve completion in this very life and swiftly escape the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
I shall dedicate [this merit] until I attain unsurpassed bodhi, becoming no different from the Buddhas;
only then shall I fulfill my great vow of repentance and finally eliminate my initial sense of shame.
The general meaning of the following six chapters—beginning with "Terror and Loathing" and "Arousing the Bodhicitta"—can be inferred by analogy.
The second fear is that, as an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*),
one has not yet escaped the evil karma of body, speech, and mind— namely, the three of the body, the four of speech, and the three of the mind.

One is constantly associated with transgressions. By reason of these causes and conditions, after the end of life, one should fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts, and undergo immeasurable suffering.
This is truly something to be startled by, to be terrified of, to be fearful of, and to be afraid of.
In such places of dread and terror, one can ultimately never escape.
Thus, one should merely contemplate with alarm and must repent with utmost sincerity, as previously described at length.
Second, there is the fear of entering the three evil paths—namely, the hells, the hungry ghosts, and the animals. One who forms this thought should be filled with solemn awe.
"Terrified" means fear; "dreadful" means terror. Such things as "startled and afraid" are as explained above.
Third, regarding "weariness and detachment": one constantly contemplates that within birth and death there is only impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self;
it is impure and illusory, like bubbles upon water that quickly arise and quickly perish, revolving and wandering back and forth like a chariot.
The wheel [of saṃsāra]: birth, old age, sickness, and death—the eight sufferings—intertwine and sear us, never ceasing for even a moment.
All of you, together, simply observe your own bodies from head to foot; therein there are only thirty-six things: hair, body hair, nails, and teeth.
Eye discharge, tears, nasal mucus, saliva, filth, sweat, the two excretions (feces and urine), skin, hide, blood, flesh, sinews, vessels, bones, marrow, fat, and grease.
The brain, membranes, spleen, kidneys, heart, lungs, liver, gallbladder, intestines, stomach, and the red and white phlegm;
these flow constantly from the nine orifices. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "This body is a collection of manifold sufferings" (the meaning of *kāya* is 'accumulation,' hence it is so described).
Everything about it is impure; what person of wisdom would ever delight in this body? Since birth and death are thus...
These various evil dharmas are truly to be dreaded and weary of.
Third, one should cultivate weary detachment: this body is impermanent, it is suffering, it is empty, it is non-self, and it is impure and false.
For one who forms such a conception, it is simply taught that the skull shall fall to the ground—this is first to observe by means of oneself.
Examine with wisdom and illuminate it; clearly understand the affairs within birth and death as being thus illusory and unreal.
The subsequent text causes the assembly to do the same, expanding upon this meaning. Regarding "mutually": this also refers to the intention of contemplating and knowing for oneself.
The entire lifetime of the Tathāgata’s temporal teachings—the Tripitaka and the twelve divisions of the canon—do not go beyond this.
The phrases "impermanent," "suffering," and "empty" indicate that because all things are empty, they are ultimately without self and without what belongs to a self;
this will be clarified in the following text. The arising and ceasing of water bubbles and the revolving of a wheel are metaphors for impermanence and unreality.

Regarding these afflictions, according to the *lakṣaṇa* school (the Abhidharma), there are six root afflictions—greed, anger, ignorance, pride, doubt, and false view—as well as twenty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
There are ten minor secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), two intermediate secondary afflictions, and eight major secondary afflictions; as the text would be too voluminous, they are not cited here.

Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "The karma of greed, hatred, and delusion causes sentient beings to fall into the hells, the realm of hungry ghosts, and the animal realm to undergo suffering.
If they are born among humans, they will be impoverished and destitute, cruel and stubborn, dull-witted, and ignorant."
The retributions for all afflictions:
due to the causes of suffering—the afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion—one undergoes the retributive suffering of the three miserable realms (*trāya*).

Once the retribution of the three miserable realms is exhausted, even if one should obtain a human body, one will be destitute, exposed, dull-witted, and deluded; all of these are the retributions evoked by afflictions. Therefore, it is said: "All..."
This is the retribution for afflictions.
Since mental karma yields such evil fruits as these, we [name] and others today take refuge in all Buddhas with a sincere heart,
seeking their compassion through repentance.
The above concludes the confession. From "Now, as for this" below, the faults and afflictions of the defilements (*kleśa*) are set forth, and so on.
Indeed, these defilements have been rebuked in various ways by all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and noble ones who have entered into the principle;
they are also termed "enemies. Why is this? Because they are able to sever the life-root of wisdom (*prajñā-jīvita-mūla*) of sentient beings.

"Sage" (*ārya*) means "correct. It refers to one who possesses correct wisdom. Aside from the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, all ancestral teachers and monks who possess wisdom universally censure their afflictions (*kleśa*).
This can be understood through such matters as the teachings on censuring desire and abandoning the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
To censure the afflictions is to regard them as enemies, as thieves, as torrential rivers, and as shackles; thus they are censured.
They are not uniform; therefore, it is said that they are "reproached in various ways. This shows that afflictions (*kleśa*) as a whole constitute a great calamity.
Below, the names of these calamities are set forth and explained in detail.
These afflictions are also termed "thieves," for they are able to plunder the various wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*) of sentient beings.

In the Abhidharma school (*lakṣaṇa-vāda*), among the eleven wholesome factors—namely, faith (*śraddhā*), shame (*hrī*), dread of blame (*apatrāpya*), the three roots of non-attachment (*alobha*) and so forth, diligence (*vīrya*), tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), heedfulness (*apramāda*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and non-harming (*avihiṃsā*)—six are designated as "thieves' accomplices" (*caura-madhya-gata*); this refers to those that facilitate the theft of one's own family treasures.
These afflictions are also called "torrential rivers," for they can sweep sentient beings away into the great ocean of suffering of birth and death.
They are also called "fetters and shackles," for they can bind sentient beings within the prison of birth and death,
preventing them from escaping.

Waves crash and surge against one another as torrential rivers; their revolution is endless and their drifting is inexhaustible. The suffering endured is profound and far-reaching, with no discernible limit or shore.
Therefore, it is likened to the great ocean.
Thus, the six realms of existence are entangled, the four modes of birth never cease, evil karma is inexhaustible, and the fruits of suffering do not end.
One should know that all of these are the faults and afflictions of the *kleśas*.
Regarding the six realms of existence (*ṣad-gati*): as stated in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, first is the realm of devas, which comprises twenty-eight heavens;

second is the realm of humans, characterized by the five constant virtues and the five precepts; third is the realm of asuras, which is subsumed under the categories of ghosts, animals, humans, and devas; fourth is the realm of hell-beings, consisting of the eight cold and eight hot hells and so forth;
fifth is the realm of hungry ghosts, comprising nine types and ten classes; and sixth is the realm of animals, categorized as those born from wombs, eggs, moisture, or transformation.

It is also called the six destinies (*ṣadgati*). Regarding the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*): these are viviparous, oviparous, moisture-born, and transformation-born. That which extends life by depending on a shell is called oviparous birth;

that which emerges from being contained within is called viviparous birth; that which arises through reliance on moisture is called moisture-born birth; and that which suddenly exists where there was nothing is called transformation-born birth.
The six paths are interconnected and the four modes of birth are unceasing; this is what is meant by the "uninterrupted cycle of rebirth" (*saṃsāra-anantara*).

This corresponds to the aforementioned retributions for the various afflictions (*kleśa*). Having concluded the exposition on the faults and calamities of the afflictions above, the following section correctly seeks repentance;
the same applies to the subsequent five sections of the text.
Therefore, today I mobilize this superior wholesome mind to seek compassion and repent.
Taking these afflictions and their faults as the superior and most excellent conditions for repentance, it is said, "with a superior wholesome mind," and so forth.
Having finished citing the sacred words above to demonstrate the faults and afflictions of the defilements, hereafter [follows] the five...
Chapter: An extensive exposition of the names and characteristics of afflictions and karmic offenses, none of which fail to arise from mental karma.
We, [the practitioners], from time immemorial until this very day, have received retribution while wandering through the six realms of existence, including those of humans and devas.
Possessing this mind-consciousness, one constantly harbors ignorance and delusion, which fill the breast in abundance.

Possessing this mind-consciousness, it arises from the fundamental faculties of mental karma; yet, being without wisdom and lacking faith, there is absolutely no aspiration for transcendence of the world.
Therefore it is said: "filling the breast in abundance," and so forth.

Or one may commit all manner of offenses due to the three poisons, or due to the three outflows (*āsrava*), or due to the three sufferings, or due to the three inversions, or by craving the three realms of existence;
such offenses are immeasurable and boundless, throwing all beings of the six destinies and four modes of birth into confusion. Today [I am] ashamed.
I feel shame and repent for all [these faults].
Greed leads to old age; hatred leads to illness; delusion leads to death; therefore, they are called the roots of the three poisons.
Furthermore, these three are the fundamental source of the evils of birth and death; hence they are called "roots. The *Abhidharma-śāstra* states: "Three..."

Regarding the outflows (*āsrava*): first, the outflow of desire (*kāmāsrava*), which consists of all afflictions of the desire realm; second, the outflow of existence (*bhavāsrava*), which consists of all afflictions of the two higher realms with the exception of ignorance;

third, the outflow of ignorance (*avidyāsrava*), which consists of the ignorance of the three realms. Because they cause the mind to flow and disperse continuously without ceasing, they are called "outflows.

Furthermore, because they cause the mind to move about, they are named "outflows. Third, regarding the three types of suffering (*duḥkha*): first, the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*). Third... [text fragment]

The realms (*dhātu*) are already suffering; the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is further characterized by suffering. There are two types of suffering due to change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*): it is suffering when pleasure changes, being equal to the three miserable destinies (*apāya*).

Third is the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*), which is the suffering inherent in the neutral state and pervades the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Regarding the "three inversions" (*viparyāsa*): they are the inversion of mind (*citta-viparyāsa*), the inversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*), and the inversion of view (*dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa*). Regarding the "three existences" (*bhava*):
these are the three realms, namely, existence in the desire realm (*kāma-bhava*), existence in the form realm (*rūpa-bhava*), and existence in the formless realm (*arūpya-bhava*).
This refers to not forgetting the causes and effects of the three realms; there is birth and there is death, hence it is called "existence" (bhava).

Such offenses as these are collectively the three poisons atop the head, extending to all offenses within the three realms of existence. Whenever the phrase "such as these" is used, it should all be understood in this manner.
Furthermore, [Name] and others, from time immemorial until this very day, have committed all manner of transgressions—
whether through the four abodes (*catur-vāsa*), or through the four floods (*catur-ogha*), or through the four graspings (*catur-upādāna*), or through the four attachments (*catur-abhiniveśa*),
or through the four conditions (*catur-pratyaya*), or through the four great elements (*catur-mahābhūta*).

All transgressions—whether those created due to the four bonds, those created due to the four cravings, or those created due to the four modes of birth—such offenses are immeasurable and boundless. They cause confusion and turmoil for all sentient beings throughout the six realms.
Today, with shame and remorse, I confess them all.

Regarding the four stations of consciousness (*vijñāna-sthiti*), the *Abhidharma-samuccaya-vyākhyā* states: the station of consciousness in form (*rūpa*), the station of consciousness in sensation (*vedanā*), the station of consciousness in perception (*saṃjñā*), and the station of consciousness in mental formations (*saṃskāra*).
Regarding the four floods (*ogha*), the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: first, the flood of desire (*kāma-ogha*), which consists of the afflictions of the desire realm;

second, the flood of existence (*bhava-ogha*), which consists of the afflictions of the two upper realms, excluding [the delusion associated with] views; third, the flood of views (*dṛṣṭi-ogha*), which consists of the views of the three realms; and fourth, the flood of ignorance (*avidyā-ogha*).

The delusion of the three realms is also called the four yokes. Regarding the four graspings (*upādāna*), the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: they are the grasping for sense-desires (*kāmopādāna*), the grasping for views (*dṛṣṭyupādāna*), the grasping for precepts and rituals (*śīlavratopādāna*), and the grasping for self-theory (*ātmavādopādāna*).

Because these can cause one's own continuum to be grasped without interruption, they are called "graspings. Regarding the four attachments, the *Awakening of Mahāyāna Faith* (*Mahāyānaśraddhotpāda-śāstra*) says:

first, attachment to arising while [truly] there is no arising; second, attachment to cessation while [truly] there is no cessation; third, attachment to annihilation while [truly] there is no annihilation; and fourth, [attachment to permanence while truly there is no permanence].

The four attachments to permanence: Regarding the four conditions (*pratyaya*), the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Yuánjué jīng*) states: first, the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), which is the conjunction of all dharmas;
second, the sequential condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), which consists of the mind and mental factors; third, the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), wherein dharmas have no basis;

and fourth, the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), wherein dharmas are ungraspable. Regarding the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), they are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element—these are called the four.

The great elements combine to form the body. ○ Regarding the "four fetters" (*bandhana*): the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states they are the fetter of greed, the fetter of delusion, the fetter of attachment to precepts and rituals, and the fetter of attachment to views.
Because one does not transcend the three realms and fails to attain liberation, they are called "fetters. ○ Regarding the "four cravings":

these are craving for sensory objects, craving for existence, craving for food, and craving for sexual intercourse. ○ Regarding the "four modes of birth": the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states they are birth from the womb, birth from an egg, birth from moisture, and [birth from transformation].
It is a transformation.
