Furthermore, [we], from beginningless time until this day, have perhaps committed all manner of transgressions due to the five abodes (*pañca-vihāra*), or committed all manner of transgressions due to the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*), or committed all manner of transgressions due to the five forms of stinginess (*pañca-matsarya*). Or...
The five views create all transgressions, or alternatively, the five minds create all transgressions.
Such afflictions as these are immeasurable and boundless; they throw all sentient beings of the six realms into confusion. Today I disclose them and repent of them all.
Regarding the five abodes (*pañca-vihāra*): the *Yongjia ji* states that "view" constitutes one abode, termed the "abode of seeing all.

Furthermore, the afflictions of thought (*vitarka-kleśa*) are divided into three abodes: first, the abode of desire-attachment; second, the abode of form-attachment; and third, the abode of formless-attachment.

Additionally, the afflictions of "dust-sands" (*rajas-aṃśu*) and the afflictions of ignorance (*avidyā-kleśa*) are combined into one abode. Regarding the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*): they cover the true meaning.
As Yongjia said: "Form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also called the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*)," which carries the meaning of "covering.
It is like the sun and moon, which are inherently bright, yet when clouds and mist obscure them, the sun and moon become eclipsed and hidden.
Likewise, the true suchness of one's own nature is covered by the five aggregates of form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; thus it becomes obscured.
Because one creates offenses due to delusion, they are also called the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), which signifies a "heap" or accumulation. Furthermore, the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* states:

"Sensual desire, ill-will, dullness and ignorance, torpor, and restlessness constitute the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*). Regarding the five types of stinginess (*mātsarya*), the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* lists stinginess regarding one's dwelling place (*āvāsa-mātsarya*).

Stinginess regarding the possessions of others, stinginess regarding praise, stinginess regarding wealth, and stinginess regarding the Dharma. Regarding the five views: the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* states:

First, the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), which is the view of a body (*kāya-dṛṣṭi*). This consists of clinging to "I" and "mine," because one clings to the body as having a self. Second, the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*).

This consists of calculating, in accordance with the [view of a] body, that there is either annihilation or permanence, thereby falling into the two extreme views. Third, the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*). This consists of clinging to the aforementioned various views as...

1. Grasping at excellence (*śreyo-grāha*): This refers to the capacity for excellence, or the attachment to all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena and so forth, falsely claiming them to be permanent, blissful, self, and pure, which is itself *nirvāṇa*.
2. Grasping at precepts and vows (*śīla-vrata-parāmarśa*): Calculating what is not a cause to be a cause. 3. False view (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*): Denying the existence of cause and effect.

Regarding the five mental states (*pañca-citta*), the *Ālayavijñāna-kārikā* says: the sudden-arising mind (*ābhoga-citta*), the seeking mind (*paryeṣaka-citta*), the determining mind (*niścaya-citta*), the defiled or purified mind (*kliṣṭa-śuddha-citta*), and the mind of uniform outflow (*nisyanda-citta*).
It is the mind. Furthermore,
from time immemorial until this day, we, [Name] and others, have committed all manner of transgressions due to the six sense organs,
or committed all manner of transgressions due to the six consciousnesses, or committed all manner of transgressions due to the six perceptions, or...
All sins are created by the six sensations; or all sins are created by the six modes of conduct; or all sins are created by the six cravings;
or all sins are created by the six doubts. Such afflictions as these are immeasurable and boundless, confusing and disorienting all sentient beings throughout the six realms.
Today, with shame and remorse, I reveal them and repent for them all.

The six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) are as follows: first, the eye faculty, characterized by the aspects of gazing with joy or anger; second, the ear faculty, characterized by the continuous process of listening and discerning;

third, the nose faculty, characterized by the attachment to or aversion toward fragrances and stenches; fourth, the tongue faculty, characterized by the tasting of sweet and bitter flavors; fifth, the body faculty...
This refers to attachment, aversion, smoothness, and roughness. The sixth is the faculty of mind (*manas*), which refers to investigation and deliberation;

that is, among the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind, these six sense organs all take consciousness as their root. Regarding the six consciousnesses, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "The eye-consciousness perceives blue and yellow as unreal;
the ear-consciousness perceives sounds of suffering and pleasure as distinct; the nose-consciousness contemplates the rotation of breath and light; the tongue-consciousness..."

Distinguishing between the heterodox and the orthodox: the body-consciousness manifests its deportment according to circumstances; the mental consciousness contemplates and follows emptiness. Regarding the "six perceptions" (*ṣaḍ-saṃjñā*):
the *Fenxuan* (Analysis of the Profound) states that for the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind, each of their respective consciousnesses has a corresponding perception.

Regarding the "six sensations" (*ṣaḍ-vedanā*): the "Chapter on Emptiness" (*Śūnyatā-parivarta*) says: the eye perceives form, the ear perceives sound, the nose perceives fragrance, the tongue perceives flavor, and the body perceives... [tactile objects].
Contact (*sparśa*). The mind experiences mental objects (*dharma*); this refers to the six sense organs receiving their respective six objects.

The "six activities" (*ṣat-karma*) refer to the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind, each having its own domain and thus each having its own activity. The "six cravings" (*ṣad-tṛṣṇā*): According to the *Abhidharma* (*Vibhāṣā*), it says:
The eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind each give rise to craving due to their respective objects of contact. Regarding the sixth, doubt:
the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states that among greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and doubt, these six are all accompanied by doubt; they are also called the "innate afflictions" (*sahaja-kleśa*).
Furthermore, [Name] and others, from time immemorial until this very day, have committed all manner of transgressions due to the seven outflows (*āsrava*),
or have committed all manner of transgressions due to the seven latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Regarding the seven outflows (*āsrava*): the *Li lun* states they are the outflow of views, the outflow of the sense faculties, the outflow of forgetfulness, the outflow of evil, the outflow of intimacy, the outflow of craving, and the outflow of mindfulness.

Regarding the seven latent tendencies (*anuśaya*): the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* states they are the tendency toward desire, the tendency toward anger, the tendency toward craving, the tendency toward pride, the tendency toward ignorance, the tendency toward views, and the tendency toward doubt.
Or due to the eight inversions they commit all manner of offenses; or due to the eight impurities they commit all manner of offenses;
or due to the eight sufferings they commit all manner of offenses. Such afflictions as these are immeasurable and boundless, agitating all sentient beings throughout the six realms.
Today we disclose them and repent of them all.

Regarding the eight perversions, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: to reckon the impermanent as permanent, the unsatisfactory as satisfactory, the non-self as self, and the impure as pure—these are the four perversions of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

To reckon the permanent as impermanent, the satisfactory as unsatisfactory, the self as non-self, and the pure as impure—these are the four perversions of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*). Regarding the eight defilements, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

The stains of recollection, the stains of non-recollection, the stains of both recollection and non-recollection, the stain of "I," the stain of "mine," the stain of intrinsic nature, and the stain of grasping at distinctions—these are the eight delusive thoughts.
Their inherent defilement is collectively termed "stain. Regarding the eight sufferings, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:
the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of association with the disliked, and the suffering of separation from the beloved.
The suffering of pain; the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks; and the suffering of the intense burning of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

Furthermore, from beginningless time until this very day, [we], such-and-such persons, have committed all manner of transgressions due to the nine afflictions (*navāghāta*), or committed all manner of transgressions due to the nine fetters (*nava-saṃyojana*), or committed all manner of transgressions due to the nine conditions (*nava-pratyaya*).
Regarding the nine grounds for resentment (*navāghātasthānāni*), the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa* states: "In the past, they were dear to me as enemies; in the past, they were hateful to me as friends;
in the past, they caused me distress as my own person. In the present, they are dear to me as enemies; in the present, they are hateful to me as friends;

in the present, they cause me distress as my own person. It is the same for the future. There are three [grounds] for each of the three periods of time; thus there are nine. Therefore, it is so called.

The nine afflictions (*nava āghātāḥ*) are precisely called the nine fetters (*nava saṃyojanāni*). "Fetter" (*saṃyojana*) carries the meaning of binding together so as not to disperse. The nine fetters are:

the fetter of craving (*anunaya-saṃyojana*), the fetter of aversion (*pratigha-saṃyojana*), the fetter of pride (*māna-saṃyojana*), the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*), the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*), the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*), the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*), the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*), and the fetter of avarice (*mātsarya-saṃyojana*).
Among these, because they are able to bring about the conjunction with suffering, they are called "fetters" (saṃyojana). Regarding the nine conditions:
first, visual consciousness conditions light, space, the sense faculty, the object, attention, the fundamental support, and the support for defilement and purification.
The object-conditioned by discrimination; the object-conditioned by seeds. Second, ear-consciousness:

conditioned by space, conditioned by the faculty, conditioned by the object, conditioned by attention, conditioned by the fundamental support, conditioned by the support of defilement and purification, conditioned by the support of discrimination, and conditioned by seeds. Third, nose-consciousness:

conditioned by the faculty, conditioned by the object, conditioned by attention, conditioned by the fundamental support, conditioned by the support of defilement and purification, conditioned by the support of discrimination, and conditioned by [seeds].

1. Seed. 4. Tongue-consciousness: conditioned by the sense organ, conditioned by the object, conditioned by attention, conditioned by the fundamental support, conditioned by the support for defilement and purification, conditioned by the support for discrimination, and conditioned by the seed.

5. Body-consciousness: conditioned by the sense organ, conditioned by the object, conditioned by attention, conditioned by the fundamental support, conditioned by the support for defilement and purification, conditioned by the support for discrimination, and conditioned by the seed. 6. Mental-consciousness: conditioned by attention...

1. The mental faculty (*manas*) takes as its objects: the fundamental support, the support for defilement and purity, the support for discrimination, and seeds. 2–7. The seven [consciousnesses] from the second through the seventh take as their objects:
the support for defilement and purity, the support for discrimination, and seeds. 8. The eighth consciousness takes as its objects:
the fundamental support, the support for defilement and purity, the support for discrimination, and seeds. These are collectively termed the "nine conditions."
Consciousness arises.
Or, one may commit all manner of offenses due to the ten afflictions (*kleśa*), or commit all manner of offenses due to the ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*).

As for the ten afflictions: first, anger (*krodha*); second, resentment (*upanāha*); third, malice (*pratigha*); fourth, concealment (*mrakṣa*); fifth, guile (*śāṭhya*); sixth, deception (*māyā*); seventh, arrogance (*mada*); eighth...
9. Envy (*īrṣyā*). 10. Avarice (*mātsarya*). Regarding the ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*): 1. The envelopment of resentment and anger is called *pratigha* (hatred). 2.

The envelopment of concealing one’s own faults is called *mrakṣa* (concealment). 3. The envelopment of mental stupor is called *styāna* (sloth). 4. The envelopment of the obscuration of the five sense-faculties is called *middha* (torpor).

5. The envelopment of playful wandering is called *auddhatya* (restlessness). 6. The envelopment of agitation in the three types of action (*karma*) is called *auddhatya* (excitement). 7. [The envelopment] arising in a secluded place...

The fetter of not feeling shame for one's own transgressions is called *āhrīkya* (shamelessness). The fetter of not feeling shame toward others regarding the commission of transgressions in public is called *anapatrāpya* (lack of dread).

The fetter of being unable to bestow wealth or the Dharma through generosity is called *mātsarya* (avarice). The fetter of the mind becoming distressed by the prosperity of others is called *īrṣyā* (envy).
These are known as the ten fetters (*daśa-paryavasthāna*).
Or, one may commit all manner of offenses due to the eleven pervasive proclivities (*paryavasthāna*).
The eleven pervasive proclivities are: lack of faith, laziness, lack of shame, lack of dread, excessive greed, excessive hatred, excessive delusion, confusion, heedlessness, stinginess, and malice.
These are the eleven pervasive proclivities. The opposite of these constitutes [the antidotes].
Eleven wholesome [factors].
Or, one may commit all manner of transgressions due to the twelve bases (*āyatana*).
The twelve bases refer to the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; these are the six internal sense bases (*indriya-āyatana*) belonging to the subject, which constitute the capacity for cognition.
"Those" refers to that which is able to see, hear, perceive, and cognize. Form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and phenomena—these are the six external sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*).

They belong to the "objective" (*sō*). The "objective" refers to the locus where seeing, hearing, perceiving, and cognizing become attached. "Entry" (*nyū*) has the meaning of mutual interpenetration.
They are also called the twelve bases (*āyatana*).
Alternatively, one may commit all manner of transgressions due to the sixteen views.
Regarding these sixteen views, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: First, the view of a self, which gives rise to the notions of "I" and "mine. Second, the view of arising...

1. The designation "one who knows and sees" refers to the knowledge and vision [of one who has attained realization]. 2. The designation "one who has a son" refers to the knowledge and vision that the three types of sensation exist. 3. The designation "one who possesses the life-faculty" refers to the knowledge and vision that the life-faculty is fully accomplished.

4. The designation "one who lives" refers to the knowledge and vision that one is capable of undertaking activities. 5. The designation "sentient being" refers to the knowledge and vision that there is the arising from the aggregation of the aggregates (*skandha*).

6. The designation "nourisher" refers to the knowledge and vision that growth occurs due to causes and conditions. 7. The designation "member of a class" refers to the knowledge and vision that all phenomena possess numerical categories. 8. The designation "person" (*pudgala*)...
1. The view that there is a knower and seer who falsely conceives "I am a person. 2. The view that there is an agent who knows and sees with hands and feet as the instrument and the object.
3. The view that there is an instigator who knows and sees, possessing the power to employ others. 4. The view that there is an originator who performs karma for future lives. 5.
The view that there is an instigator of that originator who causes others to act as well. 6. The view that there is an experiencer of the fruits of suffering and pleasure.
14. The recipient of the present [object] possesses knowledge and vision; they feel weary of suffering and pleasure. 15. The knower possesses knowledge and vision;
the five consciousnesses are termed "knowledge. 16. The seer possesses knowledge and vision; they observe forms and images with the eyes.
Or, one may commit all manner of transgressions due to the eighteen *dhātus*.
The eighteen *dhātus* consist of the six sense organs (*indriya*), the six objects (*viṣaya*), and the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*).
The term "realm" (*dhātu*) carries the meanings of analytical discernment, lineage, and boundary.
Or, one may commit all manner of transgressions due to the twenty-five *ātman*s.
These twenty-five *ātman*s are precisely the twenty-five *tattva*s. As stated in the verse of the *Śata-śāstra*:

"First, falling into the primordial darkness (*avyakta*), which is the fundamental nature of the world, there arises *buddhi*. Second, from *buddhi* comes the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), whereby the notion of 'I' (*ahaṃkāra*) arises."
The three [elements] arise from my mind; from this, the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) arises, and then the five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*). These together constitute eight.

The five sense-objects give rise to the five great elements (*pañca-mahābhūta*), and the five great elements give rise to the eleven faculties (*ekādaśendriya*). Including the above, they total twenty-four.

Furthermore, when the principle of the sovereign Self (*puruṣa-tattva*) is added, there are twenty-five principles (*tattva*). Regarding the five—form, sound, smell, taste, and touch—they are the five sense-objects.

Earth, water, fire, wind, and space constitute the five great elements (*mahābhūta*). Furthermore, regarding the eleven faculties (*indriya*): the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body constitute the five cognitive faculties (*jñānendriya*).
The hands, feet, mouth, the faculty of excretion (*mahā-śauca*), and the faculty of urination (*kṣudra-śauca*) constitute the five faculties of action (*karmendriya*).
Additionally, the mind (*manas*) is equal [to these], making eleven faculties in total. "Excretion" and "urination" refer respectively to the large and small eliminations, that is, feces and urine.
Or, one may commit all manner of transgressions due to the sixty-two views.
These sixty-two views are formed by examining the five aggregates—form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—across the three periods of time.
Each aggregate possesses four permutations; for example, it is said that "the self is large and form is small," or "the self is within form," or "the self..."

The self is large while form is small; form is within the self; the self is apart from form; the self is identical with form. The remaining four aggregates may be inferred by applying these same examples.
These five aggregates together constitute twenty [positions], which are further multiplied by the three periods of time: past, present, and future.
These constitute sixty; when added to the two fundamental views of annihilationism and eternalism, they total sixty-two.

Alternatively, due to the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*)—arising from both the vision of the truths and contemplation—and the one hundred and eight afflictions (*kleśa*), which blaze fiercely day and night, they open the gates of all outflows (*āsrava*) and commit every kind of transgression.

Regarding the ninety-eight *anuśaya*s (latent proclivities) categorized as those abandoned through seeing the truths (*darśana-heya*) and those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), the *Dazang Yilanzhan* states:

"Those abandoned through seeing the truths comprise thirty-two *anuśaya*s of the desire realm, twenty-eight *anuśaya*s of the form realm, and twenty-eight *anuśaya*s of the formless realm, totaling eighty-eight *anuśaya*s.
Those abandoned through cultivation comprise four *anuśaya*s of the desire realm, three *anuśaya*s of the form realm, and three *anuśaya*s of the formless realm."

Together with the ten *anuśayas*, these combine to form ninety-eight. They are subsumed under the [Four] Truths of Seeing (*darśana*). What are the thirty-two *anuśayas* of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)?

Under the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), there are ten *anuśayas*. Under the Truths of Origin (*samudaya*) and Cessation (*nirodha*), there are seven *anuśayas* each, excluding the view of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of adherence to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).

Under the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*), there are eight *anuśayas*, excluding the two views of self-identity and adherence to precepts and rituals. What are the twenty-eight *anuśayas* of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*)? Under the Truth of Suffering, there are nine...

The fetters (*saṃyojana*). Excluding hatred (*dveṣa*), there are six fetters each for the [truths of] origin and cessation. Excluding hatred, the views of self (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), there are seven fetters for the path.
What are the twenty-eight fetters of the formless realm? Excluding hatred, there are nine fetters for suffering.

Excluding hatred, the views of self and adherence to precepts and observances, there are six fetters each for origin and cessation. Excluding hatred, the views of self and adherence to precepts and observances, there are seven fetters for the path. Contemplate this.
They are comprised within [the fetters]. What are the four proclivities (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm? First, greed; second, hatred; third, delusion; and fourth, pride.

These four proclivities are abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) from the stage of entering toward the fruit of once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), and are only completely exhausted upon reaching the nine grades of the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmin*).
What are the three fetters (*anuśaya*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*)? First, greed; second, delusion; third, pride.

These are all abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) by one who is a candidate for arhatship (*arhattvapratipannaka*). What are the three fetters of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)? First, greed; second, delusion; third, pride.

These are exhausted only when one reaches the fruit of arhatship. Regarding the Four Noble Truths (*catuḥsatya*), they are suffering (*duḥkha*), origin (*samudaya*), cessation (*nirodha*), and the path (*mārga*). Under the truth of suffering, there are ten fetters.

This refers to the view of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), views regarding precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), lust (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), delusion (*moha*), pride (*māna*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and [the view of] wrong [precepts]. Regarding the seven afflictions (*kleśa*) each in the [truths of] Origination and Cessation:

there are only the seven consisting of views, false views, delusion, doubt, lust, hatred, and pride; therefore, it says "excluding the view of self-identity and views regarding precepts. Regarding the eight afflictions in the [truth of] the Path:

there are only the eight consisting of false views, delusion, doubt, views regarding precepts, lust, hatred, and pride; therefore, it says "excluding the view of self-identity and views regarding precepts."
These are the two views. The following cases should be understood accordingly. Suffering (*duḥkha*) is the fruit of outflows (*āsrava*); origination (*samudaya*) is the cause of outflows;
cessation (*nirodha*) is the fruit free from outflows (*anāsrava*); and the path (*mārga*) is the cause free from outflows. The *Śūraṅgama-sūtra Commentary* states:

"The view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) is here called the 'view of the body' (*śarīra-dṛṣṭi*), because it clings to the body as having a self. The 'extreme view' (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*) is the clinging to the self as being either annihilated or eternal, thereby falling into the two extremes."

Therefore, regarding the view of attachment to precepts (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*): it refers to adhering to the precepts of dogs, oxen, and so forth, [falsely] taking them to be the cause for rebirth in heaven.

Regarding the view of attachment to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*): it refers to clinging to the aforementioned views as being supreme or efficacious, or falsely regarding all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena as being blissful and pure, [mistakenly] identifying them with *nirvāṇa*.
Regarding false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*): it refers to denying cause and effect, thereby severing the seeds of virtue; this is what is called [false view].

Regarding the "one hundred and eight afflictions of wrong views": these consist of the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), with the addition of the ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), thus forming one hundred and eight.
Alternatively, it is said that they are simply the one hundred and eight views.
They throw the noble ones and the four modes of birth into confusion, pervading the three realms and filling the six destinies; there is nowhere to seek refuge.
Today I come to pray. Before the Buddhas of the ten directions, the Honored Dharma, and the Assembly of Sages, I confess with shame and remorse, repenting for all my transgressions.
Regarding the three realms: first, the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*). From the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations down to the lowest heavens, all are called the realm of desire;

because they long for and crave pleasure and desire, it is named "desire. Second, the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*). From the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna, one has not yet escaped the cage of form; therefore, it is so named.
Form. The three formless realms and the four heavens of emptiness possess only four aggregates (*skandha*) and lack the aggregate of form;

therefore, they are called "formless" (*ārūpya*). The six destinies (*ṣadgati*) are: the heavenly realm, the human realm, the asura realm, the animal realm, the hungry ghost realm, and the hell realm;
they are also called the six transmigrations (*ṣadgati*). The ten directions (*daśadig*) are: east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, above, and below; all of these exist.
This is because of the Buddha-fields and lands. May we, [Name] and others,
by virtue of the merit produced through this repentance of the three poisons and all afflictions, in birth after birth and age after age,
have the three types of wisdom become clear, the three forms of omniscience become radiant, the three sufferings be extinguished, and the three vows be fulfilled.

"May [Name] descend. In the preceding passage, the various manifestations of transgressions were extensively enumerated; thus, the confession is now complete. In the following passage, a vow is made to seek its meritorious benefits. Why is this so?
Confession ultimately extinguishes transgressions, and the extinction of transgressions ultimately gives rise to merit.
When merit arises, wisdom and its attendant qualities are naturally accomplished. Therefore, one proceeds sequentially to make vows and seek such merits.
This reveals the functional efficacy of the power of repentance. Third, regarding wisdom (*prajñā*), it consists of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
If one hears but does not listen attentively, there is no cause for receiving its nourishment. If one listens but does not reflect, there is no profound purpose or meaning.

If one reflects but does not cultivate, one will ultimately fail to realize the principle. Therefore, one must clarify the teaching of the three types of penetration (*trividha-pratisaṃvit*); this has not been seen elsewhere.
[The character] "chu" (出) appears. However, in the first fascicle of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, there are the terms *fǎdá* (法達), *yìdá* (義達), and *cídá* (辭達), as well as *jiàohuǎdá* (教化達).

It is not yet known whether these are acceptable [as equivalents]. Furthermore, "dá" (達) means "clarity" (*míng*). It may also refer to the three types of higher knowledge (*tisro vidyāḥ*): the divine eye-knowledge (*divyacakṣur-jñāna*), the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*), and the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna*).

This remains to be further examined. ○ Regarding the three sufferings (*triduḥkhatā*): the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*), [the suffering of change, and the suffering of conditioned formations]. The third...
The realms are already suffering. The desire realm is further characterized by suffering: the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*), which is the suffering that arises when pleasure perishes;

this is equivalent to the three miserable destinies (*durgati*). The suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*) pertains to the intermediate state and pervades the formless realms (*ārūpya-dhātu*).

This suffering must be extinguished. Regarding the three vows: first, the vow that all sentient beings may realize and know the Dharma; second, the vow to preach the Dharma for sentient beings with an insatiable mind; third, [the vow to...]
I vow to sacrifice my body and life to protect and uphold the True Dharma; may this vow be fulfilled.
I pray that by virtue of the merit produced from this repentance for the four consciousnesses and all afflictions, in birth after birth and throughout every lifetime, [may I...]
Broaden the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*). Establish the karma of the four faiths. Cease the four evil destinies. Attain the four fearlessnesses (*catvāri vaiśāradyāni*).
Regarding the four immeasurable minds, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states: "The straightforward mind is the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), for it is free from falsehood.
The mind of practice is the site of enlightenment, for it can accomplish all tasks. The profound mind is the site of enlightenment, for it increases merit and virtue. Bodhi..."
The mind is the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), for it is free from error. This mind should be expanded through the four faiths:

first, faith in the Buddha, which is to delight in constantly praising the Buddha; second, faith in the Dharma, which is to delight in desiring to hear the Dharma; third, faith in the Saṃgha, which is to delight in making offerings to the assembly.
Fourth is faith in the precepts. One delights in renouncing the five desires. This faith must be firmly established. Regarding the four evil destinies, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
first, the hells, including the eight cold and eight hot hells; second, the animal realm, including those that move in water, on land, and through the air; third, the hungry ghosts.
The three categories and nine types, etc., as well as the four *asuras*, are subsumed within the realms of ghosts, animals, humans, and devas; these destinies shall be extinguished.

Regarding the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states: first, the fearlessness of attaining *dhāraṇī*; second, the fearlessness of knowing the faculties (*indriya*) of others.
Third, he attains fearlessness regarding the resolution of doubts; fourth, he attains fearlessness regarding providing answers and explanations. Furthermore, it is said that these are:

fearlessness regarding all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), fearlessness regarding the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), fearlessness regarding the teaching on obstacles to the path, and fearlessness regarding the teaching on the end of suffering (*duḥkhakṣaya*).
I vow that by virtue of the merit generated through this repentance for the five hindrances and all other afflictions, may I cross over the five realms of existence,
establish the five faculties, purify the five eyes, and perfect the five aggregates.

Furthermore, the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*) are as described above; they are identical to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). First, the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), which refers to a collection of what is false and provisional.

Second, the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), which refers to the experience that nourishes craving. Third, the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), which refers to the grasping of images and the resulting mental agitation. Fourth, the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), which refers to subtle and continuous flux.

Fifth, the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), which refers to the intense discernment of objects. Regarding the five destinies (*pañca-gati*): the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "The devas..."
The path of humans and the path of devas are the two wholesome paths (*sugati*). Hell, hungry ghosts, and animals are the three unwholesome paths (*durgati*).
One should deliver all beings from these. Regarding the five faculties (*pañcendriya*), the *Ālaya-vibhāga* states: 1. The faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) is faith in the Truths.

It eliminates the net of doubt regarding the ocean of all dharmas—namely, the untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*), powers (*bala*), meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), and samādhis. 2. The faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*) maintains and upholds [the teachings].

1. The faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*): never forgetting. 2. The faculty of energy (*vīryendriya*): keeping this in mind and remaining focused upon it. 3. The faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*): profound stillness and pervasive penetration; cultivating the mind so that it is not distracted.

4. The faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*): clearly discerning the ultimate truth; illuminating and realizing it through wisdom. As for the vow to establish the five eyes (*pañca-cakṣuṣi*), the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-gāthā* says:
"The divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*) is unimpeded; the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*) is impeded and lacks penetration. The Dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*) observes only..."
Worldly people perceive emptiness with the eye of wisdom; the Buddha-eye is like a thousand suns. Illuminating diverse forms, they return to sameness.

Within the perfectly luminous Dharma-realm, there is nowhere that its reflection is not mirrored. It reveals, instructs, awakens, and leads others into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, fully possessing the five eyes.

Therefore, one vows to purify it. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: When a bodhisattva first generates the mind of enlightenment, they perceive suffering sentient beings with their fleshly eyes and give rise to compassion.

They study various dhyānas and samādhis, cultivating and attaining the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*). With their divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), they see throughout the six realms of existence as beings undergo various forms of embodiment;
their pity increases all the more, and thus they seek the wisdom-eye (*prajñācakṣus*) in order to rescue and deliver them. They attain it...

Observing that the mental characteristics of sentient beings are diverse and not uniform, one seeks the Dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣus*) in order to guide them so they may attain this true Dharma and enter into it.
Thereafter, one seeks the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*) and attains all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), thereby accomplishing the Buddha-dharmas.
Furthermore, the *Vajra Commentary* states: "The internal and external emptiness and stillness is called the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*); seeing one’s own true nature is mastery."
Equanimity is called the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). Seeing the wisdom of the prajñā of intrinsic nature is called the wisdom eye (*prajñācakṣus*).

Seeing that all phenomena are the absence of all phenomena, and seeing that all marks are the emptiness of all marks, is called the dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣus*). It sees that, in the past, there are no afflictions to be severed;
in the present, there is no self-nature to be maintained; and in the future, there is no state of Buddhahood to be sought. Thus, it is pure throughout the three periods of time.

That which is named the Buddha-eye. Regarding "accomplishing the five divisions," the *Āḍakavatī-sūtra* (Yingluo jing) states: "It accomplishes the five kinds of dharma-fragrance. First, one accomplishes the fragrance of the division of precepts to restrain the body;
second, one accomplishes the fragrance of the division of concentration to restrain the mind; third, one accomplishes the fragrance of the division of wisdom to restrain distraction;
fourth, one accomplishes the fragrance of the division of liberation to restrain inverted views; fifth, one accomplishes the fragrance of the division of knowledge and vision.

Fragrance subsumes ignorance. One teaching establishes the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañcadharmakāya*). The *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning) states: "The first part, non-active precepts (*avijñapti-śīla*), constitutes the body of morality (*śīlakāya*).

The second part, untainted pure meditative concentration (*anāsrava-vimala-dhyāna*), constitutes the body of concentration (*samādhikāya*). The third part, untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*), constitutes the body of wisdom (*prajñākāya*).

The fourth part, the three kinds of liberation (*trividha-vimukti*), constitutes the body of liberation (*vimuktikāya*). The fifth part, non-arising (*anutpāda*), constitutes the body of the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimuktijñānadarśanakāya*)."
I know and see this body.
I vow that by virtue of the merit produced from this repentance of the six types of sensation and all other afflictions, may I, in birth after birth, be fully endowed with the six supernormal powers,
fulfill the practice of the six perfections, remain undeluded by the six sense objects, and constantly perform the six sublime conducts.

The six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) are: the power of mastery over mental formations (*ṛddhividhi*), the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*), knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*), and the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*).
There are three types of the power of mastery over mental formations: first, the power of reaching [anywhere], whereby the body flies through the air like a bird without obstruction;
by shifting the distant to become near, one arrives without having traveled, vanishing from this place and appearing in that, reaching the destination in a single thought-moment. Second...

This refers to transformation: being able to make the large small and the small large, or making one into many and so forth. Third is the noble *ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna* (supernormal power of psychic transformation);

this supernormal power of psychic transformation exists only in the Buddha. There are two kinds of the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*): first, that obtained through cultivation; second, that obtained as a karmic retribution.
The supernormal power of the divine ear perceives all sounds. The supernormal power of knowing the minds of others knows the joy, anger, and fear of others.

The supernormal power of recollecting past lives knows the events of previous existences. The supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows concerns the four outflows. Regarding the practitioner who fulfills the six perfections through vows: the *Śīlasūtra* states:
First is giving, which remedies stinginess and greed and results in the reward of wealth. Second is ethical discipline, which remedies the breaking of precepts.
1. Perfecting wholesome rebirths in the good realms; 2. Patience, which remedies anger and results in the attainment of the marks and signs of a Great Being; 3.

Diligence, which remedies laziness and results in the attainment of longevity and supernormal powers; 4. Meditative concentration, which remedies distraction and results in the attainment of bliss and rebirth in the heavens;
5. Wisdom, which remedies delusion and results in the attainment of eloquence and the destruction of afflictions. These are the six wholesome karmas.
To fulfill [the sense bases], form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and mental objects constitute the six dusts (*ṣaḍviṣaya*). That which is called "delusion" is as follows:
form is like a glowing iron ball; to grasp it is to be burned. Sound is like a drum smeared with poison; to hear it is certain death.
Fragrance is like the breath of a decayed dragon; to smell it is to fall ill. Taste is like boiling honey-syrup, or like a blade smeared with honey; to lick it is to... [be cut].
Injury. Contact is like a sleeping lion: if one approaches it, it bites. The Dharma is like an elephant in a tumultuous state;

therefore, one must not be deluded by either. Sixth, regarding the "wondrous practices": in the first dhyāna of the form realm, there are three types of lower-realm practices—namely, the practice of aversion to suffering, the practice of coarse conduct, and the practice of hindrances—and three types of higher-realm practices—namely, the practice of delighting in purity, the wondrous practice, and the practice of bliss.
Furthermore, I vow that by virtue of the merit produced from this confession of all afflictions— the seven outflows, eight impurities, nine fetters, ten entanglements, and so forth—
may I sit upon the seven pure lotuses in birth after birth throughout all lifetimes.

Regarding the seven kinds of pure flowers, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: First is purity of precepts (*śīla-viśuddhi*), which is the ultimate purity of body, speech, and mind from beginning to end.

Second is purity of mind (*citta-viśuddhi*), which is the cessation of afflictions through the three vehicles and the exhaustion of fetters and outflows. Third is purity of view (*dṛṣṭi-viśuddhi*), which is seeing the true nature of phenomena and not giving rise to deluded thoughts.

Fourth is the overcoming of doubt (*vicikitsā-prahāṇa*), which is the severing of doubts regarding defilement upon seeing it. Fifth is the discernment of the path (*mārga-pariccheda*), which is [knowing] that this is the appropriate path.

Sixth, the path of practice (*pratipad*): that which is not the path should be abandoned. Seventh, the path of abandonment (*prahāṇa*): through knowledge and vision, one abandons what is to be practiced;
this is the clear and penetrating realization. Eighth, *nirvāṇa*: the attainment of the endurance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Washing with the waters of the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*).
As for the eight liberations: first, the liberation of one possessing internal form while perceiving external forms, which constitutes the first dhyāna;

second, the liberation of one not possessing internal form while perceiving external forms, which constitutes the second dhyāna; third, the liberation of the perception of purity, abiding fully therein, which constitutes the third dhyāna.
4. Contemplating the liberation of the sphere of infinite space; 5. Contemplating the liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness—both constitute the fourth dhyāna.

6. Contemplating the liberation of the sphere of nothingness; 7. Contemplating the liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—both constitute the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*).
8. Contemplating the liberation of the cessation of perception and feeling—this transcends the three realms. [The above are the seven purities. By means of...
Regarding the cultivation of causes, it is said "flower" and "sitting. Regarding the eight liberations, because they enter through the flow of the Dharma, it is said "water" and "washing.
This constitutes the nine knowledges of abandonment.

Regarding the nine types of knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*): 1. The Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuklavidarśanā-bhūmi*), which includes the five stages of mental abiding (*pañca-vastu-sthiti*), and the general and specific applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).

2. The Stage of Nature (*gotra-bhūmi*), comprising the levels of Heat (*uṣmagata*), Summits (*mūrdhan*), Patience (*kṣānti*), and the Supreme Worldly Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*). Above these, one still suppresses the afflictions of both the views (*dṛṣṭi*) and the thoughts (*saṃjñā*). 3.

The First Fruit (*srotāpanna*), which abandons the eighty-eight latent propensities (*anuśaya*) of the views pertaining to the three realms and fully realizes the Truths (*satya*). 4. The Second Fruit (*sakṛdāgāmin*), which abandons the nine grades of afflictions of the thoughts (*saṃjñā*) within the desire realm.
1. The state of delusion. 2. The fruit of the third [stage]: the exhaustion of the remaining afflictions (*klesha*) of the desire realm. 3. The fruit of the fourth [stage]:

the exhaustion of the afflictions of seeing and cultivation (*darśana-bhāvanā-kleśa*) across the three realms. 4. The Pratyekabuddha: the exhaustion of the afflictions of seeing and cultivation, further eradicating the three types of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). 5. The Bodhisattva: the exhaustion of the primary afflictions (*mūlakleśa*) of the three realms while practicing the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*).

6. The stage of Buddhahood: the sudden eradication of the afflictions of seeing and cultivation within the three realms, as well as their residual habitual tendencies, while seated upon the [Bodhi] tree.

Beneath the Bodhi tree, he sat upon grass and manifested the Hīnayāna Response Body (Nirmāṇakāya). One who can sever these nine [afflictions] is endowed with wisdom and accomplishes the practices of the ten stages (daśabhūmi).
Regarding the practitioner who accomplishes the ten stages (*bhūmi*), the *Avataṃsaka* states: "Ascending the ten stages, one cuts off the ten obstacles and realizes the ten true natures (*tathatā*).

Specifically, on the first stage, one cuts off the obstacle of being an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*) and realizes the all-pervading true nature (*sarvatraga-tathatā*). On the second stage, one cuts off the obstacle of false understanding and realizes the most excellent true nature (*parama-tathatā*).

On the third stage, one cuts off the obstacle of dullness and darkness and realizes the true nature of the noble stream (*ārya-vaṃśa-tathatā*). On the fourth stage, one cuts off the active manifestation of subtle afflictions (*anuśaya-pravṛtti*).

The obstacle to realizing the *tathatā* of non-appropriation. In the fifth stage (*bhūmi*), one abandons the obstacle to the *nirvāṇa* of the Lesser Vehicle and realizes the *tathatā* of non-conceptuality.
In the sixth stage, one abandons the obstacle to the manifestation of coarse characteristics and realizes the *tathatā* of defilement and purity.

In the seventh stage, one abandons the obstacle to the manifestation of subtle characteristics and realizes the *tathatā* that is the basis of wisdom. In the eighth stage, one abandons the obstacle to unadorned application and realizes the...
The *tathatā* of increase and decrease: in the ninth stage (*bhūmi*), one abandons the obstacle of not desiring to benefit others and realizes the *tathatā* of the basis.

In the tenth stage, one abandons the obstacle to mastery over phenomena and realizes the *tathatā* of non-conceptual phenomena. These stages, from the Joyful (*pramuditā*) and the Stainless (*vimalā*) up to the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*), constitute the ten stages.

I vow that by means of these eleven recitations of the *Chanhui-wen* (Text on Repentance) and the merits generated therein, may all afflictions regarding the twelve bases (*āyatana*) and eighteen elements (*dhātu*) be extinguished;
may the eleven kinds of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) enable me to understand their constant application, so that my mind may dwell in sovereign liberation.

Regarding the eleven kinds of emptiness, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: first, internal emptiness, because the six sense organs have no substance; second, external emptiness, because the six sense objects have no characteristics;
third, internal-and-external emptiness, because the six consciousnesses do not exist; fourth, conditioned emptiness, because the marks of arising and ceasing are absent.
1. The emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*): even non-characteristics (*animitta*) are non-existent. 2. The emptiness of that which has no beginning (*anavarāgra-śūnyatā*):

its essence is fundamentally void from the start. 3. The emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*): phenomena are fundamentally and eternally non-existent. 4. The emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*): both existence and non-existence are non-existent. 5.

The emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*): functional efficacy manifests [within it]. 6. The emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*): when the illness is gone, the medicine is discarded. 7. The great emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā*): the teachings of the Hīnayāna are absent herein.
The eleven dharmas are empty; you must certainly aspire to understand this. Once the mind is constantly applied and has understood emptiness, one will spontaneously attain the samādhi of liberation.
Therefore, it is said that the mind dwells in sovereign freedom.
One is able to turn the wheel of the twelve aspects of the Dharma (*dvādaśākāra-dharmacakra*).
As for this wheel of the twelve aspects of the Dharma, it consists of three turnings of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* wheel: first, the turning of demonstration; second, the turning of exhortation;

and third, the turning of realization. Each turning has four aspects, namely suffering (*duḥkha*), origin (*samudaya*), cessation (*nirodha*), and the path (*mārga*). Three sets of four thus constitute twelve. First...
First, the turning that demonstrates [the truths] says: "This is the nature of suffering as oppression; this is the nature of origination as that which invites [suffering];
this is the nature of cessation as that which is realizable; this is the nature of the path as that which is to be cultivated. Second, the turning that exhorts cultivation says:
"This is suffering; you should know it. This is origination; you should abandon it. This is cessation; you should realize it. This is the path; you should cultivate it."
[The Buddha] practiced. Regarding the third turning toward realization, he declared: "This is suffering; I have already known it and shall not know it again. This is the origin;
I have already abandoned it and shall not abandon it again. This is cessation; I have already realized it and shall not realize it again. This is the path;
I have already cultivated it and shall not cultivate it further. With these four dharmas—suffering, its origin, and so forth—he made this proclamation three times.
Because these are known, it is said that there are three turnings and twelve aspects. As for "wheel" (*cakra*), this is spoken by way of analogy:

just as a worldly chariot wheel has the function of pushing and crushing, as well as the function of revolving, so too do these four dharmas revolve and enter into the minds of sentient beings, crushing and destroying afflictions (*kleśa*) to realize *nirvāṇa*.
Therefore, it is called the Wheel of Dharma with twelve aspects (*dvādaśākāra-dharmacakra*).
Fully endowed with the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) and immeasurable merits, all are perfectly complete.
Having made this vow, one takes refuge in and pays homage to all Buddhas.
Regarding the eighteen unique qualities, the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states: "The three karmas of body, speech, and mind are without fault; there is no lack of meditative concentration."
His mind is free from divergent thoughts; his mind is free from lack of equanimity. His aspiration does not diminish; his mindfulness does not diminish;
his diligence does not diminish; his wisdom does not diminish; his liberation does not diminish; his knowledge and vision of liberation does not diminish.
His bodily actions follow wisdom; his verbal actions follow wisdom; his mental actions follow wisdom. He knows the past.
Unimpeded in the present; unimpeded in the future—these constitute the eighteen [unshared qualities].
As for the "unshared qualities" (*āveṇika-dharma*), these are supramundane dharmas that belong exclusively to the Buddha alone, as they are not shared with the two vehicles.
Regarding the "eighteen and so forth," there are further immeasurable merits beyond these that cannot be fully described. I pray that you may seek them.
Only when all [these practices] are fully and perfectly accomplished does one truly fulfill the great resolve of my repentance.
Those who wish to seek repentance must first pay homage to the Buddha as the foundation for purifying transgressions; therefore, they should make this vow and take refuge, saying: [etc.]
Homage to Vairocana Buddha. Homage to our Original Teacher Śākyamuni Buddha.
Homage to Amitābha Buddha. Homage to Maitreya Buddha. Homage to Dragon-Species Supreme Honored King Buddha.
Homage to Dragon Sovereign King Buddha. Homage to Jewel-Victorious Buddha. Homage to Awakened-Flower Samādhi-Sovereign King Buddha.
The *Kṣitigarbha Sūtra* states: Furthermore, in the past, during inconceivable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, there was a Buddha in that world named Buddha-Flower Samādhi-Sovereign King Tathāgata.
During the period of the Semblance Dharma, there was a Brahmin girl whose accumulated merit from past lives was profound and who was protected by the various devas.
Her mother, however, believed in heterodox teachings and constantly disparaged the Triple Gem. She did not...
Long ago, her life ended and her spirit fell into the Avīci Hell. At that time, the woman beheld the image of the Tathāgata King of the Samādhi of the Sovereignty of Awakening Flowers;

as she gazed upon and paid homage to the Honored One’s countenance, her reverence and admiration redoubled. She thought to herself, "The Buddha is named Great Awakening and possesses all-encompassing wisdom;
he must surely know the destination of my mother after her death. Suddenly, she heard a voice from the air.
The Buddha said, "I am one whom you look up to and worship. Seeing that you were grieving for your mother, I have come to inform you.
Simply sit upright and contemplate my name; you shall then know the place where your mother has been reborn.
At that time, the woman immediately prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and contemplated for one day and one night. Suddenly, she saw herself arrive at the shore of a sea. Because of her mindfulness—
By the power of the Buddha, she was naturally free from fear. A king of ghosts named Wudú (Non-Venomous) bowed his head in greeting and came forward to welcome her, saying to the Holy Woman:
"This is the first of the seven concentric seas on the western side of the Great Iron Ring Mountains.

For sentient beings who have committed evil, if within the seventh week there is no one to continue their lineage and perform meritorious deeds for them, they must first cross this sea before [crossing] the three seas."
Within this [realm] lies the Great Hell. I pray that the Noble Lady will return quickly. Since the daughter of King Śuddhodana was born into the heavens, three days have now passed.

It is said that she has heard that her filial son has prepared offerings and cultivated merit for her by making donations at the stupa and temple of the Tathāgata Buddha-Flower-Samadhi-Sovereign-King. Not only has the mother of the Bodhisattva attained liberation from the earth...
In this Avīci Hell, on that very day, all the sinners were reborn together. At that time, a Brahmin woman made a great vow, saying:
"May I, throughout all future kalpas, employ every possible skillful means to bring liberation to all sentient beings who must endure the suffering of their karmic offenses.
The King of Ghosts named Amṛta (The Untoxic) was none other than the present-day Bodhisattva Vasumitra (Wealth Chief). As for the Brahmin woman...
This is none other than Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva.
Homage to the Buddha Kāṣāyadhvaja. Homage to the Buddha Siṃhanāda. Homage to Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva.
Homage to Samantabhadra Bodhisattva. Homage to Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva. Homage to Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva.
The *Kṣitigarbha Sūtra* states: Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying, "I only pray that the World-Honored One will extensively explain the causal ground of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha:
what practices did he perform and what vows did he establish, such that he was able to accomplish the inconceivable?"

Regarding this matter, the Buddha told Mañjuśrī: "Suppose, for example, that in a trichiliocosm—namely, all the grasses, trees, thickets, forests, rice, hemp, bamboo, reeds, mountains, rocks, and atoms of dust—one were to count each single object and make it into a single Ganges River."
There is one Ganges River of sands; for each grain of sand there is one world-system; within each world-system, there is one atom for every kalpa;

and within each kalpa, the number of accumulated atoms constitutes the entirety of that kalpa. Since the time the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha realized the fruit of the tenth bhūmi, his [realizations] have been a thousand times more than this number.
How much more so, then, regarding the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha’s [merits] while among the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas?
Earth.
Homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāvyūha. Homage to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.
Having paid homage to all the Buddhas, we next proceed to repentance (continuing from what preceded and initiating what follows).

Now, regarding the discourse on repentance (*pratikramana*), its essence lies in reforming the past and cultivating the future, extinguishing evil and promoting good. When people dwell in this world, who can be without transgression?
Even those who have studied the Way still give rise to afflictions when their mindfulness lapses; even Arhats manifest physical and vocal karma due to their residual habits.
How much more so for ordinary beings—how could they possibly be without faults?
"Reforming the past and cultivating the future" means reforming the transgressions of the past and cultivating the fields of merit for future lives;

it means extinguishing the evils of the three poisons, the six sense faculties, and so forth, and promoting the goodness of the six perfections, the myriad practices, and so forth. Regarding "the student" (*xué rén*):

the word "study" (*xué*) signifies emulation. One emulates the refined cultivation of the path and its practices by the ancient sages and former worthies; therefore, it is called "study. As it is said, "Diligence..."
Cultivate precepts, concentration, and wisdom; extinguish greed, anger, and delusion; realize the mind and penetrate its source—therefore one is called a śramaṇa.
Those of such caliber may truly be called students of the Way. Yet, if there is even the slightest negligence, one has already lost mindfulness.
As it was said of old: "To be absent for even a moment is to be like a dead person. Now it is said that losing mindfulness gives rise to afflictions.
This is precisely the meaning intended here. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "It is not that they do not turn their minds [toward enlightenment].

Yet even great Arhats still possess subtle delusions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. As for those who are dull-witted Arhats, can they possibly be free from the habit-energies of their fetters (*saṃyojana-vāsanā*)?
By 'habit-energies of the fetters' is meant the residual tendencies accumulated since the time of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), which have not yet been completely dissolved."
Furthermore, as for the phrase "how much more so": if even those who have emerged from the fetters are like this, how much more so those still within them?
Yet, the wise possess prior awakening and are thus able to repent and reform; the foolish conceal their faults, causing them to spread and entangle.
Consequently, through long nights of accumulated habituation, there is no prospect of awakening until dawn.
To conceal means to know that one has committed a transgression yet to hide it and fail to disclose it; thus, the offense increases daily. As the *Lunyu* says:
"The faults of the petty man must be glossed over. To gloss over is to embellish them. The petty man dreads correcting his faults but does not dread self-deception;
therefore, he inevitably glosses over them to make his offenses more serious. This is what that refers to. For this reason, one must necessarily disclose them.
[The Master] Lu then performed a repentance. Regarding the wise person’s repentance for transgressions: it is like cutting grass;
one must pull out its roots so that it will not grow again. Therefore, it is called "reforming and repenting. As for the fool who conceals [their faults] and does not bring them forth:
it is like grass whose roots are buried deep within the soil. Moistened by dew and rain, it spreads and creeps, flourishing day by day and growing ever more luxuriant.
As their sinful karma gradually deepens, if they do not confess and reveal it, they will be as if dwelling in the midst of celestial darkness;
ultimately becoming deluded and obscured, they will see nothing at all. Even when they fall into the suffering and affliction of the three miserable realms, they will not know its cause.
Therefore, it is said that there will be no time for awakening.
If one confesses with a sense of shame and remorse, it will not only extinguish these transgressions,
but will also increase immeasurable merit and establish the wondrous fruit of the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa.
The benefits obtained through repentance are as wondrous as this. Below, the method for the rite of repentance is further elucidated.
Those who wish to practice this method should first externally solemnize their physical demeanor while gazing upon and honoring the sacred images, and internally arouse a spirit of reverence.
Contemplate the thought of the Dharma and pray with sincere earnestness.
To be "externally solemn" means to maintain a sense of uniform gravity and reverent decorum. Regarding the *Avatamsaka Sūtra*, Chapter on the Vows and Practices:
"First, pay homage to all Buddhas. If, at the time of performing this rite of repentance, one looks left and right and secretly engages in speech or laughter, how could this be appropriate?

If one’s demeanor during formal ritual is not solemn, it means there is no reverence within. The *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states: "Gazing up at the Honored Countenance, the eyes do not for a moment depart.

When performing prostrations and respect, it is precisely appropriate to look with the eyes while focusing the mind upon the object of veneration. If there is no reverence, even this act of gazing and honoring is empty;
how much more so is the case for mental visualization? One should know that true reverence does not lie merely after the seven types of mental application.
Two kinds of thoughts arise. What are these two? First, one reflects to oneself: "This life of mine is difficult to preserve forever;
it may perish in a single morning. I do not know when this body might be restored, were I not to encounter the Buddhas and the worthy sages."
If one suddenly encounters evil friends and commits various sinful karmas, one will further fall into deep pits and perilous realms.
This body is formed by the temporary conjunction of the four great elements; when these four elements disperse, this body perishes.

How much more so, since it is like a spark from a stone or a flash of lightning—its impermanence is unfathomable. If one does not prepare in advance, regret will come too late. One should still fear this.
This is because once one loses this human body, it will not be regained for ten thousand kalpas.

The "deep pits and perilous realms" are metaphorical expressions for the three miserable paths and the eight difficulties; they are likened to being "deep" because it is difficult to escape them, and likened to being "perilous" because one suffers afflictions therein.
Second, one reflects to oneself: "In this life of mine, although I have encountered the True Dharma of the Tathāgata, I have not acted for the sake of the Buddha-dharma;
I have not succeeded to the lineage of the Sages, nor have I purified my body, speech, and mind, nor have I dwelt in wholesome dharmas."
Those who do not practice for the sake of the Buddha-dharma find it difficult to obtain a human body and difficult to hear the Buddha-dharma.
Now, having encountered the Sangha, if one still cannot practice—first, reflecting that this body is impermanent and that upon death one will fall into the evil realms with no prospect of escape;
second, reflecting that the evils of this body cannot be concealed from the Buddhas and the deities, and that one will ultimately arrive before King Yama.

Regarding the various sufferings one undergoes, there are these two kinds of thoughts: a natural sense of shame and remorse, and a sense of dread that leads one to urgently seek repentance, not daring to deceive oneself.
[One should] cause the Buddha-dharma to flourish and manifest, so that the Holy Way may prosper and never be severed.
This is called succeeding to the lineage of the sages.
Yet now we have secretly committed evil deeds and further concealed them, saying that others do not know and that they do not see.
To harbor secret evils in one's heart while remaining haughty and without shame is truly the height of worldly folly and delusion;
not only can such a person not succeed in propagating the Buddha-dharma, but they instead privately indulge in such talk.
Because they commit evil deeds in private, believing that the Buddha neither knows nor sees them, their actions of body, speech, and mind become all the more profound and grave.
Once it is confessed, the karmic offenses melt away like ice. (The character *te* means "evil. I privately thought that Buddhas and Bodhisattvas neither know nor see;
however, in reality, Buddhas and Bodhisattvas know and see everything, as stated in the following passage. Therefore, it is said:
"There is nothing more foolish and deluded than this in the world."
There are currently the Buddhas of the ten directions, the great Bodhisattvas, and the celestial spirits and immortals;

how could they ever fail to behold with their pure divine eyes the evil deeds we have committed? Furthermore, the spirits of both the hidden and the manifest record our transgressions and merits with absolute precision, down to the finest detail.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Aniruddha sees Jambudvīpa as if looking at an *āmala* fruit in the palm of his hand;
the various bodhisattvas see hundreds of thousands of worlds; and the Tathāgatas of the ten directions perceive all pure lands, as numerous as motes of dust, with nothing that escapes their vision.
Yet the clear sight of sentient beings does not exceed the span of a finger-joint. The *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "O Deva..."
With their eyes, they can see the sentient beings within the sands of worlds in the ten directions who have accomplished evil deeds of body,

speech, and mind, and who, due to the causes and conditions of slandering the noble ones and holding wrong views, shall fall into the miserable realms upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life— [including] those in the dark realm of hungry ghosts and those dispatched by the messengers of Yama.
The Manifest One is the deity of intelligence and rectitude. Since the cause is without error, the fruit is ultimately without mistake.
The following specifically points to the fact that the retribution of the fruit is without error.
Now, regarding a person who has committed offenses: after their life ends, the ox-headed jailers record their spirit and bring them before Yama.

At the place of King Yama, the right and wrong are investigated and scrutinized. At that time, all adversaries come forward as witnesses (this refers to those who confront one in judgment), each saying:

"In the past, you slaughtered my body—roasting, boiling, steaming, or grilling it (this refers to confrontations with non-human beings)—or you previously plundered all my wealth and separated me from my kin (this refers to confrontations with human beings). Only today do I [speak thus]..."
You have fallen into our hands; we now have direct evidence before us. How can you dare to conceal [the truth]—for "concealment" (huì) means to hide or suppress?
You must simply accept your past misfortunes with a willing heart and bear them in full.
"Records" (lù) means to take and collect them. ○ Yánluó (Yama): A Sanskrit term;
its correct form is *Yamāra*, which means "tranquil rest. It is also called *Yamarāja*, meaning "the two worlds. He is the general administrator of the realm of ghosts (*pretas*).

Because this is the name of the netherworld where both suffering and pleasure are experienced, it is called "the two worlds. An ancient saying states: "The elder brother and the younger sister are the twin kings," referring to suffering and [pleasure].
"To enjoy together" refers precisely to this. "Slaughtered, butchered, boiled, and roasted" refers to the karma of killing living beings and eating their flesh.

"Stripped, robbed, and separated" refers to the karma of stealing and seizing by force. Regarding the two instances of the word "xiān" (formerly/first) in the phrase "you xiān" or "or xiān," one should know that both mean "in the past" or "in former times.
Because of the act of stripping and robbing, one may even [be reborn as] a father's... [or] a mother's... [body].
The son is in the north; the brothers are in the east and west, and so forth. Therefore it is said, "I am separated from my kinsmen. As for the phrase "only today has it become convenient":
previously, because the karmic conditions had not yet ripened, it seemed inconvenient; now that the time for the retribution of karma has arrived, it is truly difficult to escape.

Thus, one finds the opportunity [to receive retribution]. Regarding "willingly accepting one's portion": it means that the retribution for a crime should correspond precisely to the magnitude of that karmic offense.
Therefore, the one who undergoes the retribution accepts it with a willing heart, exactly according to their allotted share.
This is precisely what is meant by investigating and punishing according to the gravity of the offense.
As clarified in the sūtras, within the hells, people are not punished unjustly (the phrase "not punishing unjustly" is explained below).
If one has forgotten the various sins committed during their ordinary life, then at the moment of death, all the various signs of the places where those evils were created [will appear].
They all appeared before him, each saying, "In the past, while you were in my presence, you committed such-and-such a transgression.

How can you now seek to conceal it? The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "The three realms are but mind; the myriad dharmas are but consciousness. They arise according to what the mind creates and manifest according to what the mind perceives;
there is nothing to be concealed. Furthermore, the *Śūraṅgama* says: "At the time of death, before warmth and sensation have departed from the body, [the karmic record of] one's life..."
"Good and evil appear simultaneously and all at once"—this is precisely that meaning. "Each says, 'In my past... and so forth; these are words of mutual accusation.
At that time, the person who committed the offense has no place to hide; thereupon, King Yama gnashes his teeth in reproach and, leading [the offender] away—
Cast into hell, one must pass through immeasurable kalpas, with no way to seek escape. This matter is not far off; it does not concern others.

(From here below, the text urges one to reflect upon one's own transgressions and confess them. It is precisely my own body that acts and my own body that receives the retribution. Though father and son share the closest intimacy, once the moment of reckoning arrives, there is no one who can take one’s place.
We have all together obtained this human body, free from various ailments; each of us—
Exert yourself! Strive as if contending for your very life; when the great terror arrives, it will be too late for regret.

Ordinary people often believe that evil karma can be concealed, and thus they do not contemplate repentance; had they known early on that in the end nothing can be hidden, they would have acted differently.
What do you think? It would be best to first confess and repent before the Buddha, hoping thereby to escape [retribution]. Be careful not to be indolent.
However, after repenting, you must reform your ways and ensure that you never commit such acts again; only then may you hope to be spared. If, however, you rely merely upon your confession—
To further create new calamities and yet hope to escape them—such a thing has never existed. Reflect upon this, be cautious, and you must exert yourself.
○ Regarding "reproach," it is as when one says: "Foolish person, seed of hell! While you were in the world, you were unfilial toward your parents."
"You are possessed by false pride and lack the Way; you have no sense of shame or remorse. The place where you are now born is called the Avīci Hell.
Do you find pleasure in undergoing such suffering and affliction? Thus he rebukes him with these piercing words, solely for the purpose of causing the person to reform and start anew.
Furthermore, because the king sees that the individual has forgotten their transgressions and remains unaware of them, he censures them.
"To entrust" means to hand over this sinner to the Avīci Hell; therefore, throughout kalpas, there will be no way to seek deliverance.
"The assembly together" refers to the confession master exhorting the practitioners to recognize their transgressions and repent swiftly, without indolence or laxity.
"When the time of great terror arrives" means that impermanence suddenly comes upon one.
The flowers before one’s eyes fall to the ground; the four elements disperse. The path ahead is vast and desolate, and it is unknown where one shall go.
Moreover, if one has not prepared the provisions for the journey during one's ordinary life, is this not truly terrifying? Do not wait until the suffering of retribution descends upon you.
At that time, there will be no way to escape; therefore, one must cast aside life and forget the self, striving to seek repentance before it is too late.
For this reason, with a sincere heart, we seek mercy and repent: from beginningless time until this very day, we—[the practitioners]—have [committed such offenses].
Accumulating ignorance, it obscures the mind and eyes; following the nature of secondary afflictions, one commits offenses throughout the three periods of time.
That which is said to have existed since beginningless time refers to the past eons being incalculable, and the offenses committed therein likewise being incalculable.

How much more so now, in this life, where one remains unawakened; thus, with the ignorance and afflictions of the present moment, one opens eighty-four thousand gates of worldly toil (*kleśa*), committing sins beyond counting.

The cycle of future births and deaths has no end, and as one transmigrates through the four modes of birth and the six realms, changing form after form, how can one not stand in awe? Therefore it is said: "If this body does not [attain realization] in this life..."
[To] cross over. Toward what time shall one further cross over this body? One should know that the courageous and diligent transcendence of the three realms occurs precisely in this present life;
do not, by any means, let it slip away. The following two chapters again take up beginningless ignorance to repent for the transgressions and evils of the three periods of time.
The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is fundamentally luminous; originally, there are no sinful karmas. Because of [ignorance]...
It is said that because one is obscured and clouded by afflictions (*kleśa*) and lacks clarity, it is called "following after afflictions," and so forth.
Thus, the statement, "From beginningless time, the deluded mind has drifted through the ocean for vast eons amidst the waves of birth and death," refers precisely to this.
Furthermore, the "accumulation of ignorance" (*avidyā*) means that there is no light of wisdom; one is unable to fully comprehend objects.
The mind obscures the faculty of the mind; therefore, it follows this [obscuration] to create various evil karmas. Thus, it is said to have the nature of secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
Alternatively, through indulgence in defiled attachment, the affliction of craving arises; or through hatred and anger, the affliction of harboring malice arises; or...
The affliction of mental confusion and delusion that fails to comprehend; the affliction of self-exaltation and arrogance born of pride;

the affliction of doubt and hesitation regarding the Right Path; the affliction of false views that deny cause and effect; the affliction of attachment to a self through ignorance of dependent origination;

the affliction of clinging to nihilism or eternalism due to being迷失 (lost) regarding the three periods of time; and the affliction of dogmatic adherence to views arising from associating with unwholesome dharmas. Bias...

I now, with utmost sincerity, repent of all afflictions arising from following false teachers and clinging to precepts and rituals, as well as all afflictions resulting from the arbitrary conceptualizations of the four types of grasping.
Ordinary beings take only the two maladies of dullness and distraction as the root of birth and death;
"dullness" (kùn) refers to the state of being agitated and distracted. Doubt, lack of faith, and indecisiveness are all the faults of being shrouded by ignorance (*avidyā*).
Whether preceding or following [this], it is no different in every case: heaven is a false construction, and hell has no reality.

To speak thus is to utter words that slander the Peerless One. Failing to recognize that causes and conditions are empty and illusory, one consequently fails to understand that the Four Great Elements are fundamentally void.
Thereby, one clings to the view of self and gives rise to afflictions. The two views of annihilationism and eternalism are simply the two views of existence and non-existence.
Those of like mind are called "companions," and those who dwell nearby are called "intimates. Since these are termed "evil dharmas," there must surely be those who possess them.

And thus one approaches it.
