"When a donor originally gives away even a single hair’s breadth or a single grain of rice, they intend it for the sounding of the drum and bell throughout the ten directions, so that it may be heard alike by those far and near, and enjoyed by both the holy and the ordinary."
Both shall accomplish the path; they will provide secret support to their donors, who will thereby obtain boundless merit.

Yet now we see ignorant sentient beings who either consume the food of the Sangha, or make use of its flowers and fruits, or follow about the slaves belonging to the Sangha, or ride upon the animals belonging to the Sangha, or privately borrow monastic property and fail to return it, or use their official power to seek out the faults of the Sangha, and so forth.

The full enumeration would be inexhaustible. As for those eminent monks who guard [the property] and refuse to give it away, how could they merely be pitying laypeople for suffering retribution in the future?
They also know that those in charge of affairs will share in the calamity in their future rebirths. *Zhuangzhuang Lu* says:
"If one steals even a single coin from the permanent endowment, the interest grows by three fen and seven li per day and night. On the second [day...]"
Day and night, the benefit is superior and even more long-lasting. In future lives, one will repay this by becoming an ox or a horse.

This is why it is said that what is easy to do in a single lifetime becomes a hardship for ten thousand kalpas. If one gives up even a single coin to enter the permanent endowment (*sangha-ratna*), the daily and nightly increase in merit is likewise so.
In Sanskrit, *cātudisa-saṃgha*; in the language of Tang, "the Saṃgha of the four directions."

*Wu*. This is erroneously called *zhāotí* (Jiātí). It refers to the property held in perpetual trust for the ten directions. An ancient saying goes: "A single blade of grass is held in perpetual trust;
I urge you not to seek it [for private gain]. In the Buddha-land there are monasteries; in the underworld there is Lord Yama. Be cautious!

Regarding those who use these funds in a confused and improper manner—for instance, using money intended for the casting of sandalwood statues to burn as incense, or using funds for the release of living beings [for other purposes]—[they incur grave karmic retribution].
To mix funds for the ordination of monks and then use those funds to build temples constitutes a sinful karmic offense; how much more so to use them for private self-interest?
The *Sui-fu jue-yi jing* (Sutra on Resolving Doubts Regarding Sin and Merit) states: "If a donor originally intended to commission an image of Śākyamuni but changes it to Amitābha;

if they originally intended to produce the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* but change it to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*; if they originally intended to build a monk’s quarters but change it to provide food for the monks; if they originally intended to give..."
To divert offerings intended for two groups into one group, or those originally intended for the ten directions into those present before one, violates the donor’s intent.
Likewise, to give what was promised for this place to another place constitutes an offense.

According to this text, if there is surplus pigment from a Buddha image, it must not be used to create the forms of Bodhisattvas, sages, or similar figures, because the status of the Teacher and his disciples is distinct.

One must not use materials interchangeably. The *Wubai wenshi lü* (Vinaya of Five Hundred Questions) states: "If one uses the colored pigments belonging to the Buddha to create the forms of birds or beasts, one incurs an offense;
however, there is no offense if it is for the purpose of making offerings before the Buddha."

Or by means of various goods—grain, rice, firewood, salt, fermented soybeans, sauce, vinegar, vegetables, fruits, money, silk, bamboo, wood, brocades, banners, canopies, incense, flowers, oil, and candles—one acts according to one's own whims and intentions, either using them for oneself, giving them to others, or plucking flowers and fruit belonging to the Buddha, or using the property of the Saṃgha;
thus, through the wealth and property of the Triple Gem, one privately benefits oneself. Such are these transgressions.
Immeasurable and boundless. Today, with shame and remorse, I repent it all.
Alternatively, the phrase "with various objects" runs directly through the following six phrases beginning with incense and flowers; all of these refer to various material offerings.

"According to circumstances" means according to the voices of others; "following one's own intent" means following one's own will. "Mālā" refers to flower garlands and necklaces; see the character *yin* (因).
One must not confuse its application for oneself or others. For example: making images, making scriptures, building stupas, or constructing monasteries.

Furthermore, the funds for the monastic community’s recitation of sutras and the performance of repentance rites, as well as the money offered by donors for feeding the Sangha, making offerings, and releasing living beings—all such items are the property of the Triple Gem.
If one is unable to repay these obligations to the Triple Gem, yet nevertheless conceals or misappropriates them for personal use, [one commits an offense].
This is called seeking private self-interest.
Furthermore, from time immemorial until this day, whether acting as friends, associates, teachers, monks, or fellow students, [one has acted in such a manner].

Parents, brothers, and the six classes of kinsmen and relatives dwell together and reside together; they provide for one another’s hundred and one necessities. Those who share the same purpose are called *peng* (companions);
those who mutually respect one another are called *you* (friends). The preceptor is called the *shi* (teacher); the pure assembly is called the *seng* (sangha).
Aunts, maternal uncles, paternal uncles, and so forth are called the "six kinsmen. Among such groups, when they are in one place, they may be able to provide for one another's needs completely.
This is but one hundredth part of what is required. Regarding necessary items, they may instead deceive, defraud, and mislead one another to use them for private purposes;

or, among neighbors and those living nearby, they may shift fences and expand walls to encroach upon others' lands and dwellings, altering boundary markers and changing signs to plunder [their property].

Regarding wealth and property, they encroached upon and monopolized fields and gardens; under the pretext of public business, they appropriated others' shops and residences, as well as lands in the wilderness.
For such boundless and immeasurable transgressions, I now repent them all.
*Tuò* (拓) means to push forward. To "push forward" (*yituò*) implies encroachment. *Biāo* (標) means to mark. To "alter" (*gǎiyì*) implies the sense of shifting or encroaching.
"Looting" (*lǔlüè*) refers to seizing by force with torches and weapons. "In the name of public affairs" (*jìngōng*) means to exploit official business for one's own private interests.
*Dǐ* (邸) means a lodging; it also means to arrive, referring to the place where one arrives. *Diàn* (店) means a shop; it is where goods are placed for sale.
"Yu" means to sell goods. "Zhun" means to gather; it may refer to a place where people congregate in the mountains or wilds.

Furthermore, since beginningless time, there have been those who have besieged cities and destroyed towns, burned villages and demolished stockades, or who have stolen and sold free citizens, lured away the servants of others, or even unjustly oppressed the innocent, causing them to perish by the blade or be subjected to forced labor.
Chains. Family ties shattered and dispersed; flesh and bone separated by birth; scattered across different lands; life and death utterly severed.
For such immeasurable and boundless transgressions as these, I now repent them all.

"Wǎng" (枉) means to be wronged or oppressed. "Cú" (殂) means to pass away; it signifies death. "Yuán" (緣) means cause or condition; it may also be written as "yuán" (園), meaning a garden. "Yìyù" (異域) and "tāxiāng" (他鄉) both mean a foreign land or a place other than one's own home.

Furthermore, from time immemorial until this very day, whether in commerce and trade, or in shops and markets, we have used light scales and small measures, reduced dimensions by a fraction of an inch, and stolen even the smallest increments of grain.
We have deceived others with measures of *gui* and *he*, exchanging coarse goods for the fine, or short items for the long.
Through hundreds of such cunning deceptions, we have sought profit in the slightest amount. All such transgressions, we now fully repent.
"Merchants trade": they appraise and negotiate prices to purchase goods and exchange them for profit. "Market transactions" refers to exchanging what one has for what one lacks.
"Inches and spans" refers to the measurements of length. "Fen and zhu" refers to the marks on a scale, such as the *li* (one-hundredth of an ounce).
Regarding the numerical values for weights: twenty-four *zhū* constitute one *liǎng*; one *zhū* is equal to one *liǎng* and four-tenths plus seven *máo*.
Six *sù* constitute one *guī*; ten *guī* constitute one *cuō*; ten *cuō* constitute one *chāo*; ten *chāo* constitute one *sháo*;
ten *sháo* constitute one *hé*; ten *hé* constitute one *shēng*. Even when speaking of the most minute of things, these cannot be deceived or falsified.
To take [these]... (Omission mark) — all such matters here refer to commerce and trade in the marketplace. To involve even a single instance of deception or fraud is equivalent to theft.

Furthermore, from time immemorial until this very day, there have been those who break through walls or climb over them, those who waylay and plunder on the roads, those who evade debts and interest, those who betray trust and violate agreements, those who deceive with their faces while taking by heart, or those who seize by force contrary to the Way—whether against spirits, ghosts, birds, beasts, or humans.
Regarding living beings, they may falsely resort to divination and physiognomy to seize people’s wealth and treasures.

In this way, they even seek profit through profit, employing evil means and excessive greed, never feeling satiated or satisfied. Such transgressions are immeasurable and boundless, beyond the power of words to fully describe.
Today we pray. Before the Buddhas of the ten directions, the Honored Dharma, and the Assembly of Sages, we repent for all our transgressions:
breaking through walls or climbing over fences to spy or steal; blocking roads and plundering—this refers to those who intercept travelers on the road to rob them;
and refusing to repay debts or interest, violating agreements and betraying trust by borrowing and failing to return what was lent. We repent of such acts of deception.
To bear false witness is to violate an old covenant; it is a breach of the covenant. To deceive face-to-face means to deceive one’s face to face.
To take by private intent means to plot and seize through a secret mind; these are all categories of theft.
Since ghosts and spirits partake of blood and flesh, there exist the four modes of birth for birds and beasts. One should know that ghosts and spirits, too, each have their own gains.
When people see objects, they immediately bully others to seize them. To seek profit through profit means to add profit upon profit.
To seek evilly or to seek excessively means to rely on one’s power to coerce others.
I pray that by virtue of this repentance,
the extensive repentance for the karma of theft above having been completed, I may now, below, make vows to seek the accomplishment of merit and virtue.

Through the merit produced by the repentance of crimes such as robbery and theft, may I, in birth after birth and life after life, obtain wish-fulfilling jewels and have the seven treasures rain down constantly.
Exquisite garments, a hundred flavors of delicious food, and various medicinal decoctions—whatever they require according to their wishes arrive as soon as they are thought of.
All sentient beings harbor no thoughts of theft or plunder; they are all able to have few desires and be content, neither indulging in nor being stained by worldly things.

They always delight in giving and practice the path of providing relief, relinquishing their heads, eyes, marrow, and brains as easily as they would spit or snot, dedicating these acts toward the fulfillment of *dāna* (generosity).
The pāramitās;
the seven treasures and eight precious gems, such as gold, silver, and lapis lazuli;

and exquisite jewels, fine garments, delicious foods, and medicinal decoctions that arrive the moment they are thought of—these appear spontaneously before one, just as in a Buddha-field. [Yet] the karma of theft and plunder is abundant.
This arises from poverty, or it occurs because of a lack of contentment. Now, may all that is required be obtained as wished; may there naturally be no thought of theft or seizure;
and may one be able to practice fewness of desires and contentment, fulfilling the perfection of giving. It is fitting to make such a vow.
The Dānapāramitā: the true perfection of giving that reaches the other shore. [The above concludes the repentance for the karma of theft.
We, [Name] and others, now further repent of the sins of greed and attachment.
The following is the repentance for the karma of sexual desire of the body.
The Sūtra says: "It is solely because of desire that one is confined within the prison of ignorance and submerged in the river of birth and death, unable to know how to emerge."
Sentient beings, for the sake of these five desires, have wandered through birth and death since time immemorial.

Throughout all the lifetimes they have passed through over kalpas, the bones accumulated by all sentient beings would equal Mount Vipula in Rājagṛha, and the milk they have drunk from their mothers' breasts would likewise be vast.
The blood shed from one's body exceeds the waters of the four oceans.

Likewise, the tears shed from the eyes while weeping for the death of parents, brothers, and other six types of kinsmen and relatives exceed the waters of the four oceans. Therefore it is said: "Where there is craving, there is birth."
When craving is exhausted, it ceases. Thus, one knows that craving for birth and death is the root.

The Brahmajāla Sūtra says: "If a Buddha’s disciple engages in sexual misconduct themselves, teaches others to engage in sexual misconduct, or [participates in] the causes of sex, the conditions of sex, the methods of sex, or the karma of sex—even with the females of animals, the females of devas or ghosts, or engaging in sex through improper orifices—the Bodhisattva should..."
To bestow pure dharmas upon others, yet instead arouse lust in all people, constitutes a *pārājika* offense. "Desire" refers here to sensual desire.
As for the "prison of delusion," it means to be mired in ignorance and folly without reflection, like being confined in a prison with no way to escape.
The depth of affection and the cycle of birth and death are as profound as rivers and oceans.
Regarding the "five desires" (*pañca-kāma-guṇa*)—wealth, form, fame, food, and sleep—the present context specifically refers to sexual desire; the other four are mentioned only by way of association.

Throughout the births of successive kalpas, the quantity of one's own bones, milk, blood, and tears is immense. This clearly demonstrates the vastness of birth and death throughout the kalpas, and the suffering therein is likewise [immeasurable].
The endless and inexhaustible cycle of birth and death has nothing other than craving as its root.
Therefore, once the mind of lust is extinguished, birth and death are likewise extinguished.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "The sin of sexual desire can cause sentient beings to fall into the hells or as hungry ghosts to undergo suffering.
If they are born among animals, they will receive the bodies of pigeons, sparrows, mandarin ducks, and the like. If they are among humans, their wives will not be chaste."
One obtains a retinue that is contrary to one's wishes. Since sexual desire yields such evil fruits as these, I now, with utmost sincerity, seek compassion and repent.
This section first clarifies the retribution for sexual desire; below, we shall repent for the transgressions of sexual desire.

"Zheng" (貞) means "true purity. It refers to those who do not follow the whims of their kinsmen; all those who are neither honest nor pure, the ignorant and dull-witted who are difficult to transform, and the violent and fierce who are difficult to tame—these are all such as these.

Furthermore, from time immemorial until this very day, you may have stolen others' wives or concubines, abducted other women, violated the integrity of the pure, defiled bhikṣuṇīs, and destroyed their brahmacarya;
you may have coerced others unrighteously, looked upon them with turbid and lustful eyes, or mocked them with lewd speech;
or perhaps you have brought shame upon others' families and sullied the reputations of the virtuous and good.
Above, the repentance for the retribution of sexual desire has been completed. Below, the characteristics of the offenses of sexual desire are extensively cited and further repented of.
*Fanxing* (梵行) is here translated as "pure conduct" (*brahmacarya*); it refers to the pure precepts.

Because the mind abounds in sexual impurity, it is called a "turbid mind. "Color" (*se*) refers to the act of engaging in lust; since its name is synonymous with the "fire of desire," it is called "evil gazing. This arises because one harbors sexual impurity.
Because of this mind, it is called a "turbid mind. Because one constantly contemplates improper forms, it is called "perverse vision.
It can be understood that a person who practices correctly does not look upon perverse forms. "Chao" refers to jesting and mockery.
Or having committed impure acts with five kinds of men; such offenses as these are immeasurable and boundless.
Today, with utmost sincerity, I repent them all.
As for "men," they are likely those such as members of the *lìyuán* (orchestra) or singing boys. As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:
"One should not delight in keeping young disciples, śrāmaṇeras, or small children. Furthermore, they are performers who play stringed instruments and lead the chanting;
in the West, they are called "incense-seekers" (*xúnxīngrén*). Regarding the "five kinds of people," they give rise to intense jealousy and transformation.
Half. Regarding the five kinds of impotent persons: the upper portion concludes the repentance; the lower portion sets forth vows to achieve virtue, stating:
"By the merit produced through this repentance for the sins of lustful desire and so forth, may we, in birth after birth and age after age, naturally transform..."

He was born not from a womb, pure and radiant, endowed with the marks and signs of excellence and luminous splendor. His six sense faculties were clear and bright; he was sharp, intelligent, and profoundly discerning.
He realized that affection and craving are like shackles and fetters, and he viewed the six sense objects as being like illusions and transformations.

He felt a definitive revulsion toward the realms of the five desires, such that even in his dreams he did not give rise to improper thoughts. Neither internal nor external causes and conditions could ever...
Movement. Having performed repentance and made vows, one takes refuge and pays homage to the Triple Gem.

One shall be born either in the Western Land or in the pure lands of the ten directions, always attaining birth by transformation from a lotus flower, unlike the birth from a womb in the five turbidities of this evil world.
○ The six emotions become clear and bright; the six sense organs are unimpeded and sharp. Being...
That which is on the feet is called a *zhì* (shackle), and that which is on the hands is called a *gù* (manacle); these refer to such things as fetters for the ankles and cuffs for the wrists.
Having already finished repenting for the three karmas of the body, one should now, in due order, repent for the four evil karmas of the mouth.

The upper section is the repentance for the three [misdeeds] of body; the lower section is the repentance for the four [misdeeds] of speech. The headings of the text clarify this themselves. This is the repentance for the four karmas of speech:
namely, harsh speech, false speech, frivolous speech, and double-tongued speech.
The Sūtra states: "The transgressions of verbal karma can cause sentient beings to fall into the hells or the realm of hungry ghosts to undergo suffering.
If they are born among animals, they will take the form of an owl, a cuckoo, or a [name*] bird; those who hear their cries cannot help but feel loathing."

If born among humans, their breath will always be foul; whatever they say, people will not believe or accept; their kinsmen will be discordant, and they will constantly delight in quarreling and contention.
First, the evil fruits of verbal karma are clarified. Below, the four types of verbal misconduct are repented in sequence. The Brahmajāla Sūtra states:
"If a Buddha’s disciple speaks falsehoods themselves, teaches others to speak falsehoods, employs skillful means to speak falsehoods, or provides the causes for speaking falsehoods..."
The conditions for false speech, the nature of false speech, and the karma of false speech:

if a Bodhisattva constantly gives rise to right speech and right view in all sentient beings, yet instead gives rise to wrong speech, wrong view, and so forth toward others, this constitutes a *pārājika* offense.
○ The "owl" (*xiūliú*) refers to the strange bird known as the "strange owl" (*guāichī*). There are many names for the owl; one name is *xiūliú*, and another is...
It is called the *jiji* (owl), also known as the *gēgē*. It sees nothing during the day; at night it flies out to feed on mosquitoes and gadflies.
Whether the *qūgē* is the same as the *gēgē* remains uncertain. If one refers to the *qūyù*, this is the modern-day "eight-syllable bird" (*bāgē*);
it is neither a monster nor an evil creature, so why should it be loathed? Furthermore, it is said to be a bird of foul voice and excessive lust. [If it] were born among humans...
[In the] middle [of the text]: "If these words [were uttered], one might even fall into the realm of animals," and so forth.
Since verbal karma yields such evil fruits as these, we now take refuge in the Triple Gem with utmost sincerity and repent of them all.
This is the repentance for the retribution of the aforementioned offenses.
From beginningless time until this very day, we have committed various sins within the four modes of birth and the six realms of existence through the karma of harsh speech.
Our words have been coarse and vulgar, our utterances violent and overbearing, regardless of whether the person addressed was honorable or lowly, a relative or a stranger.

Being base, whenever things do not go as they wish, they immediately harbor anger and resentment, resorting to verbal abuse, defamation, and insults so vulgar, obscene, and foul that nothing is left unsaid.
This causes others to harbor grievances that they never forget for the rest of their lives, leading to a succession of calamities and the formation of enmity without end.
The general confession of the retributions for the evils of verbal karma is now complete. Herein, the four types of evil verbal karma are extensively enumerated and confessed in succession.
This text consists of four parts, which may be observed. Regarding "harsh speech" (惡口): it refers to resentment, abuse, and the utterance of malicious curses.
It is called *kuaṅ* (獷), meaning it is like a dog that cannot be approached; it refers to words that are ugly, coarse, and violent, and are unbearable to hear.
Those who hear this are precisely such people. "Vile and indecent" refers to that which is loathsome and unbearable; hence it is said they "go to no end.
"To bring about calamity and enmity" refers to the accumulation of misfortune throughout eternal kalpas; hence it is said there is "no end to it."

Furthermore, there may have been instances where we have provoked resentment against Heaven and Earth, reviled the spirits and deities, disparaged the sages and worthies, or slandered and defiled the virtuous and good.
The karmic offenses arising from such evil speech are immeasurable and boundless; today, with utmost sincerity, we repent for them all.
"Resentment and verbal abuse" refers to those such as the angry devas who revile the earth, curse the rain, and rebuke the wind.
"Censure" means to suppress or to banish. "Defamation and pollution" refers to using evil words and foul language to falsely slander and tarnish one's pure reputation;
hence it is said, "defaming and polluting the virtuous."
Furthermore, from time immemorial until this day, through the karma of false speech, they have committed various offenses.

Driven by a desire in their minds for reputation and gain, they conceal their true feelings and employ deception; with clouded hearts and shameless faces, they point to existence as emptiness and point to emptiness as existence;

they say they have not seen what they have seen, and say they have seen what they have not seen; they say they have not heard what they have heard, and say they have heard what they have not heard; they say they know...
They do not know, yet they claim to know; they have done something, yet they claim not to have done it; they have not done something, yet they claim to have done it.

They deceive the worthy and the sages and delude the people of the world. Even in their conversations with fathers and sons, rulers and ministers, relatives and old friends, they never speak with sincerity.
This causes others to mistakenly place their trust in them, leading to the ruin of families and the downfall of nations—all of which stems from this source.

One who speaks falsely leaves no trace or evidence; because they act with deceit, it is called "concealing one's true feelings. To claim something exists when it is empty, or to speak thusly in falsehood, is entirely a matter of concealing one's emotions and practicing deception.
It is a state of darkening the mind and possessing thick-skinned shamelessness, wherein one remains in a state of self-deception.
One's own mind is such that one has cause for shame before others;

thus it is said that they "obscure their minds and possess thick-skinned impudence," creating false illusions and constantly praising themselves, claiming to have attained the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments, and ānāpāna-smṛti (mindfulness of breathing).
"Deceivers and illusionists" refers to those who borrow the heterodox arts of external paths (tīrthika) to delude people.
"Constantly praising themselves" refers to such statements as, "I directly govern the whirlwind below; earth-spirits and ghosts all come to my abode," which are all instances of self-praise.

"Attaining the four dhyānas" refers to the two characters "attained" (de); because one directly governs the sixteen contemplations below, one attains [the fruits of] srotāpanna and so forth. "Attained."

Regarding the four dhyānas (*catur-dhyāna*): this refers to attaining the meditative absorptions of the heavens of the four dhyānas. There are three heavens in the first dhyāna, three heavens in the second dhyāna, three heavens in the third dhyāna, and nine heavens in the fourth dhyāna;
thus, there are eighteen heavens in the realm of form (*rūpa-dhātu*) in total. The *Zongjing lu* states:

"First, those who hold heterodox views practice by rejoicing in higher realms and loathing lower ones; this is the dhyāna of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Second, those who correctly believe in cause and effect..."

To practice by means of joy and aversion is the dhyāna of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*). To practice having realized the principle of the emptiness of sentient beings and attained the path of partial truth (*ekadeśa-satya*) is the dhyāna of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).
To practice having mastered the two types of emptiness—of persons and phenomena—is the dhyāna of the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*).

Regarding the four formless absorptions (*catasra ārūpya-samāpattayaḥ*), these refer to the meditative concentrations of the four heavens of the formless realm. The first is the concentration of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-samādhi*).

Second is the concentration of the sphere of infinite consciousness; third is the concentration of the sphere of nothingness; fourth is the concentration of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
These four are the empty heavens of the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), and are thus called the four formless concentrations (ārūpyasamāpatti). Ānāpāna was discussed previously.
One attains the stage of *srotāpanna* through the contemplation of the sixteen aspects, up to the stage of *arhat*, the attainment of a *pratyekabuddha*, and the non-retrogressive *bodhisattva*.

Regarding the "contemplation of the sixteen aspects," the treatise states: The initial stage of the faculties is called the "dharma of warmth" (*uṣmagata*). This is a general mental application (*ālambana*) upon the common characteristics of phenomena (*dharmas*), being a specific differentiation of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
Thus cultivated, it is capable of burning the fuel of the afflictions (*kleśa*); it is the precursor sign (*pūrvanimitta*) to the fire of the Noble Path (*āryamārga*).
It is like the process of drilling for fire, where first the signs of heat arise; [in this way, one] is able to fully observe the objects of the Four Noble Truths.
By means of this, one fully cultivates the sixteen aspects (*ākāra*). One contemplates the Noble Truth of Suffering by cultivating four aspects: First, impermanence (*anitya*):

because that which exists returns to non-existence, it is called impermanent. Second, suffering (*duḥkha*): because it is accompanied by the characteristic of affliction, it is called suffering. Third, emptiness (*śūnya*): one observes emptiness.
Because it is originally non-existent, it is called "emptiness. Fourth is "non-self": because there is no self-mastery, it is called "non-self.
Next, one contemplates the Noble Truth of Origination by cultivating four aspects: first, "cause," because it produces a corresponding fruit, it is called "cause"; second, "origination."
It is called "origination" (*samudaya*) because it is able to produce the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*). It is called "arising" (*jāti*) because it is able to draw forth birth and death.
It is called "condition" (*pratyaya*) because it is able to bring about mutual conjunction. Next, one contemplates the Noble Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-āryasatya*) by cultivating four aspects:

first, "cessation" (*nirodha*), so called because it is diametrically opposed to birth and death; second, "tranquility" (*śānta*), so called because it eliminates the fire of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Third, "Excellent" (*praṇīta*): it is called excellent because it surpasses all other phenomena. Fourth, "Detached" (*niḥsaraṇa*): it is called detached because it is able to abandon birth and death.
Furthermore, one next contemplates the Noble Truth of the Path by cultivating four aspects: First, "Path" (*mārga*): it is called path because it leads to the state beyond categories (*asamskṛta*).

Second, "Correctness" (*nyāya*): it is called correctness because it is not inverted or erroneous. Third, "Practice" (*pratipad*): it is so called because it is that which is trodden by the feet of the noble ones.
These are called the "Practices. Because they forever transcend birth and death, they are called "Departures.

Taking the four noble truths as the object of observation above, cultivating the four aspects of practice is termed the "Sixteen Aspects of Observation. When the practitioner has cultivated this stage of Heat (*ūṣmagata*), they next give rise to the stage of Summits (*mūrdhan*).
Like a mountain peak where a person does not remain long, if there are no obstacles, one will surely pass beyond this mountain and reach...
If one encounters various obstacles on that mountain, one immediately retreats; if there are no obstacles, one will certainly reach the stage of Patience (*kṣānti*).

Having entered the stage of Patience, because one is extremely capable of enduring the objects of the Four Noble Truths, one next gives rise to the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), which is preeminent among all worldly states.
Thus, by contemplating the objects of the Four Noble Truths, one cultivates the sixteen aspects (*ākāra*) in their entirety and gradually approaches the Path of Seeing.

The roots of goodness regarding the Truths do not take the desire realm as their object. If one gives rise to untainted *dharma-kṣānti* (receptivity to the Dharma) with respect to the objects of the Noble Truths, this receptivity is therefore called *dharma-jñāna* (knowledge of the Dharma).
[One then] attains the four *dhyānas*, the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*), *ānāpāna-smṛti* (mindfulness of breathing), and the sixteen aspects of contemplation;
these are called "attaining the practice and heading toward" [the fruit]. One attains the stage of *srotāpanna*; included within this interval are the *sakṛdāgāmin* and *anāgāmin*.
From the *Sakṛdāgāmin* up to the *Arhat*, as well as the *Pratyekabuddha* and the non-retrogressive *Bodhisattva*—these are called those who have attained the fruits.
Those who enter by way of training (*śaikṣa*) are the *Srotāpanna*, *Sakṛdāgāmin*, and *Anāgāmin*. Those who enter by way of no-more-training (*aśaikṣa*) are the *Arhat* and the *Pratyekabuddha*.
As for "those in training" (*śaikṣa*), it means they train because their intention is not yet fulfilled. As for "those beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*), it means...
Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas accomplish their practice through the cultivation of various self-benefiting deeds; they should act solely for the sake of benefiting others.
As the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "The Srotāpanna is called 'one who has entered the stream';
the Sakṛdāgāmin is called 'one who comes back once'; the Anāgāmin is called 'one who does not come back. Regarding the Arhat, there are three meanings, namely: *arhat* (worthy),...
The "Arhat" (Killer of Thieves) refers to one who is free from birth; the "Pratyekabuddha" (Solitary Realizer) refers to one who appears in an age without a Buddha.
"Bodhisattva" is translated in full as *bodhisattva*; in the language of China, it means "Awakened Being."
Devas come, nāgas come, spirits come, ghosts come, and whirlwind earth-ghosts all arrive at my place, manifesting wonders to delude the masses and seeking my veneration and the fourfold offerings.
Such false speech gives rise to immeasurable and boundless karmic offenses.
Today, with utmost sincerity, we repent all together.
The devas, nāgas, spirits, and ghosts cannot see us constantly. The "whirlwind" is what is currently called the "demon army wind.
The "local ghosts" are the ghosts within one's own region. The two lines beginning with "seeking their reverence" precisely correspond to the aforementioned "longing for [their presence]."
The intention for fame and gain. The four types of material offerings (*caturvidha-pūjā*) are: food and drink, clothing, bedding, and medicine.
In the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, these are termed the "four attachments.
Furthermore, from time immemorial until today, one has committed various transgressions through the karma of frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*), using such words as...
Flourishing and ostentatious; their calligraphy and ink-strokes are艳丽 (yàn lì—gorgeous and brilliant). They gloss over faults and embellish errors.

They skillfully compose songs and lyrics that depict seductive charms and portray licentious manners, causing those of mediocre or inferior capacity to be moved by passion and lose their true nature. They become addicted to wine and lust, unable to turn back from their depravity.

Or they indulge their private vendettas, forgetting public justice. Though they may be loyal ministers, filial sons, men of ambition, or benevolent persons, they are forced to act [contrary to their principles].

They composed chapters and writings to vilify them. Later generations read these works and consequently accepted them as truth. This caused those [sages] to harbor grievances in the depths of the underworld with no means of vindication.
Thus, the karmic offenses arising from such frivolous speech are immeasurable and boundless. Today, with the utmost sincerity...
I repent of them all.

As for frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*): it consists of embellishment and adornment—namely, clever words, skillful jesting, elegant compositions, flowery rhetoric, lewd expressions, and seductive songs.
All these are *puṣpita* (flower-like), being ornate, beautiful, and refined; they are gorgeous, fresh, and radiant. Thus, it is able to...
They gloss over their errors to cause others to believe and submit. Observe their clever fabrications, descriptions, and imitations;

they are nothing other than the pursuit of cleverness and minor acts of craftiness and deception. They feign appearances and sounds, even employing songs and short stories to make people find pleasure in them.
This causes them to become so deeply immersed in delusion and attachment that they are unable to turn back of their own accord.
As for those who indulge in private enmity, they act according to their own whims and natures, failing to regard upright men and gentlemen. They shift blame onto others and seize upon faults;

they set traps and ensure that [the victim] is defiled, leaving no way to offer an explanation. Consequently, the deceased must harbor resentment in the depths of the underworld with no means of clarifying their innocence.
Furthermore, from time immemorial until this very day, through the karma of double-tongued speech, they have committed various offenses:

praising to one's face while slandering behind one's back; employing a hundred forms of artful speech, saying this to that person and that to this person; caring only for their own benefit and disregarding the harm done to others;

slandering and creating discord between sovereign and minister, and falsely defaming the virtuous and good, thereby causing suspicion and jealousy between sovereign and minister, and disharmony between father and son, and husband and [wife].
Wives are separated; relatives are distanced and estranged; the grace of teachers and preceptors is lost; and the path of friendship is severed.

Extending even to the fanning of strife between two nations, they break their oaths and lose their joy, binding themselves in resentment and waging war, thereby killing and wounding the common people. Thus, the karmic offenses arising from double-tongued speech are immeasurable and boundless.
Today, with utmost sincerity, I confess and seek [purification] before the Buddhas of the ten directions, the Honored Dharma, and the Assembly of Sages.
Alas! I repent of them all.
As for double-tongued speech: it is to be compliant to one's face while being contrary behind one's back, sowing discord between this person and that.

"Suspicion, jealousy, and doubt" are words born of fear and resentment; these arise solely from slander and defamation, whereby the Way of the Five Relationships and the amity between two states are destroyed.
It is because of this that they each fall into confusion and uncertainty, even harboring resentment and hatred that cannot be resolved; all of this stems from this very point.
For instance, it is as when one knows only how to benefit oneself while disregarding the harm done to others, and so forth.
I pray that by virtue of this confession of the four evil karmas of speech,
and having already completed the sincere confession above, I may now make aspirations to seek the merit of the four virtuous karmas of speech.
By the merit thus produced, in birth after birth throughout all lifetimes, they shall possess the eight qualities of vocal resonance and attain the four types of analytical eloquence;

they shall always speak words of harmony and benefit, their voices being pure and elegant, such that all delight in hearing them, and they shall skillfully understand the various local dialects and languages of sentient beings.

Whatever is spoken should be timely and accord with the faculties [of the listeners], so that those who hear it may immediately attain realization, transcend the mundane, enter the state of sagehood, and open the eye of wisdom.
Having finished repenting and making vows, take refuge in and pay homage to the Triple Gem.
The Buddha possesses eight qualities of voice. The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states: first, the extremely beautiful voice; second, the soft and supple voice;

third, the harmonious and appropriate voice; fourth, the voice of venerable wisdom; fifth, the voice free from effeminacy; sixth, the unerring voice; seventh, the deep and far-reaching voice; eighth, the inexhaustible voice. Regarding the four types of eloquence (*pratibhāna*):
first, the eloquence of meaning (*arthapratibhāna*), which clarifies the meaning of all phenomena; second, the eloquence of dharma (*dharmapratibhāna*).

1. The ability to proclaim the names of dharmas. 2. Eloquence (*pratibhāna*): the speech capable of explaining those names. 3. Delightful eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*): one must necessarily delight in speaking.

These first three constitute the great eloquence that emits light. [One should] make a vow, saying: "Due to a lack of wisdom and a lack of eloquence in all past verbal karma, I now seek to always speak words that are harmonious, beneficial, and so forth."* *Note:
The original text contains a lacuna marked by ○; the bracketed section provides a reconstruction based on the context of the preceding list of eloquences.*

One should be familiar with the languages and dialects of the four quarters. The customs of the four directions, the local accents of the Chinese and the barbarians, and the regional tongues are each different.

One who skillfully understands sentient beings is like one who understands the cries of the birds of the nine heavens; the speech of the beasts of the nine earths is likewise included therein. As stated previously:
first repent for the three [misdeeds] of the body, next repent for the four [misdeeds] of the mouth; as for the remaining obstacles, they shall be removed in successive order.
"Chen" (Exposition) refers to the text that sequentially lays out the six sense faculties.

Having already completed the repentance for the three actions of the body and four actions of speech, we shall now, in due order, repent for the karmic obstructions committed by the six sense faculties.
From beginningless time until this very day, we—[the practitioners]—have [committed these offenses].
Below this, the transgressions of the six sense organs are first enumerated and repented.
Sometimes the eye is deluded by forms; it becomes stained with craving for dark and yellow, red and green, crimson and purple, as well as rare curios and precious ornaments.
Or, one grasps at the characteristics of men and women—whether tall or short, black or white—their seductive postures and charms, giving rise to unlawful thoughts.
This enumerates the characteristics of the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*).
Alternatively, the ear may crave pleasant sounds— such as the notes of the musical scale (*gong-shang*), stringed instruments, wind instruments, or vocal performances—
or it may seize upon the characteristics of the voices, speech, weeping, or laughter of men and women, thereby giving rise to unwholesome thoughts (*adharmasaṃjñā*).

Next, the characteristics of the faculty of hearing are described: the sounds of the musical scales *gong*, *shang*, and the strings and pipes do not transcend the five notes—*gong*, *shang*, *jiao*, *zhi*, and *yu*.

Or, when the nose relies upon famous incenses such as aloeswood (*cendana*), sandalwood (*tandan*), dragon’s blood (*longxue*), musk (*mosha*), *yujin*, and *suhe*, one gives rise to improper thoughts.
The characteristics of the olfactory faculty are listed: it is like the musk deer.

Or, the tongue craves excellent flavors—fresh, delicious, sweet, and rich. Sentient beings nourish their four great elements with the flesh and blood of others, thereby further increasing the root of suffering and giving rise to unrighteous thoughts.
The characteristics of the tongue-faculty are set forth. Regarding the four great elements (*mahābhūta*): first, the earth element, which refers to solidity, density, and obstruction;

second, the water element, which refers to downward moisture and the nourishment of craving; third, the fire element, which refers to upward flaming and the production of anger; fourth, the wind element, which refers to fanning, blowing, and movement. Furthermore, regarding the six elements:
fifth is the space element, which refers to the non-perception of boundaries or surfaces; sixth is the consciousness element, which refers to the myriad phenomena.
The root source: by killing and consuming the flesh and blood of sentient beings to nourish the four great elements, one will receive even more suffering as retribution in future lives;
hence it is said that this further increases the root of suffering.
Or, regarding bodily pleasures such as flowers, embroidery, brocade, fine silks, all smooth textures, and garments of the seven treasures—by indulging in these, one gives rise to unrighteousness.
[He] forms conceptions,
enumerating the characteristics of the body-faculty;
or his mental thoughts are largely distracted, and his sensory contacts and inclinations deviate from the Dharma.
I shall now set forth the characteristics of the faculty of mind.

Because of these six faculties, the sinful karma created is immeasurable and boundless. Today, with utmost sincerity, I confess before the Buddhas of the ten directions, the Honored Dharma, and the Assembly of Sages.
Having completed the confession of the six kinds of transgressions, one now makes vows to seek the accomplishment of the six kinds of merit.
By the merit of having confessed the faculty of the eye, may this eye penetrate and clearly see the pure *dharmakāya* of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions,
without perceiving them through dualistic characteristics.

The "non-dual characteristic" means that there are no two characteristics of eye and form. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* says: "There is a Buddha, a World-Honored One, who has attained the true divine eye;
constantly abiding in samādhi, he perceives all things without dual characteristics. Kumārajīva said: "He does not create the two characteristics of 'refined' and 'coarse' regarding form.
Sengzhao said: "The 'true divine eye' refers to the eye of the formless Dharma-body; ten thousand forms fill its vision."
It is as if it were before one's eyes; there has never been a moment it was not settled, nor a moment it did not see. Thus, there are no two distinct characteristics of eye and form.
I pray that by the merit of this repentance of the ear-faculty, may these ears always hear the Buddhas and sages of the ten directions.

I shall practice the True Dharma as it has been taught. By the merit of this repentance regarding the faculty of the nose, I pray that this nose may constantly smell the fragrance of the Accumulated Merit (Gandhavyūha) that enters the station of the Dharma, and may abandon the impure stench and filth of birth and death.
The Vimalakīrti Sūtra states: "In a region above, beyond Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of forty-two Ganges Rivers, there is a land named Saṃghagandha.
The Buddha there is named Gandhottamakūṭa. The fragrance of that land, compared to the fragrances of humans and devas throughout the ten directions, is [unparalleled]."
It is the most supreme. The Tathāgata Gandhottamakūṭa teaches the Dharma without words or letters;
he merely causes each bodhisattva to sit beneath a fragrant tree, and upon smelling this wondrous fragrance, they immediately attain the Samādhi of the Treasury of All Virtues.

Therefore, I pray that you will hear the fragrance of the Gandhottamakūṭa’s entry into the stage of Dharma. Furthermore, from every single pore of the bodies of all the bodhisattvas of the Tathāgata Gandhottamakūṭa...
All are fragrant.
By the merit of this confession of the faculty of the tongue, may this tongue always partake of the food of Dharma-joy and the bliss of dhyāna,
and never crave the flavors of the flesh and blood of sentient beings.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: The Buddha asked Pukkusa: "What dharma did you experience that brought you such joy? He replied: "A bhikṣu named Balaṃ was sitting beneath a tree.
At that time, five hundred chariots passed by. Someone asked him, 'Do you see the multitude of chariots?

He answered, 'I do not see them. Again he asked, 'Do you hear the sound of the chariots? He answered, 'I do not hear it. [The man] asked, 'Were you sleeping at that time? He said, 'I was not sleeping.'"

At that time, while he was on the road, the man sighed, saying, "The sound of the carriage wheels is *li-li*. I have been awake and yet did not hear it; how single-minded is his application! It is truly rare to reach such a state.

He deeply admired the man’s resolve, and the man subsequently attained the joy of the Dharma (*dharmaprīti*). When one enters realization through Zen meditation (*dhyāna*), the wondrous Dharma naturally brings delight, and the principles of Zen gladden the heart;
this is what is meant by being satiated with the flavor of the Dharma (*dharmarasa*). Thus, the Ritual for the Feast (*zhāiyí*) says: "When..."
"May sentient beings take the joy of dhyāna as their food and be filled with the delight of the Dharma. This means that they take the joy of the Dharma and the bliss of dhyāna as their sustenance.
As the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra says: "Though they partake of food and drink, they take the joy of dhyāna as their flavor.

And the Ekottarika-āgama says: "There are five supramundane foods: first, the food of the joy of dhyāna; second, the food of aspiration; third, the food of mindfulness; fourth, the food of liberation..."
Food: the five dharmas are the food of joy in the Dharma. Mencius said, "To be satiated by virtue" means to be satiated by benevolence and righteousness;

therefore, one does not desire the flavors of rich meats and fine grains. The Gate of Emptiness takes the joy of the Dharma and the delight of meditation as its food, rather than taking physical nourishment as its flavor. This should be considered in conjunction with the above.
By the merit of this confession of the faculty of the body, may this body be clothed in the robe of the Tathāgata, don the armor of patience,
lie upon the bed of fearlessness, and sit upon the seat of the emptiness of dharmas.
The "Dharma Master" chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: "One should enter the Tathāgata’s chamber, don the Tathāgata’s robe, and sit upon the Tathāgata’s seat;
only then should one extensively expound this sūtra for the fourfold assembly. The Tathāgata’s chamber is the mind of great compassion toward all sentient beings.
The Tathāgata’s robe is the mind of gentleness and patience. The Tathāgata’s seat is..."
The emptiness of all phenomena is the cultivation of the Tathāgata’s dharma of quiescence; because it carries the sense of being worn, it is called "clothing.

Because patience has the sense of being firm and solid, it is called "armor"—armor being golden mail. Because dwelling among the multitude without fear has the sense of peace and happiness, it is called a "bed.
Because the four formless meditative absorptions have the sense of stillness and concentration, they are called a "seat."
By the merit of this repentance of the mental faculty, may this mind achieve the ten powers and master the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*).

May it profoundly contemplate the truth of the equality of emptiness within the two truths (*satyadvaya*), and through the wisdom of skillful means (*upāyaprajñā*), enter the stream of the Dharma, increasing in clarity with every thought-moment.
This reveals the Tathāgata’s great patience regarding non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Regarding the five sciences (*pañca-vidyā-sthāna*), the *Mahā-śāstra* states: First is the science of grammar (*śabda-vidyā*), which refers to the interpretation of glosses and the classification of characters.

Second is the science of arts and crafts (*śilpa-karma-sthāna-vidyā*), including technical skills, mechanical devices, and the calculation of yin-yang and calendrical cycles. Third is the science of medicine (*cikitsā-vidyā*), including incantations and the warding off of evil influences.

1. Medical Science (*cikitsā-vidyā*): through medicine, stones, and acupuncture. 2. Logic (*hetu-vidyā*): examining and determining the heterodox and the orthodox, and investigating and verifying the true and the false.

3. Inner Science (*adhyātma-vidyā*): thoroughly elucidating the wondrous principles of cause and effect within the five vehicles. One must vow to penetrate these five sciences. Regarding the two truths:
first, the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); second, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). As for the conventional truth, within the gateway of Buddha-activities, one does not abandon...
There is one Dharma: as in exhorting ministers to loyalty, sons to filial piety, states to order, and families to harmony;
in promoting goodness to reveal the bliss of heaven, and rectifying evil to manifest the suffering of hell—all these rely upon conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

As for the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it reveals the principle of primordial quiescence: the single nature is all-pervasive, and within the ground of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), not even a single thing is received.
"Dust" refers to all phenomena as being *tathatā* (suchness). To bring the three vehicles back to the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) is based upon the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
Regarding these two truths and the principle of the equality of emptiness, one should vow to contemplate them deeply.

To be fully endowed with the ten powers and the five sciences while understanding the two truths and the principle of the equality of emptiness constitutes skillful means and wisdom; it is not "dry wisdom. From this...

Arising from the wisdom of skillful means, there are the ten sublime practices (daśa-pratipatti), and so forth. Regarding the ten sublime practices: first, the sublime practice of the non-duality of form and mind;
second, the sublime practice of the non-duality of internal and external wisdom; third, the sublime practice of the non-duality of cultivation and nature;
fourth, the sublime practice of the non-duality of cause and effect stages; fifth, the sublime practice of the non-duality of defilement and purity; sixth, the [sublime practice of] reliance...
1. The wondrous practice of the non-duality of the correct response to stimuli; 2. The wondrous practice of the non-duality of self and others;
3. The wondrous practice of the non-duality of the three karmas; 4. The wondrous practice of the non-duality of provisional and ultimate truths in preaching the Dharma; 5.

The wondrous practice of the non-duality of receiving moisture [of the Dharma] and benefiting one’s retinue; These are the ten wondrous practices. Because they are based on non-duality, they are called wondrous practices.
The ten sublime practices all arise from the sphere of skillful means and wisdom. Regarding "entering the flow of the Dharma," the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:
"When desire and attachment are dried up and exhausted, and the faculties no longer encounter their objects, there is nothing but pure wisdom; one possesses wisdom that is dry [of defilement]."
This is called the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuklavidarśanā-bhūmi*). The habit-energies of desire are first dried up, yet one has not yet connected with the Tathāgata’s stream of Dharma.
By means of this very mind, one flows into the perfect and subtle; delusive thoughts are extinguished, and the Middle Way becomes purely true. This is called the Abiding in Faith (*śraddhā-vihāra*).
One is then able to give rise to the ten sublime practices, which is the state of connecting with the Tathāgata’s stream of Dharma. This is what is meant by "flowing."
Entering the Perfect and Subtle is precisely this. Regarding "Great Patience toward Non-arising": "Non-arising" refers to the dharma that is neither born nor extinguished.

As for "patience" (*kṣānti*), it is so named because while this dharma is about to be realized but not yet realized, one is like a person enduring a situation—neither harboring resentment nor venting anger.
"Great Patience toward Non-arising" is the unsurpassed Dharma of the Tathāgata’s One Vehicle.
Therefore, it is called "Great.
Having made the vow, one takes refuge and pays homage to the eternally abiding Triple Gem.
This making of the vow constitutes the concluding confession of the general repentance.

"In Jiulong of Western Shu, there is a spring named Samadhi. It washes away grievances and transgressions; Kanakavatsa reveals the true source."
Pure and penetrating the profound mysteries, its Dharma has spread widely. Regarding the phonetic explanations:

With great kindness and great compassion, you pity all sentient beings; with great joy and great equanimity, you rescue all conscious creatures.
Adorned by the radiance of your marks and signs, the assembly now reverently takes refuge and pays homage to the Buddha, calling you the Great Compassionate Father.
Kindness is able to bestow happiness; compassion is able to uproot suffering. Thus it is said of kindness and compassion.
The "Great" refers to the parents of the world, who possess compassion and cherish their children and grandchildren, yet this is limited to a single lifetime.
If a child is unfilial, ungrateful, or violates righteousness, they give rise to resentment and anger, and their compassionate heart becomes diminished;
thus, it is not called "Great. The compassionate hearts of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are not like this; when they see suffering sentient beings, their heart of pity increases.
"Weighty. This refers to even entering the Avīci Hell amidst great wheels of fire to undergo immeasurable suffering on behalf of all sentient beings.
Such compassion exceeds that of one's own parents by immeasurable and boundless degrees; therefore, it is called "Great.
"Pity" (mǐn) refers to the act of feeling sorrowful compassion and cherishing others. "Sentient beings" (zhòngshēng) refers to those within the six realms and four modes of birth.

It is said: "From the essence of the father and the blood of the mother, the seed of one's own spirit, and so forth, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) arise through the production of various phenomena;

therefore, they are called 'sentient beings' (*sattva*). Regarding "joy" (*muditā*): it is to rejoice when other sentient beings are freed from suffering and attain happiness. Regarding "equanimity" (*upekṣā*): [it is to remain impartial].
"Equality toward enemies and kin" means being free from feelings of hatred or attachment. "To deliver" refers to pulling others out of suffering and providing them with refuge.
"Sentient beings" refers to the class of living creatures who possess consciousness; this refers to the aforementioned beings within the six realms of existence.
These two phrases praise the Buddha’s four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*). The Buddha’s reward body (*saṃbhoga-kāya*) and response body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*) both possess thirty-two marks.
The [thirty-two] marks, the eighty minor characteristics, and the eighty-four thousand rays of light—this praises the adornments of the Buddha.
As for "taking refuge" (*namas* in Sanskrit), it is translated here as "taking refuge in one's life. This refers to seeing that the Buddha’s compassionate vows are vast and profound.
One immediately surrenders one’s very life with utmost sincerity to take refuge in him; hence it is said, "with a sincere mind," and so forth. "Li" (禮) means respectful salutation.
Furthermore, "li" signifies "to tread upon" or "to advance. It implies that there is a measure for advancing and retreating, and a distinction between the honorable and the humble.
Because the humble pays respect to the honorable, it is called "respectful salutation" (*jingli*). First, one uses these four phrases to extol and praise the Buddha.
This collectively expresses the awakening of the initial resolve and signifies the utmost sincerity and earnest devotion.

In the lower fascicle of the *Cibei Shuishan Chanhua* (The Ritual of Water Repentance through Compassion), all Buddhas, out of compassion for sentient beings, have expounded the general methods for the water repentance ritual arena (*dōjō*). Now, we shall take refuge.
