Homage to Kāshyapa-dhvaja Buddha. Homage to Simhanada Buddha. Homage to Mañjushri Bodhisattva.
In the *Pǔchāo sānmèi jīng* (The Sutra on the Samādhi of Universal Transcendence), the Buddha said: "That I have now attained Buddhahood is entirely due to the grace of Mañjuśrī;
he was originally my teacher. All the countless Buddhas of the past were his disciples, and those of the future will likewise be brought about by the power of his grace.
Mañjuśrī is truly the father and mother within the path of the Buddhas. At that time, the assembly reflected: "Since Mañjuśrī is already with the Buddha..."
[Question: Why has he not yet attained Buddhahood? [Answer: The Buddha said: "Mañjuśrī has deeply entered skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) to extensively transform sentient beings;
therefore, he has not yet completed the Way. Furthermore, it should be known that Mañjuśrī is divided into three Buddhas who attain enlightenment across the three periods of time.

He has already attained Buddhahood long ago—who could say he has not attained it? The past Buddha, Nāgottararāja (Dragon-Species Supreme King), is one who has already attained it; this is the present [Mañjuśrī].
The Buddha Ratnākara-śrīgarbha-maṇi-koṭi-nicaya has already attained realization; the Buddha Samantadarśin of the future is one who shall attain it.
This is recorded in various sutras and is not a mere speculative assertion. Because he now sails against the current to deliver sentient beings, he is called a Bodhisattva.
Homage to Samantabhadra Bodhisattva. Homage to Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva. Homage to Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva.
Homage to Mahāvyūha Bodhisattva. Homage to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.

In the *Bodhisattvavyākaraṇa-sūtra*, the Bodhisattva Guṇakara addressed the Buddha, saying, "In which land will the two great beings, Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, attain equal and perfect enlightenment?

The Buddha replied, "After the True Dharma of Amitābha Buddha has ceased, Avalokiteśvara will attain equal and perfect enlightenment, and his name shall be the Tathāgata Samantaprabhā-guṇaparvatarāja. In that [land]...

The Buddha-land shall be named *Saṃcita-sarvaratna-vyūha*. After his parinirvāṇa, Mahāsthāmaprāpta will immediately attain equal and perfect enlightenment in that land, becoming the Tathāgata named *Susthita-guṇaratnarāja*. As for Mahāsthāmaprāpta, he shall never enter extinction;
there is no further need for him to be supplemented.

Having paid homage to all the Buddhas, one next performs repentance. Having already completed the repentance for the three actions of the body and four actions of speech above, one shall now repent for all obstacles regarding the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.
This continues from what precedes to initiate what follows. The preceding section on the confession of sins committed through the three karmas is now complete.
Below follows the confession of karmic obstacles regarding the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha—the karma created within the divisions of the Triple Gem—as described in detail in the subsequent text.
Nevertheless, regarding the three karmas and six sense organs, even within the categories of the Three Jewels, whether it be merit or karma, none arise apart from one’s own mind.
If one’s own mind is pure, and one is reverent, sincere, and respectful without indolence, then there is no transgression that will not be extinguished and no merit that will not be produced.
Otherwise, though one may speak of performing repentance rituals and chanting in harmony with others, if one seeks to eliminate transgressions...
As for the claim that merit is extinguished [upon rebirth], this too is likely not necessarily the case;

reflect upon it. In the sutras, the Buddha said: "A human body is difficult to obtain; the Buddha-dharma is difficult to hear; the Sangha is difficult to encounter; and faith is difficult to give rise to."
The six sense faculties are difficult to possess in full; a virtuous friend is difficult to find.

Yet now, through the roots of merit planted in past lives, we have obtained this human body with its six faculties intact, and furthermore, having encountered a virtuous friend, we have been able to hear the True Dharma.

Within this interval, each of us has nonetheless failed to exert ourselves with total diligence; I fear that in the future we shall sink long into myriad sufferings, with no time of escape in sight. For this reason, today—
With utmost sincerity, seek compassion and repent.
In a sutra, while the Buddha was walking with Ānanda and resting, he took some soil with his fingernail and asked Ānanda:
"Which is more, the soil on my fingernail or the soil of the great earth? Ānanda replied: "The soil on your fingernail is but a tiny fraction."

"Extremely so. The soil of the great earth is infinite. The Buddha said, "Those who obtain a human body are like the soil upon a fingernail; those who lose a human body are like the soil of the great earth.
Furthermore, it is said that when the Buddha was traveling, he happened to arrive at Kacangalā (Kakuda-vana) and took some soil there to provide this same analogy.
Alas! We and the multitude, upon hearing this single phrase regarding the difficulty of obtaining a human body, should immediately—

One should give rise to great fear, with shame and remorse intersecting in one's heart. Throughout the two periods of six watches of the day and night, one should contemplate: by what dharma was this human body obtained?
Only in this way does one begin to correspond with the method of repentance. The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states:

"If the five precepts are not observed, the path to the realms of humans and devas is cut off; if the five precepts are firmly upheld, humans and devas are joined. It is precisely at this point that it lies."

Be careful not to treat this with negligence. That one has now obtained a human body so difficult to find, and that one is now hearing the Buddha-dharma so difficult to hear, is entirely due to the spiritual resonance of past virtues.
You should give rise to joy and gratitude, and must apply yourself with total sincerity, diligence, and supreme reverence.
Do not allow yourself to become lax or indolent, thereby inviting the various faults and transgressions described below.

Be cautious. The preceding section briefly clarified the causes for the arising of obstacles; the confession is now complete. The following section extensively enumerates the causes for the arising of obstacles and performs a thorough confession.
These causes all reside in the single phrase: "being unable to exert oneself with total sincerity and diligence."
This connects directly to the following text. Being unable to venerate with a sincere heart—down to the various faults and afflictions regarding the Triple Gem—none arise beyond this.
One shall see this for oneself upon encountering the text.
We, from time immemorial until this very day, have constantly had our minds shrouded by ignorance and our intentions obstructed by afflictions.
Thus, we were unable to show full-hearted reverence toward the images of the Buddhas, while instead despising sentient beings and harming our virtuous friends.
They destroy stupas and demolish monasteries; they burn sutras and images; they shed the blood of the Buddha.

Or, while dwelling themselves in magnificent halls, they place sacred images in lowly and filthy locations, subjecting them to smoke and sun, wind, rain, and dew, defiling them with dust and dirt, and allowing them to be damaged by sparrows and rats.
They live and sleep together with these images without ever showing them reverence; or they remain naked before the images, never decorating them or providing any protection.
To cover lamps and candles, to lock and shut temple buildings, and to obstruct the light of the Buddha—such transgressions as these, today with utmost sincerity, I repent them all.

First, regarding the karmic obstruction of being arrogant toward the Buddha: those who have been unable to venerate with a wholehearted respect [the Triple Gem]... [Regarding] people today toward the Triple Gem...
Before the images, they are unwilling to perform prostrations and offerings; this is precisely what is meant by "being right here. As for the burning of scriptures and images:

just as all printed Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, as well as those made of paper, are to be burned, so too, once the affairs of the ritual site are concluded, it is entirely inappropriate to cremate everything. Therefore, Yunqi [Zhuhong] prohibited its use in his religious regulations.
"One who sheds the blood of a Buddha" refers to those such as Devadatta who pushed down a mountain; likewise, those of today who scrape gold from the Buddha’s face are also [included].
Within the halls of flowers, lofty pavilions, and deep chambers, the lowly and vulgar are places of impurity.
"Dust" (*chen*) refers to obscuration. "Dun," "fu," and "weng" refer to the rising of dust; "fu-weng" describes the appearance of dust swirling upward. Regarding "reverence" (*li-jing*):
a single prostration to the Buddha extinguishes sins as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. For one who lacks reverence, how can they be free from karma?

"Nakedness" (*lu-lu*) means to have the body bare and exposed, with not even a thread of clothing hanging upon it. All such [conditions] arise because one is unable to exert oneself with a wholehearted diligence. Thus it reaches this point.
Thus it is; all subsequent cases are to be understood according to this pattern.
Furthermore, from time immemorial until today, one may have handled scripture scrolls with impure hands during the midst of the Dharma;
or, while facing the scriptures, have engaged in improper or worldly speech; or have placed them at the head of the bed, failing to show reverence when sitting or rising; or—
Opening and closing boxes and chests, [causing] insects to devour them until they rot and decay; or having the heads and shafts fall off, or the fascicles lose their order;

or having them torn, displaced, omitted, or erroneous, with the paper and ink shattered—having neither cultivated these for myself nor being willing to circulate them, I now, with utmost sincerity, repent of all such transgressions.
Next, the repentance for the karmic obstacles of minor offenses against the Dharma.
Regarding "the Dharma," this refers to the Buddha-dharma consisting of all the scriptures and teachings of the Tripitaka and the twelve divisions of the canon.

As for "impure hands," whenever one has not yet washed or combed oneself in the early morning, or after performing the functions of nature, or even when handling any defiled objects, in all such cases, one should...
Washing and rinsing: if one does not wash and rinse, it is collectively termed "impurity. One must use pure water to wash one's hands before being permitted to hold sacred scriptures.
Therefore, there are verses and mantras for washing the hands within the teachings that explain this in detail elsewhere;

these are not cited here. Regarding "unlawful speech" (*adharma-vāk*) and so forth: this refers to intermittent talk, miscellaneous chatter, and even vulgar or coarse conversation. All such things [are to be avoided].
This is improper, colloquial language. The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Wherever this scripture resides, there is a Buddha present.
Since you do not show it respect, how can you be without fault? *Qiè* (篋) refers to a chest or box.

A single fascicle, or several fascicles grouped together, constitutes a "section" (*bù*); a complete set constitutes a "case" (*zhì*). "Disordered" (*shīcì*) means that the sequence has been inverted and lacks proper arrangement.
Furthermore, "omissions and errors" refers to what has been dropped or left incomplete. "Torn and broken" means that the characters and phrases are missing or damaged.

Regarding "transmission": it is called "transmission" (liuchuan) because it circulates among people; "chuan" (transmit) means to pass on. It is a continuous, endless circulation from one person to another.
Some listen to the sutras while sleeping on the ground; some recite them while lying on their backs; some speak aloud or laugh, thereby disturbing others who are listening to the Dharma.
Some misinterpret the Buddha’s words or provide perverse explanations of the Sage’s intent. They preach what is not the Dharma as the Dharma, and what is the Dharma as not the Dharma.

They declare non-offenses to be offenses, and offenses to be non-offenses. They describe light transgressions as heavy, and heavy transgressions as light. Some copy passages from the beginning and place them at the end, or copy passages from the end and place them at the beginning. At the beginning...
They place the later [teachings] within the middle, and the middle within the earlier and later. They employ flowery rhetoric to establish their own scriptures.

Whether for the sake of gain, reputation, or honor, they preach the Dharma to others without a heart of virtue and morality. They seek out the faults of Dharma masters to engage in debate, attacking them unreasonably.
They do not seek profound understanding or the supramundane Dharma, but instead treat the Buddha’s words with contempt while respecting false teachings.
To disparage the Mahāyāna and praise the path of the Śrāvakas—such transgressions as these are immeasurable and boundless; I repent them all.

This refers to the confusion of the Dharma. From "lying on the ground, sleeping face up" onwards, it refers to various forms of disorder and extreme irreverence toward the Dharma—that is, the true Dharma of both the mundane and supramundane worlds.
"Non-Dharma" refers to the false teachings of both the mundane and supramundane worlds.
The Dharma. ○ Regarding the six phrases on "teaching what is not the Dharma as being the Dharma," these are precisely the points where erroneous understanding and deviant explanations occur.

○ Even such statements as "Heaven is a false fabrication" and "Hell is not a true teaching," or "Alcohol and meat do not obstruct Bodhi," and "Lust does not hinder the True Nature," and so forth—all share the same intent as these:
they are instances of erroneous understanding and deviant explanation. ○ "Repetition" refers to the precepts.

Regarding the four *pārājika*, eight *pārājika*, ten *pārājika*, and so forth in the Vinaya, the "light" refers to the light offenses within the precepts, numbering from thirty-nine or forty up to forty-eight, etc.
The four phrases beginning with "abridgment" (*chao*) may be categorized according to the three levels of the aforementioned two categories of "light" and "heavy.
For example, in the Vinaya, the first section (*pūrvabhāga*) is the most serious; the middle section (*madhyabhāga*) is somewhat heavy and somewhat light.
The latter part is purely trivial. Those with false understanding have simply copied it; one can see how they have confused matters of gravity and lightness for future generations.
Let the wise examine this closely. ○ Regarding the embellishment of literary expressions to establish one’s own treatises:
this refers to being skillful at using dharma-discourse to adorn one's own views and then interpolating them into the scriptures. ○ Seeking the Dharma.
This is a transgression of the Master. To reach the point of praising the path of the *śrāvakas* is precisely for the sake of gain and reputation;
it is a state devoid of the mind of the Way and its Virtue. The *Compendium of Essential Passages from Various Sutras* (*Zhujing yaoji*) says:

"If one does not benefit sentient beings with a heart of compassion, but instead greedily seizes wealth and goods—whether by drinking alcohol, eating and drinking with women, or selling oneself to seek riches—such is the 'Dharma-giving' (dharma-dāna) of this kind."
The fruit is very slight. One is born among the devas as a wise bird capable of reciting verses;

this is called the inferior grade of the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*). If one preaches the Dharma to others for the sake of fame or to surpass other Dharma masters, the retribution obtained is likewise slight:
one is born among the devas and receives middling extraordinary rewards, or is born among humans; this is called the middling grade of the gift of Dharma.

Giving. If, with a pure mind, one practices the gift of Dharma for the sake of increasing the wisdom of sentient beings and causing them to abide in the True Dharma, rather than for the sake of wealth or profit—such a gift of Dharma benefits both oneself and others;

there is no person more supreme, and its merit remains inexhaustible even until Nirvana. This is called the superior grade of the gift of Dharma. As for being stingy regarding the Buddha-Dharma and being unwilling to give it...

To reveal [these things] to sentient beings and obstruct the wisdom-light of others, such that they are later reborn in remote regions where the Buddha-dharma does not exist, is still a transgression.
Furthermore, from beginningless time until today, one may have created obstacles within the Saṃgha or killed an Arhat.

They cause schisms in the Saṃgha; they harm those who have resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta; they sever the seed of the Buddha, causing the Noble Path not to flourish. Or they rob and strip practitioners of the Way;
they whip and torture śramaṇas, subjecting them to flogging and forced labor, or assailing them with harsh words and slander.
Or they violate pure precepts and corrupt dignified conduct; or they urge others to abandon the Eightfold Noble Path and instead accept and practice the five [wrong] dharmas; or they falsely...
I now repent of all such sins as these: assuming a physical form to spy upon and steal from the permanent [Dharma-body].
Next, I repent of the karmic obstacles of despising the Sangha. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "Devadatta was unable to harm the Buddha, so he sought to break the harmony of the Saṃgha.
The Buddha said to Devadatta: 'If one who has already caused a schism in the Saṃgha is able to reconcile it, that person shall attain birth in heaven.'"
O Deva, if one causes a harmonious Saṃgha to be divided, one falls into hell.

If one intentionally slanders a harmonious assembly of monks, creating schism—whether it be an Arhat, one who possesses the unsurpassed bodhicitta, or anyone who is a seed of the Buddha—one murders them, divides them, and harms them; therefore, this is called "annihilation."
"Buddha-seed" refers to those who possess the Way and virtue; thus they are called "Way-men" (*dàorén*). They are also of the same class as the *śramaṇas*.
In the *Pózhūmó jīng* (Sūtra on Destroying All Māras), the Buddha said: "There are three kinds of *bodhi*.
If a person, although having resolved upon *bodhicitta*, merely delights in self-benefit in seeking liberation, it is therefore called the *bodhi* of the *śrāvaka*."

Furthermore, although one has generated the bodhicitta, if one does not delight in practicing the Mahāyāna teachings but instead gives rise to the thought of contemplating all conditioned phenomena (*pratyaya-dharma*) and acts in accordance with what is thus observed, it is therefore called the enlightenment of a *pratyekabuddha*. Moreover, if there is another person...
Having generated the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, one further exhorts others to generate such a mind as well.
Without giving rise to weariness toward the body of saṃsāra, one desires to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings, causing them all to attain liberation.
Because one universally bestows one’s own merit and benefit upon all, it is called "unsurpassed bodhi."
This concludes the preceding section. The text is identical to that concerning the seven heinous offenses (*saptānantarya*), which may be understood accordingly. In Sanskrit, *arhat*;

here translated as "slayer of thieves," "worthy of offerings" (*dakṣiṇīya*), and "one who has attained non-arising" (*anutpāda*). These are the three titles. In Sanskrit, *śramaṇa* (also rendered as *sāmaṇa*, *samana*, etc.); here translated as "diligent in cessation.

This means to diligently cultivate precepts, meditative concentration, and wisdom, while ceasing and extinguishing greed, anger, and delusion, thereby gathering the mind and attaining the fundamental source.
"Originally, for this reason he was called a śramaṇa," and so forth. Regarding the "five dharmas prior to right view": these are the five worldly dharmas of nirvāṇa, namely:

worldly phrases (*loka-pada*), worldly bonds (*loka-bandhana*), worldly dharmas (*loka-dharma*), and worldly attachments (*loka-abhiniveśa*). These are termed the five dharmas of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
As for "peeping and spying," it refers to watching and waiting for an opportunity.
Or they expose their bodies, or enter with light clothing and undue haste before the scriptures and images; or they place impure feet upon temple halls and stupas;
or they enter monasteries wearing sandals or wooden clogs; or they spit and expectorate in the halls and rooms, defiling the grounds of the Buddhas and the Sangha;
or they ride in carriages or on horseback, jostling and colliding with the temple buildings—all such acts give rise to immeasurable karmic obstacles regarding the Triple Gem.
Boundary. Today, with utmost sincerity, I confess before the Buddhas of the ten directions, the Honored Dharma, and the Noble Assembly.
"Naked" (*lu-lu*) means to be bare-bodied; to have one's body exposed is called being naked. "Light clothing" (*qing-yi*) refers to small garments;

to wear small garments that are light and skipping about is called being intrusive (*tang-tu*). Furthermore, "intrusive" (*tang-tu*) is the same as *cong-tu*; it means to be disrespectful. A bhikṣu does not wear...
The three robes for prostration are also called "light robes. *Tángtū* refers to sandals; it is also the inner lining of footwear. *Jiè* (屐) refers to wooden clogs.
Furthermore, *lǚ* (履) refers to slipper-like sandals without heels, while *jiè* (屐) refers to foot-socks with a casing.

A sutra states: "Wearing clogs to see the Buddha, one will be reborn in the country of Horse Hooves (*Aśvavāra*). *Sanskrit: Saṃghārāma*; this is translated as "Garden of the Assembly" (*Zhòngyuán*). It refers to the pure assembly.
This is the place where they dwell. "To push and shove" refers to thrusting, jostling, and lightly brushing against one another.
May they, in birth after birth throughout all ages, always encounter the Triple Gem, honoring and revering them with never a moment of weariness.

May there be celestial silks and exquisite fabrics, necklaces of various jewels, hundreds of thousands of musical performances, rare and famous incenses, and flowers and fruits of brilliant clarity—all that exists in the world.
I shall always make offerings. If anyone attains Buddhahood, I will go first to entreat them to open the gate of ambrosia.
If they enter nirvana, may I always be able to present the final offering.

The upper part concludes the confession; the lower part concerns the making of vows to accomplish virtue, preaching the Dharma to deliver sentient beings, and thereby opening the gate of ambrosia (*amṛta*).
This is precisely the turning of the wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra-pravartana*). Ambrosia is named the medicine of immortality; by consuming it, one lives long and does not die.
By analogy, if one attains the Buddha-dharma, one immediately realizes the eternally abiding Dharma that is neither born nor extinguished; hence it is so called.

This is the "Cloud of Ambrosia. The "Gate" (Mén) carries the meaning of passage for both entry and exit, as it causes people to be born from birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and enter the Dharma-gate of the Buddha.

Regarding the "Presentation of the Final Offering": according to the *Jīnglù yìxiàng* (Heterogeneous Aspects of Sūtras and Vinaya), when the Buddha was about to enter *parinirvāṇa*, there was a son of a craftsman from the city of Kuśinagara named Cunda.
He wept and addressed the World-Honored One, saying: "From this day forward, we [shall have no more...]"
"Lord, there is no one to save us from our poverty and suffering. We wish to follow the Tathāgata and seek food for the future.
We pray only that you will compassionately accept our humble offering and then enter parinirvāṇa. The Buddha said, "I shall now eliminate your poverty for you.
With the rain of the unsurpassed Dharma, I shall drench the field of your body so that the sprouts of the Dharma may grow, and I shall cause you to be fully endowed with *dāna* (generosity)."
[The Buddha spoke of] the *pāramitās*. Cunda wept aloud and addressed the great assembly, beseeching them all together to pay homage and exhorting the Buddha not to enter *nirvāṇa*.
The Buddha told Cunda, "Such is the nature of the Buddhas' Dharma; so too is it with all conditioned things (*saṃskṛta*). Prepare quickly what you intend to offer; it is not fitting to delay.
At that time, devas and humans all came to present offerings, but the Buddha accepted none of them. The great assembly cried out, "Excellent! (Sādhu!)
"Cunda, you have accomplished great merit. Our offerings would otherwise have been in vain;

yet, because the World-Honored One wished to fulfill the hopes of the assembly, he manifested immeasurable Buddhas from each and every pore, and each of those Buddhas was accompanied by an immeasurable community of bhikṣus, all of whom received the offerings.
The Tathāgata Śākyamuni himself accepted the food offered by Cunda and partook of it."
It filled eight *shu*. By the Buddha’s supernatural power, it completely sufficed for the entire great assembly.
Within the community of monks, they cultivated the six points of harmonious respect, attained the power of mastery, caused the Three Jewels to flourish, and propagated the Buddha-way above.
To transform sentient beings below, there are six points of harmony:
first, harmony of body in dwelling together; second, harmony of speech in being without contention; third, harmony of mind in shared joy; fourth, harmony of precepts in practicing together;
fifth, harmony of views in shared understanding; sixth, harmony of benefits in equal distribution. To cultivate these six harmonies is—

One cannot attain respect [in this way]. Therefore, it is said that one cultivates the six points of respectful harmony (*ṣaḍ-abhivādanīyāni*). The statement that there is "nothing that is not respected" also carries this same meaning.
Regarding the various grave and light offenses committed toward the Triple Gem as described above, all should be repented; as for the remaining evils...
The upper part concludes the confession; the lower part concludes the preceding section by introducing the subsequent one.
Regarding "the remaining evils," this refers to those mentioned above which were not fully exhausted in the explanation; therefore, the term "remaining" is used again.
Now, following the sequence, we shall again perform repentance, continuing from what preceded to what follows, as it is said in the Sūtra:
"There are two types of brave men: first, those who do not commit offenses themselves; second, those who, having committed them, are able to repent."
Furthermore, there are two kinds of pure dharmas (*śukla-dharma*) that can eliminate the various obstacles for sentient beings: first, self-reproach (*hrī*), which is not committing evil oneself;
second, shame (*apatrāpya*), which is not causing others to commit it. One who possesses self-reproach and shame may be called a human being; if one lacks self-reproach and shame, one is not.
They are no different from birds and beasts. Therefore, today with utmost sincerity, we take refuge in the Buddha and perform repentance according to the Dharma.
This citation of the scriptural text is an exhortation to act in accordance with the Dharma. "Vigorous" refers to being diligent and self-reliant; "white" refers to purity.

"White" (śukla) refers to pure words. *The Perfect Interpenetration of Exoteric and Esoteric Teachings* states: "Regarding the merits of white dharmas (*śukladharma*), one need only possess the two qualities of shame (*hrī*) and remorse (*apatrāpya*).
These alone can eliminate all obstacles for sentient beings; without requiring wealth or treasures, these merits are spontaneously accomplished.
Therefore, they are called 'white dharmas. Furthermore, the two characters 'shame' and 'remorse' also carry the meaning of wisdom and faith."

From time immemorial until this very day, we may have believed in heterodox and inverted views, killing sentient beings and making offerings to *chi-mei*, *wang-liang*, ghosts, and spirits, hoping thereby to prolong our lives, yet in the end we were unable to achieve this.
Or we may have spoken falsely of seeing ghosts and feigned divine speech. We now repent of all such transgressions.
This is the confession of the characteristics of these perverse inversions. Below, all [faults] arise because of ignorance, lack of faith, and the absence of shame and remorse;
thus there exist various evils such as perverse inversions and the like. This connects directly to the following text.

Regarding the two phrases "if one lacks shame and remorse" [from above], which constitute the formal confession: *chimei* (魑魅) refers to the essence of aged objects and the monsters of mountains and marshes; *wangliang* (魍魎) is large...
The "Power Ghost" (Lìguǐ). If one hopes for longevity, one must know that not only will it not be attained, but furthermore, one will find it difficult to avoid the sufferings of hell.

As for those who falsely claim to see ghosts or feign divine speech—such as those who "summon the dead to capture ghosts," who weigh the fortunes of children and women through shamans, who open halls for spirit possession, or who summon spirits to speak incoherently—all such practices are of this nature.
The "Sinner" refers to the confession. The subsequent sections are the same.
Furthermore, from beginningless time until this day, one may have acted with arrogance and insolence, being self-exalting and conceited;

or, relying on one's lineage, one may have treated all others with contempt, looking down upon the lowly because of one's own nobility, or using strength to oppress the weak; or, one may have indulged in drinking and incited strife.

I do not avoid intimacy or distance; I remain muddled and intoxicated all day long, failing to recognize the honorable from the lowly. For such transgressions as these, I now repent them all. This is the sequential confession of arrogance.
"Arrogance" (*ābhimāna*) means haughtiness and insolence. "Dissolute" (*pramatta*) means unrestrained. Regarding "lineage" (*gotra*): it refers to a noble and superior clan;
to rely on one's own high status and to be self-exalting and conceited, etc. To treat others with contempt because of one's own nobility.
The two phrases [regarding] "the base" explain the preceding phrase "disrespect. The Sūtra states: "The transgressions of one who drinks alcohol are immeasurable.
If one holds a vessel of alcohol and gives it to another to drink, they shall be handless for five hundred lifetimes; how much more so if they drink it themselves?
How much more so if they cause strife and disorder, and so forth... even teaching others to drink constitutes an offense of a light defilement. [This concerns] drinking alcohol.
One commits thirty-six kinds of transgressions. The *Dazang yilan* states: being unfilial toward one’s parents;
treating elders with contempt; failing to revere the Triple Gem; lacking faith in the sutras and the Dharma; slandering śramaṇas; exposing the faults of others;
constantly speaking falsehoods to deceive people; spreading rumors of evil deeds; engaging in double-tongued speech and harsh words that wound others; and being the root cause of illness and strife.
The root of this is that one’s ill repute spreads abroad; people detest and loathe them. They reject and exclude the sages and worthies, bringing resentment upon Heaven and Earth.
They neglect their duties and squander their family wealth. Constantly devoid of shame and remorse, they know not how to feel abashed. Without cause, they beat their servants and slaves;
they recklessly kill living beings, commit adultery with the wives of others, steal the property of men, distance themselves from virtuous people, and associate with...

Associating with the wicked, constantly harboring anger and resentment, and being filled with grief day and night; being pulled eastward and dragged westward, held to the south and bound to the north;
falling headlong into ditches or lying by the roadside; falling from carts or horses; encountering rivers and drowning; holding lamps and losing them to fire;
perishing from the heat in the summer months, and freezing to death in the cold weather—these are the thirty-six kinds of loss.
Some indulge in food and drink without moderation; some eat raw fish and minced meat, or consume the five pungent herbs;

they defile scriptures and images with their foul odors and pollute the pure assembly with their presence. They act according to their own whims and desires, knowing no limits, distancing themselves from virtuous people while associating closely with evil friends.
I now repent of all such transgressions.
This is the "Repentance of the Manifestation of Impurities," which refers to indulgence in desires and cravings. Regarding delicacies: minced fish, raw minced fish, or pungent and stinking foods;
and the five pungent roots (*pañca-garaka*). The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states: first, garlic; second, leeks—that is, chives and scallions; third...

1. *Cicong* (慈葱) is the domestic onion (*gṛñjana*). 2. *Lancong* (蘭葱) is the small garlic (*laśuna*). 3. *Xingqiu* (興蕖) is the coriander (*hiṅgu*). These constitute the five pungent roots (*pañca-gandhaka*).
Regarding the consumption of pungent foods, there are five faults: first, they involve many transgressions; when eaten cooked, they arouse lust, and when eaten raw, they increase anger.

Second, the gods are distant; even if one is able to preach the Dharma, the various devas remain far removed. Third, the ghosts are near; the ghosts lick one’s divine essence (*śukra*), and one constantly dwells with ghosts.
Fourth, merit is exhausted; as one’s merit daily diminishes, there is no long-term benefit. Fifth, Māras gather;

Māras come to preach the Dharma, thereby reviling and destroying the prohibitions and precepts. Those who revile and obstruct the pure assembly are tainted by foul odors that defile all those observing the fast.
This is because [I have failed] to serve virtuous friends and the assembly.

Or perhaps I have been arrogant and hypocritical, stubborn and self-willed, defiant and aggressive, ignorant of human feelings, judging myself right and others wrong, and harboring vain hopes for fortune.
All such transgressions, I now fully repent.
These are the manifestations of violent and tyrannical conduct for which I repent: being conceited and full of self-importance due to one's talents;

feigning virtue and practicing deception through hypocrisy; being indolent and acting according to one's own whims with arrogance and self-will; being stubbornly self-assertive and displaying unrestrained audacity.
To act with arrogance and defiance is, in general, to mean non-compliance.
Whatever one obtains that is improper and received through unwarranted overstepping is called "fortuitous gain" (jiaoxing).
Or when facing wealth, they fail to yield; lacking integrity and a sense of shame, they live by slaughtering meat and selling liquor through deception and fraud.

Or they engage in lending at interest, calculating profits by the hour and selling their days for gain; they amass wealth with stinginess and parsimony, greedily seeking more without satiety. Receiving offerings from others, they feel neither shame nor remorse.
Or, lacking the virtue of the precepts, they pointlessly accept the faithful offerings of the laity. All such transgressions as these, I now fully repent.

This is the confession of the characteristics of greed and deception. "To slaughter" means to butcher; it means to kill. As for "butcher," it refers to one who cuts the flesh and knows whether a cow is large or small.
"To purchase" (in the context of *gu*) means to buy. The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states:

"If a child of the Buddha personally sells alcohol, teaches others to sell alcohol, or [participates in] the causes of selling alcohol, the conditions for selling alcohol, the methods of selling alcohol, or the karma of selling alcohol—this is the cause that gives rise to sin through such alcohol."

Regarding the causal conditions: if a Bodhisattva should give rise to the wisdom of clarity and penetration toward all sentient beings, yet instead gives rise to a mind of delusion and perversion toward them, this constitutes a *pārājika* offense. Regarding "income and expenditure with interest":

lending money at usury, calculating the principal and interest through accumulation, is called "income and expenditure with interest. The principal is the parent, and the interest is like the child; therefore [the term is used].
"Yun" means "to cease. Now, people of the world lend money at interest, claiming that the monthly rate does not exceed five percent;

this is called "selling the days by the hour," a form of accumulation through greed. Lacking the virtue of pure precepts, yet accepting the offerings of donors, one finds it difficult to digest such gifts of faith;
therefore, it is said that one "vainly receives the offerings of faith. [This leads to] lust, killing, and theft.
Drinking wine to the point of delusion, as well as the aforementioned behaviors such as showing no restraint regarding wealth and living by means of deception—
all these are collectively termed "lacking precepts and lacking virtue."
Or beating slaves and servants; driving menial laborers and officials without regard for their hunger or thirst, or their cold or heat;
or dismantling bridges and blocking paths—such transgressions as these, I now repent of them all.
This is the repentance for the manifestation of such cruelty:
whether through indulgence and self-indulgence, neutral mental wandering, playing games of chance and go, gathering in crowds, drinking alcohol, eating meat,
mutually harassing one another, engaging in aimless chatter, or discussing worldly affairs from year to year— thus wasting one's heavenly life in vain.
Day and night, throughout the first, middle, and last watches, they do not practice meditation or recitation, but remain indolent, lazy, and lie prostrate all day long.

They do not attend to their minds regarding the six objects of mindfulness (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*). Upon seeing the superior achievements of others, they immediately give rise to envy; harboring cruel and poisonous thoughts, they fully arouse the afflictions (*kleśa*).
This causes the fierce winds of various evils to blow upon the firewood of their transgressions, keeping it constantly ablaze without respite. (3)
Even the slightest wholesome karma is utterly consumed by this fire. Once all wholesome dharmas are exhausted, one becomes an icchantika and falls into the great hells with no prospect of escape.
Therefore, today we offer our most earnest prayers and prostrate ourselves before the Triple Gem of the ten directions to confess all our transgressions.
This is the confession of the manifestations of negligence: *Chupu* (chess/checkers) refers to gambling games; it is the equipment for wagering.
*Weiqi* (Go) was created by Yao, and Dan Zhu excelled at it. Regarding alcohol: Yi Di created *jiu-lao* (fermented liquor), and Du Kang created *shu-jiu* (rice wine). Regarding the eating of meat:
The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states that it severs great compassion and constitutes a minor secondary offense (*laghu-āpatti*). Furthermore, regarding eating...
There are ten faults of eating meat. As stated in the *Lan-yi*: First, all sentient beings have been one's own kin since beginningless time.
Second, when sentient beings see a meat-eater, they are immediately struck with fear. Third, it destroys the faith of others. Fourth, it causes the mind of compassion to become thin and diminished.
Fifth, it increases the habitual tendencies of a malevolent rākṣasa. Sixth, it prevents the practice of incantations and arts. Seventh, [it harms] sentient beings...
One's body and life are no different from oneself. Eighth, one is distanced from the worthy sages of the heavens, while evil spirits cause terror.

Ninth, it is produced from impurity. Tenth, at death, one falls into the evil realms. "To disturb" means to confuse or to agitate. "To bid farewell" refers to a banquet for those departing on a journey. Regarding the "beginning, middle, and end":
those who seek supreme bodhi should appropriately practice meditation and recitation with diligence day and night.
One must be diligent; it is not permissible to be idle for even a moment and thus let [this opportunity] go to waste. Therefore, the *Śālistamba Sūtra* (Yijiao jing) says:
"You bhikṣus, by day you should diligently cultivate wholesome dharmas so as not to miss the proper time. During the first watch and the last watch of the night..."
Do not allow these practices to fall into neglect. In the middle of the night, recite the sutras to regulate yourself.
Do not, on account of sleep, let this one life pass in vain without attainment. As for "Chan" (禪), it is a Sanskrit term, *dhyāna*, which here means "tranquil stillness.

It refers to stilling discursive thoughts, forgetting external conditions, investigating the nature of one's own mind, and suddenly awakening to the principle of non-arising; this is what is currently called "investigating Chan" (*chánzhen*).

"Recitation" refers to such acts as the holding of mantras, the recitation of sutras, and the mindfulness of the Buddha. Because one does not cultivate these practices, one falls into the two maladies of torpor and distraction.
Within the cycle of birth and death, is this not to waste one's natural lifespan in vain and to pass the years and months to no purpose?
○ "Seeing the superior deeds of others" refers to such matters as the mindfulness of the Buddha, the practice of Zen meditation, and the holding of recitations. (6)
As for mindfulness: mindfulness of the Buddha is to regard him as the compassionate teacher; mindfulness of the Dharma is to regard it as the mother of the Buddhas of the three periods of time;

mindfulness of the Sangha is to regard them as the field of merit for humans and devas; mindfulness of the heavens is to seek long life and peace; mindfulness of the precepts is to purify body and mind;
mindfulness of giving is to universally relieve poverty. These are the six recollections. One whose mind does not attend to these matters will become lax in this practice.
Negligence. One can know that there is no awakening whatsoever. Evil karma belongs to wind; afflictions and anger belong to fire.
Because they are fanned by the winds of accumulated habitual karma, the fires of sin blaze fiercely, burning away the path to Bodhi. Therefore it is said: "All are consumed by fire.
Regarding "slight goodness in the three karmas": the various evils mentioned above do not exceed the ten non-virtuous actions and so forth.
The slight goodness found today does not go beyond the five precepts and ten wholesome acts. Because evil overcomes this slight goodness, it is said that "both are consumed by fire.
This is precisely the harm wrought by the affliction of envy. *Icchantika* in Sanskrit means "one whose wholesome mind has fallen away," and is also called "one who lacks faith."
All the various transgressions I have committed in the past—whether light or heavy, coarse or subtle;
whether committed by myself, incited by others, or rejoiced in by me;
whether committed through the coercion of force or even by praising those who practice unwholesome dharmas—I now, with utmost sincerity, confess them all.
This summarizes the preceding text. As for all other karmic offenses, one should again earnestly seek repentance and disclose them.

May, by virtue of the merit arising from this repentance of all evils, one be compassionate and harmonious, loyal and filial, humble and patient, know propriety and possess a sense of shame throughout every life, and first inquire after others' welfare, cultivating goodness, correctness, prudence, purity, and righteousness.
May they distance themselves from evil friends and constantly encounter virtuous conditions. May they restrain the six sense-faculties and guard the three karmas.
May they endure toil and suffering with a mind that never retreats, establishing the vow for Bodhi and not failing sentient beings.
Having made these vows, I take refuge in and pay homage to all Buddhas.
The preceding general confession is hereby concluded. May I, by virtue of this, attain the virtues of the vows:

from "benevolence and harmony" to "ultimate righteousness and yielding," these are worldly dharmas; from "far removed" to "sentient beings," these are supramundane dharmas. Below is the conclusion of the confession.
The Sūtra says: "Be humble toward all bhikṣus and remain far removed from a mind of self-exaltation. The Way arises from modesty and withdrawal; virtue arises from tranquility and harmony.
Thus it is said. To know shame is to be close to courage; the meaning of this also lies therein. To cultivate goodness, correctness, and prudence;
to cultivate compliance with the guidance of the virtuous; to give rise to no heart of opposition or resentment; to be upright, prudent, and dignified—to understand [this] is [the Way].

It means being free from indulgence in passions, partiality, and crookedness. "Evil friends" refers to those who practice the ten unwholesome deeds; "wholesome conditions" refers to the practices of the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions.
"Turning the light back to reflect within" means gathering the mind and returning to the truth; hence the phrase "gathering and collecting," etc.

The "six feelings" (liùqíng) refer to the consciousnesses of the six faculties—eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—which are called the six feelings; they are categorized as consciousness and emotion.
This is because it gives rise separately to craving, attachment, and so forth. "Hàn" (捍) refers to the meaning of courageous and vigorous diligence (*vīrya*).
If one looks at the text according to its structure, the middle fascicle should conclude at this point, as the repentance for karmic obstructions (*karmāvaraṇa*) has been completed.
Homage to Vairocana Buddha. Homage to our Original Teacher Śākyamuni Buddha.
Homage to Amitābha Buddha. Homage to Maitreya Buddha. Homage to Nāgottamarāja Buddha. Homage to Nāgeśvararāja Buddha.
Homage to Ratnasaṃbhava Buddha. Homage to Bodhimaṇḍitaviśveśvararāja Buddha. Homage to Kāṣāya...
Dhvaja Buddha. Homage to Siṃhanāda Buddha. Homage to Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva.

In the *Ratnakūṭa-mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā*, it is said: "May it be my vow that when I attain Buddhahood, the worlds of all Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges shall become a single buddha-field named 'Universal Vision' (*Samantadarśana*).
The bodhisattvas then said: "The buddha-field attained by Mañjuśrī is equal to that of Maitreya..."
"Is it equal to the adornments of Amitābha Buddha’s buddha-field? The World-Honored One replied:
"Suppose, for example, there were a person who split a single hair into one hundred parts, and with one part took a single drop of water from the great ocean.

That drop would represent the adornments of Amitābha Buddha’s buddha-field, while the waters of that great ocean would represent the adornments of Samantadarśin Buddha’s buddha-field—and even more than that."
Homage to Samantabhadra Bodhisattva. Homage to Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva. Homage to Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva.
Homage to Mahāvyūha Bodhisattva. Homage to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.

Having paid homage to all the Buddhas, one next performs repentance. Previously, the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) has been repented of, and the obstacle of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*) has been repented of;
the remaining obstacle of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*) shall now be set forth and repented of in due order.
The confession of the karmic obstacles of afflictions is hereby completed. Regarding the confession of the obstacle of karmic retribution at this point:

among these retributions, there are those of the hells, animals, hungry ghosts, and asuras; furthermore, there are immeasurable other retributions within the realms of humans and devas—all of which constitute karmic retribution.
From here, one shall perform confession sequentially for each of them in turn.

The Sūtra states: "When the retribution of karma arrives, there is no place—neither in the void nor in the midst of the ocean, nor by entering a mountain city—that can provide a refuge from which one may escape without receiving the retribution. Only through the power of repentance can it be eliminated."

This citation from a sutra is provided to offer encouragement. The *Catuḥ-bhrātṛ-sūtra* states: Four brothers studied the path of the immortals and attained the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
When their past karmic retributions arrived and they realized their lifespans were ending, each of them thought to use their supernormal power of flight to soar away.
Wherever they went, they were unimpeded. Each, by means of their supernormal powers, avoided death in their own way: one leaped into the air and concealed his form;
one entered the marketplace where there was no place for many people to search;

one entered the great ocean, traveling three million three hundred and sixty thousand *li* without reaching the bottom, remaining within its depths; and one split open a mountain to hide his form within the rock.
In leisure, he considered that the counterpart of impermanence could not be sought out from anywhere, for death is unavoidable for all hereafter.
Those who enter the void die and fall to the earth like ripe fruit falling; those who enter the marketplace die amidst the crowds;
those who enter the sea die to be devoured by fish and turtles; those who hide in the mountains die to be eaten by birds and beasts. The Buddha, having observed and known this, [taught accordingly].
This refers to these four people who, wishing to abandon their past karmic conditions, have not yet eliminated the three poisons; how can they find peace and liberation from this affliction?
How do we know this is so? When Śakra Devānām-Indra manifested the five signs of decline, his heart was overcome with fear, and he took refuge in the Triple Gem with sincere devotion.

The five signs will then vanish, and one shall attain an extended lifespan. Such instances as these are clearly elucidated in the sutras and teachings; their occurrences are not limited to a single case.
Therefore, we know that repentance truly has the power to extinguish calamities.
This refers to a single instance used as a verification. The *Avadāna-sūtra* states: There was a Śakra-devendra whose five celestial virtues had departed from his person;

knowing for himself that his merit was exhausted, he was filled with great sorrow. He thought to himself, "Within the three realms, there is only the Buddha who can rescue beings from suffering and calamity.

He went to the place where the Buddha was, at which time the Buddha was sitting in meditation, having entered the Samādhi of Universal Salvation (*Sarvasattva-paritrāṇa*). The Great Emperor paid him homage.
Prostrating himself on the ground, he took refuge with a sincere heart in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Holy Sangha.

Before he had even risen, his life suddenly departed, and he was reborn as a son within the womb of a mother donkey at a potter’s workshop. At that time, the donkey broke loose and ran among the clay vessels, trampling and destroying the unfired pottery.
Her master beat her, and she immediately suffered a miscarriage. His spirit returned once more and became a Heavenly King. Thus spoke the Buddha.
The Samādhi-awakening praised him, saying, "Excellent! That at the moment of death you took refuge in the Triple Gem—your karmic retribution is now exhausted, and you shall no longer suffer.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the stage of Srotāpanna.

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that there are five signs of decline for the devas: first, the flowers upon their heads wither; second, sweat breaks out from their armpits; third, their robes constantly...
1. Defilement; 2. Foul odor from the body; 3. Dislike for one's own seat. These are the five great signs of decay that indicate certain death.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharmakośa* states: 1. The fragrance of one’s clothing vanishes; 2. The bodily radiance suddenly extinguishes; 3. Water droplets cling to the body after bathing; 4.

One’s natural disposition becomes agitated and restless; 5. The two eyes twitch and roll. These are the five minor signs of decay; if one encounters superior conditions, they may still be resolved, and thus do not necessarily signify death.
This is a sign. That he has now been granted an extension of his celestial years must surely be due to the minor five signs of decay (*pañca-kṣaya*). Śakra-devānām-indra is none other than Śakradeva.
Thus, one should know that from the section on repentance until the end of the text, it is all intended to exhort and inspire future generations.

One must certainly recognize for oneself that one's karmic obstacles are heavy and profound; one must resolutely repent to extinguish them, thereby avoiding the calamity of regret that is difficult to remedy later.
However, if ordinary persons do not encounter the guidance and encouragement of virtuous friends, there is no evil they will not commit, which leads to this state.
When one's great life is about to end, at the moment of ultimate exhaustion, the evil manifestations of hell all appear before one.
At that time, remorse and fear arrive together. Having failed to cultivate goodness in advance, one only repents when facing the end. What can be achieved by repenting later? It will be of no avail.
Calamities and misfortunes await in different places; they lie in wait in advance. One must proceed alone into the realm of hell;

one can only press forward into the fiery cauldrons, where body and mind are shattered and the spirit suffers agony. At such a time, if one wishes to seek even a single prostration or a single confession, how could it ever be possible?
This is raised as a report to warn those who are deluded. "To encourage" means to exhort; "to praise" means to extol, and it also implies to assist.
"To guide" means to lead; "to initiate" means to enlighten. "To exhaust" means to reach the ultimate limit. "Calamity and misfortune" is synonymous with disaster.

Regarding "different places," it means that the retributions vary according to the lightness or gravity of the offenses. Even before a person’s life has ended, the underworld has already pre-allocated their karma from this lifetime.
It is clear that the retribution for sinful karma awaits in advance. "Ssu" (宿) means "of old"; "yu" (預) means "in advance.
"Yen" (嚴) means to prepare with solemnity to await the arrival of the sinner. "Ch'ü" (趣) means "swiftly," and it also implies "urgency" or "compulsion.
"Po" (鑊) refers to a large cauldron or cooking vessel. A "fire-cauldron" (huo-po) is precisely the location of the hells. The following section serves as an exhortation to inspire future generations.
Furthermore, you all must by no means rely upon your prime youth, your wealth, treasures, or power, nor indulge in indolence, laziness, or self-indulgent negligence.
When the suffering of death arrives, it makes no distinction between old and young, poor and rich, noble and humble; it utterly destroys all and comes suddenly.
Do not let others know of it. For human life is impermanent, comparable to morning dew; though the outgoing breath may still remain, the incoming breath is difficult to preserve.
Why then do you neglect this and fail to repent?
This says that human life is impermanent; it truly means that one only regrets when facing the ultimate end.

When regret reaches a point where it can no longer avail, one must know that impermanence is swift and the timing of birth and death is uncertain. When impermanence suddenly arrives, there will be no time to repent.

Taking advantage of this present state of health, one should rightly apply oneself with diligence. By no means should you console yourself with the thought that you are still young, thereby leading to later regret.
An ancient sage once said: "Do not wait until old age before you study the Way; the solitary graves are all but the young.

and (5) the deluded grasping of it as a horse. The five factors regarding phenomena (*dharma*) are: 1. The basis of phenomena, which is the mind-only (*cittamātra*). 2. If one is not careful, suddenly one day one will personally encounter such matters; will one then not feel regret?
This is called "Heavenly Bliss with an End. In Sanskrit, *Subhadra*; this means "Good Virtue" (*Hǎoxián*) in Chinese, and "Excellent Sage" (*Shànxián*) in the language of Táng.
In Sanskrit, *Udraka Rāmaputra*; this means "Fierce Joy" (*Měngxǐ*), or alternatively "Ultimate Joy.
It is the name of a seer (*ṛṣi*). Regarding the karmic retribution of Udraka Rāmaputra, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The seer Udraka."
Having attained the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), he flew to the royal palace. The king’s consort received him by touching his feet in prostration.

As soon as her hand touched him, he lost his supernormal powers. He requested a carriage from the king and departed, whereupon he again cultivated the five supernormal powers with single-minded devotion.
However, the birds’ chirping disturbed his mind. Next, he went to the water’s edge to seek meditative concentration, but again he heard the fish fighting;

he immediately gave rise to anger and said, "I shall kill every one of these fish and birds. After a long time, this man attained concentration and was reborn in the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Later, when his lifespan there ended, he descended to be reborn as a flying weasel (*bi-li*) as retribution, killing various fish and birds and committing immeasurable sins.
Falling into the three evil realms is like the skill of a wildcat: it can only kill fish;
now, as a flying wildcat, it kills even birds to carry out its evil, thereby causing it to fall into the evil realms. One must be cautious regarding even a single thought of anger!
"Holy fruit" refers to the supreme, wondrous fruit of *nirvāṇa*. "Infant" means to receive; it also means to touch.

This uses the minor sufferings of worldly affairs as a metaphor for the great [sufferings]. Even when facing the minor sufferings of the bustling government offices, one knows they are to be feared;
yet when compared to the immeasurable manifold sufferings of hell, one does not fear them and fails to cultivate goodness beforehand.
Is this not extreme folly? Is this not a greater error? Is it not terrifying? Is it not fearsome? Below, the assembly raises their voices in lamentation.
The above has been a general statement that the retribution for transgressions is inevitably unavoidable; therefore, one must rely on the power of repentance to effect its eradication.

This suffering urges one to abandon sinful retribution. It is said that among human beings there is none who is without sin;

Therefore, with utmost sincerity, we seek compassion and repent.

What are the six retributions? For all sentient beings, the evil retributions summoned by the karma created through the six consciousnesses emerge from the six sense organs.

First is the retribution of sight, which draws forth evil fruits. When this karmic activity of seeing intersects with other factors, at the moment of death one first sees fierce fires filling the ten directions;
the deceased’s spirit and consciousness fly downward and, riding upon smoke and fire, enter the Avīci Hell.
In the hells, two types of perception are revealed: first, clear vision, in which one sees various evils and gives rise to immeasurable fear;
second, dark vision, in which one perceives nothing in silence and gives rise to immeasurable dread. Such visions of fire can, when burned upon the ears, become boiling cauldrons and molten copper;
when burned upon the breath, they become black smoke and purple flames; and when burned upon the sense of taste, they become scorched pellets and iron gruel.
The burning sensation can turn [the body] into hot ashes, stoves, and charcoal; the burning of the mind can cause sparks to scatter and fly. Second is the hearing of retribution.
When this hearing karma intersects, at the time of death, one first sees the heavens and earth submerged in waves.

The consciousness then rides these currents into the Avīci Hell, manifesting two signs: first, when opening the ears to listen, there is all manner of clamor and confusion; second, when closing them...
Listen: when silent, there is nothing heard. Thus, when the wave of hearing pours forth, it can become censure and interrogation;
when sight pours forth, it can become thunder and poison; when breath pours forth, it can become rain and insects; when taste pours forth, it can become pus and filth;
when touch pours forth, it can become beasts and ghosts; when thought pours forth, it can become lightning and hail.
It crushes the heart and soul. Third is the retribution of smelling. When this karma of smelling intersects, at the time of death, one first perceives poisonous vapors filling the consciousness.
These surge from the earth and enter the Avīci Hell, manifesting two signs: first, the "open hearing," where foul odors suffocate the mind;
second, the "blocked hearing," where the senses are obstructed and one falls into a state of stupor. Such is the retribution of smelling that assails [the dying person].

When it encounters the breath, it can become a solid substance or a foot-covering; when it encounters sight, it can become fire or a torch; when it encounters hearing, it can become drowning or submersion;
when it encounters taste, it can become hunger or a refreshing flavor; when it encounters touch, it can become a tear or a rotting corpse;
when it encounters thought, it can become ashes or a miasmic fog. These four are the retributions of taste. When these karmic conditions of taste intersect, they manifest at the moment of death.

At the time of death, one first sees an iron net completely covering [the body]. The consciousness descends through it and becomes suspended in the net, hanging upside down as it enters the Avīci Hell.
Two manifestations arise: first, when inhaling, ice forms and cracks; second, when exhaling, fire burns and causes putrefaction. Thus one experiences these flavors;
