However, when metal and stone are encountered through hearing, they can become sharp weapons; when encountered through breathing, they can become a great iron cage;
when encountered through touch, they can become bows and arrows; and when encountered through thought, they can become a rain of glowing iron.
These are the five types of retribution for touch. When such karmic contact occurs, at the time of death, one first sees four mountains closing in from all sides, leaving no way out.
The conscious spirit is driven into the Avīci Hell, where two kinds of manifestations arise: first, contact through conjunction, wherein mountains press against the body;

second, contact through separation, wherein the body and mind are butchered and torn asunder. Through such contact by conjunction, when experienced through touch, it becomes a crushing press or a grinding mill;
when experienced through sight, it becomes burning and heat; when experienced through hearing, it becomes the clashing and striking of blows. When experienced through...
When one ceases [to breathe], it can result in being tortured and bound. When one experiences [sensations] through the body, it can result in being plowed and shackled.

When one experiences [sensations] through thought, it can result in being seared and roasted. These six are the retributions of thought. When these thoughts and karmic actions intersect, at the time of death, one first sees a violent wind blowing away the spiritual consciousness;
blown upward into the void, it swirls and falls back down into the Avīci Hell, manifesting two signs.
First is lack of awareness: one wanders wildly in extreme delusion. Second is non-delusion: if one awakens to it, there is suffering. Such is perverse reflection.

When reflection is bound, it can become the directions and the objects [of perception]. When views are bound, they can become the mirror and the witness. When hearing is bound, it can become ice and frost.
When breath is bound, it can become the fiery chariots and fiery enclosures [of hell]. When tasting is bound, it can...
Crying out and wailing, they undergo transformations into large and small forms; within a single day, they die ten thousand times and are born ten thousand times.
These are called the ten causes and six effects of hell, all of which are created by the deluded ignorance of sentient beings and are the retributions summoned by their own karma.
Next, one further repents of the retribution for the shedding of body and head in the Hell of the Mountain of Knives and the Forest of Swords;

one repents of the retribution for being burned and boiled in the Hell of Cauldrons of Boiling Water and Furnaces of Burning Charcoal; and one repents of the retribution for being scorched in the Hell of Iron Beds and Copper Pillars.
Repent of the retribution for the sins of the "chariot-fire" hell and the "splitting gravel" hell. Repent of the retribution for the agonizing pains of the "tongue-pulling" and "plowing-field" hells.
As for the "sword-mountain" and other such hells, these are likewise the results summoned by the habit of anger among the ten habits. And so forth.
As for "embers," these are also what is summoned and experienced through the fire within the sixfold mutual retribution.
As for "gravel," it refers to small stones; it carries the sense of being ground to pieces.
I repent for the karmic retribution of the Iron Ball and Molten Copper Hell, where the five internal organs are consumed and rotted away.

I repent for the karmic retribution of the Iron Grinding Hell, where bones and flesh are ground into dust. I repent for the karmic retribution of the Black Rope Hell, where limbs and joints are severed and torn apart.

I repent for the karmic retribution of the Ash River and Boiling Excrement Hells, where one suffers from distress and suffocation. I repent for the karmic retribution of the Salt Water and Cold Ice Hells.
The retribution for the sin of being naked and frozen involves the skin of the hells splitting open.
"The five internals" refers to the five viscera. As for "ashes and powder," they are dragged with ropes, following the worldly custom of dismembering a corpse.
I repent for the retribution of the crimes of mutual slaughter and harm committed in the hells of jackals, wolves, hawks, and dogs.

I repent for the retribution of the crimes of mutual grappling, seizing, hacking, and stabbing committed in the hell of weapons and clawed talons. I repent for the retribution of being roasted on spits in the hell of fiery pits.
I repent for the retribution of my offenses that result in the body being shattered like two stones grinding against each other in the Crushing Hell (Saṃghāta).
I repent for the retribution of my offenses that result in being torn apart in the Black-Eared Crushing Hell (Kālasūtra).
Or, as a jackal may harm a dog, and a dog may harm a jackal, it is said they "mutually harm one another. As for "claws," this refers to the spurs of a rooster.
The talons of birds such as hawks and the spurs of roosters—indeed, any blade edge possessing a backward-pointing barb—is called a *ju* (spur).
Zhao Guanghan was skilled at employing the "hook-and-spur" (*gouju*) technique. A hook with a spur is compliant when swallowed but resistant when spat out;

it causes people to enter its mechanism without being able to escape, thereby using the hook to extract hidden intentions. It is used for seizing with the hands, striking, hacking, and cutting with a blade.

"Beating, seizing, hacking, and stabbing" are all descriptions of the states of suffering. "Kha-kha" (磕) is the sound of stones striking one another. As for the "Mass-Compressing" (*Saṃghāta*) and "Black-Eared" (*Kālakarṇī*) hells:
in some, various objects are pressed together, and the ears and eyes are shrouded in darkness; furthermore, there is the agony of being sawn apart and scraped with knives.

I repent for the retribution of being hacked and minced in the Dark and Obscure Flesh Mountain Hell. I repent for the retribution of being sawn apart and nailed to the body in the Hell of Fragmentation.
I repent for the retribution of being butchered and sliced while suspended upside down by iron clubs in the Hell of Hanging.
I repent for the retribution of grievous anguish in the Burning Heat and Screaming Hells. I repent for the long, dark night of oblivion between the Great and Small Iron Ring Mountains.
Unaware of the retributive offenses regarding the Three Luminaries, I repent for the Apapa Hell,
the Ababa Hell, the Atata Hell, and the Alala Hell.
From the highest to the lowest, throughout the various hells, beings undergo such sufferings;

that each of these differs from the others is entirely due to the ox-headed jailers, horse-faced yakṣas, and their like, who, by means of their great power, pursue, drive, and coerce them into such states.
Nevertheless, all of this is summoned and experienced through the karmic power of sentient beings themselves; it is fundamentally not the work of the gods.
Descending [into hell] is not caused by others; one must know this for oneself and not remain self-deluded.
○ *Papo boba tātā rala*. These are the sounds of those enduring the cold within the Cold Hells.
Thus, within all these eight cold and eight hot hells, there are further eighty-four thousand subsidiary hells (*kalāpaka-naraka*) that serve as their retinues.
This refers collectively to the aforementioned hells; the "eight hot" are the eight primary hells, and the Avīci is one of them.
Furthermore, because the Avīci Hell is so vast, it is called the "King of Hells. As for the eight cold hells: first, Arbuda;
second, Nirarbuda—these two are named after the blisters that form and split when the body is oppressed by the cold; third, Aṭaṭa.
Fourth, Hu-hu-pa; fifth, Hu-hu-pa. These three are named after the sounds produced by those suffering from cold and pain.
Sixth, Utpala; seventh, Padma; eighth, Mahā-padma. These three are named after the way their bodies split open like the three types of lotuses:
first, the blue lotus; second, the red lotus; third, the great red lotus. These constitute the eight.
The cold hells. [There are] eight hot hells, including the *saṃjīva* (Reviving), which refers to being cut, pierced, ground, pounded, blown upon, and revived;

second, the *kālasūtra* (Black String), which refers to being measured with black strings before subsequently being cut and sawed; third, the *saṃghāta* (Crushing), which refers to the arrival of various instruments of torture that crush and mangle one another;
fourth, the *raurava* (Wailing), which refers to the sound of piteous wailing produced when oppressed by manifold sufferings; fifth...

1. Great Crying (*Mahāraurava*): Being oppressed by extreme suffering, they cry out with great lamentation. 2. Heat (*Tapana*): Being tormented by heat that pervades the body, they undergo extreme suffering that is unbearable.
3. Intense Heat (*Pratāpana*): From within and without, both their own bodies and those of others emit fierce flames, which burn and harm one another.
There are eight Avīci hells. When experiencing the suffering of their retribution, both life and form are uninterrupted for five [periods].

Each of these eight hot hells has four gates, and each gate has four subsidiary hells, namely: the Pit of Hot Ashes (Kukūla), the Quagmire of Corpses and Excrement (Kuṇapa), the Forest of Razor-Sharp Blades (Kṣuramārga), and the River of Boiling Water (Vaitaraṇī).
Since one hell thus consists of sixteen [sections], the eight hells together comprise one hundred and twenty-eight.
Eighteen: all are called the *Utsada* (AUXILIARY HELLS). Connected to the eight great hells, they form one hundred and thirty-six seats.

Sentient beings wander therein; because their suffering increases upon their suffering, they are named *Utsada*. Committing the ten non-virtues and the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*) oneself brings about rebirth in the eight great hells.
Teaching others to commit such heinous crimes brings about rebirth in the sixteen *Utsada* auxiliary hells, numbering eighty thousand and so forth.

This refers to the Kumbhīpa (Pot) Hell. A brief account appears in the *Lianghuangchan* (The Imperial Repentance of the Liang Dynasty), though the eighty-four thousand varieties have not been fully detailed therein.
"To take as kinsmen" means to regard them as one's own kindred; this refers to those within the eight cold and eight hot great hells.
In total, there are one hundred and twenty-eight *yūtsaṅga* (auxiliary) hells.

Within all these various hells, there are further eighty-four thousand *kalpa* (sub-hell) compartments that correspond internally and externally to the great hells, each belonging to and interrelating with them.
Because these manifold sufferings combine to constitute the great hells, they are called "retinues" (*parivāra*). They correspond precisely to the small [hells] within the great hells.
The various hells combine to form them, much like a person has large or small retinues; yet these are not truly retinues.
Those within the various hells act as their masters, and those who serve as their retinues are so called because they are like attendants following a master.
Thus, they are termed "retinues."

Within this, there are the sufferings of transgression: the agony of roasting and boiling, flaying the skin and scraping the flesh, hacking the bones and pounding the marrow, extracting the entrails and pulling out the lungs—immeasurable sufferings that cannot be heard and cannot be described. *Namo Buddha*.

"Brushing" means scraping; it means sweeping. "Shaving" means scraping and shaving; both carry the sense of flaying and excising. ○ When it comes to repentance at this point, how could one not be struck with horror and feel defiled?
*Namo Buddha*. Moment by moment, thought after thought, prepare your provisions early and make an urgent reform so as not to incur such suffering.
These "provisions" are precisely the merit and wisdom that you cultivate. ○ Five hundred [years] among humans...
One human year constitutes a single day and night in the hells, and their lifespan there is one thousand such years.

Since beginningless time, as for the parents from whom we have taken birth—if even those who have committed only grave offenses have not known how many times they have undergone such suffering, this is already the case in these minor hells;
how much more so for King Avīci, where sixty small kalpas of the human realm constitute but a single day and night?
Their lifespan is twenty thousand years; what end can there be to their suffering?
There is yet an immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable duration of time that is difficult to describe fully—how one should not fail to feel deep regret!
If one does not prepare provisions in advance, nor swiftly reform with a sense of shame, the sufferings of hell await in solemn anticipation. How could one not lament this?
How unafraid! The Sūtra says: "Reciting the Buddha’s name even once extinguishes the grave offenses of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas.

When the Master of Repentance reaches this point in his narrative and chants "Namo Buddha," he does so with ultimate compassion, deeply pained by the fact that all sentient beings suffering within the hells are none other than those whose causes and conditions are rooted in beginningless evil karma. Thus it comes to pass...
This is so; however, it is not necessarily the case for everyone, nor is it necessarily so for myself from beginningless time.

Therefore, I offer this general prayer of mindfulness of the Buddha, confessing my faults with earnest supplication and seeking compassion through repentance. I pray that you will grant me the eradication [of these faults], that I may be free from all suffering and affliction, and attain the bliss of liberation.
Those who are here among us today may have been our parents throughout countless lifetimes since beginningless time, or all manner of our kinsmen and associates.
After we and they pass away, we may once again fall into such a hell as this.

Today, with cleansed hearts and earnest prayers, we prostrate ourselves, bowing our heads to the ground before the Buddhas of the ten directions and the Bodhisattvas of the great earth, seeking their compassion and repenting our transgressions.
May all these retributions for past offenses be utterly extinguished.

The above constitutes the recollection of suffering and the conclusion of the repentance for the retribution of the hells; hereafter follows the making of vows to leave suffering behind and attain happiness.

I vow that by virtue of the merit arising from this repentance for the retributions of the hells and other realms, may the iron city of Avīci be immediately shattered and entirely transformed into a pure land.
May the names of the evil paths and all other hells cease to exist; may all instruments of suffering be transformed into conditions for joy;

may the mountains of blades and trees of swords become forests of jewels; and may the boiling cauldrons and glowing coals be transformed into lotus blossoms where beings are born through miraculous transformation. [May the ox-headed jailers...]
They completely abandoned violence and cruelty, giving rise to compassion for all and harboring no evil thoughts.

The sentient beings in the hells were freed from the fruits of suffering and ceased creating further causes; they equally experienced peace and happiness as if in the third dhyāna, and simultaneously all gave rise to the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment.
Having finished the repentance, with a sincere heart, take refuge in and pay homage to the eternally abiding Triple Gem.
The sublime bliss detached from joy constitutes the third dhyāna. Among the pleasures of the human realm, none surpasses this. The "third dhyāna" refers to the heavens of the third dhyāna:
first, the Heaven of Limited Purity (Parīttaśubha); second, the Heaven of Immeasurable Purity (Apramāṇaśubha); and third, the Heaven of Universal Purity (Śubhakṛtsna). These three heavens—
There is no male or female, nor sexual desire; they take the joy of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) as their sustenance.

Therefore it is said that they no longer create causes, experiencing peace and happiness equally, as in the third *dhyāna*. "To give rise to the mind of the Unsurpassed Way" means to give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Regarding the Sanskrit term *anuttara* and so forth, in the language of China (Huayan), it means "Unsurpassed."
To the One Perfectly and Fully Enlightened.
Homage to Vairocana Buddha. Homage to our Original Teacher Śākyamuni Buddha.
Homage to Amitābha Buddha. Homage to Maitreya Buddha. Homage to Nāgottamarāja Buddha. Homage to Nāgeśvara Buddha.
Homage to King Buddha. Homage to Ratnashrī Buddha. Homage to Bodhikusumavijitāviśvarāja Buddha.
Homage to Kāshyapa-dhvaja Buddha. Homage to Simhanada Buddha. Homage to Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva.
Homage to Samantabhadra Bodhisattva. Homage to Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva. Homage to Kshitigarbha Bodhisattva. Homage to Mahāvibhūṣaṇa.
Bodhisattva! Homage to the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.

Having paid homage to all the Buddhas, I shall next perform repentance. Having already finished repenting for the retributions of the hells, I shall now repent for the retributions of the three evil realms.

Connecting the past and initiating the future: Below this, within the repentance for karmic retribution, are the retributions of the three evil paths—namely, the animal path, the hungry ghost path, and the asura path.
Together with the aforementioned hell path, these are called the four evil paths.
In the Sūtra, the Buddha said: "A person of great desire suffers much affliction because they seek many gains.
A person who knows contentment is peaceful and happy even when lying upon the ground. One who lacks contentment finds no satisfaction even while dwelling in heaven."
Yet when people of the world suddenly encounter urgent distress, they are able to relinquish their wealth without regard for its quantity;
they do not realize, however, that this body stands upon the edge of the deep pits of the three miserable realms, and that with a single breath not returned, it must fall into them.
This section on repentance reveals the suffering of those who seek much yet remain unsatisfied due to their stinginess; it is performed as a repentance on their behalf.
Here, the "three realms of misery" (san-tu) specifically refers to hell, hungry ghosts, and animals, for the meaning of the text does not pertain to the asuras.
Suddenly, a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) exhorted him to cultivate merit, so as to provide the provisions for wholesome dharmas in the future.
However, clinging to this stingy mind, he was unwilling to act accordingly.
Out of compassion for his suffering due to such transgressions, the spiritual friend came to exhort him to practice wholesome dharmas and cause that [stinginess] to be extinguished.

"Sin. Even the cultivation of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom, as well as the performance of various meritorious deeds, may all be called the provisions for wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃbhāra*).
For one to think thus is extremely foolish and deluded. Why is this so? In the sutras, the Buddha said that at the time of birth, one does not carry [anything with one]."
One comes with not a single coin, and one departs at death without carrying a single coin away. One exhausts the body through accumulation, resulting only in anxiety and distress;
it benefits oneself not at all, serving only the interests of others. With no goodness upon which to rely and no virtue to depend on, one’s life ends in falling into the various evil realms.
"Ji" (賫) means "to carry" or "to provide with provisions"; it refers to what is used while traveling on the path.

Since these things do not benefit oneself, even if they are one's own possessions, they still become the property of others. Because of stinginess and greed, one lacks goodness and virtue, and thus is reborn in the evil realms.
Therefore, today we take refuge in the Triple Gem and sincerely repent.

The preceding section, which generally clarifies the repentance for the karmic retribution of stinginess and greed, is now concluded. Below, the three paths are individually opened, and we shall proceed with sincere repentance in their proper order;
first, we repent for the realm of animals.
Next, I further repent for the retribution of ignorance within the realm of animals;
I repent for the retribution of bearing heavy burdens and pulling plows to repay past debts within the realm of animals;

I repent for the retribution of lacking autonomy and being hacked, pierced, slaughtered, and dismembered by others within the realm of animals; I repent for the realm of animals that are footless, two-footed, or four-footed.

The retribution for the offense of having many feet. I now repent for the retribution of being eaten by various small insects within the body hairs, feathers, scales, and shells of those born in the animal realm.
Thus, there are immeasurable karmic retributions within the animal realm;
today, with utmost caution, I repent for them all.
This is the repentance for the animal realm. Regarding the animal realm, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:

"If these sentient beings, due to their original causes, committed offenses by coveting material things, they will take form according to those objects upon encountering them; these are called 'strange ghosts. When the objects are exhausted and the retribution is finished..."
Born into the world, they mostly become owls; when their retribution is fulfilled, they become humans, yet remain mixed with the dull-witted.

Greed for sensual form is their transgression. Encountering wind, they take shape and are called *pātra* ghosts (drought spirits). When the wind dissipates and their retribution is exhausted, they are born into the world, mostly as omens of calamity;
when their retribution is fulfilled, they become humans, yet remain mixed with strange species. Greed and delusion are their transgression. Encountering animals, they take shape and are called...

They become *mehi* ghosts. When their retribution for animal existence is exhausted, they are born into the human world, mostly as members of the fox species. Once they have fully repaid [their debt] and become humans, they join the ranks of the commoners.
Through greed and resentment they commit offenses; encountering *gū* (poisonous charms), they take form as what are called "insect-poison ghosts.

When the *gū* is extinguished and their retribution is exhausted, they are born into the human world, mostly as members of the venomous species. Once they have fully repaid [their debt] and become humans, they join the ranks of the wolves. Through greed and obsessive memory...
Due to their offenses, they encounter decay and take form, being called *pishāca* ghosts. When their decayed and impoverished retribution is exhausted, they are born into the human world;

for the most part they become parasitic worms, and once their debt is repaid, they become humans. Combining with subtle elements due to the offense of greed and arrogance, they encounter vital energy (*prāṇa*) and take form, being called hungry ghosts (*preta*).
When that energy dissipates and their retribution is exhausted, they are born into the human world; for the most part they become food, and once their debt is repaid, they become humans.

When a person merges with the category of the supple (*róu-lèi*), and commits the offense of greed and deception, they encounter the obscure (*yōu*) and take form; this is called a *yàn-guǐ* (suffocating ghost).

When the obscure dissolves and retribution is exhausted, they are born into the human world, mostly as clothing. Once their debt is repaid and they become human, they merge with the category of the laboring (*láo-lèi*), and commit the offense of greed for light.
Encountering the refined (*jīng*), they take form; this is called a *wǎngliǎng-guǐ* (goblin). When the refined dissolves and retribution is exhausted, they are born into the human world.

For the most part, they are of the corresponding type; when their retribution is fulfilled, they become human beings. When combined with the category of literary texts, greed constitutes an offense. Encountering illumination, they take form and are called "ghosts who employ others.
When illumination ceases and retribution is exhausted, they are born into the world. For the most part, they are auspicious omens; when their retribution is fulfilled, they become human beings.
When combined with the category of luminous beings, greed constitutes an offense. Encountering a human being, they take form and are called "ghosts who transmit messages. Human beings...

When the retribution for past offenses is exhausted, one is born into the world of humans. For the most part, one follows the common herd; once the debt is repaid, one becomes a human being and joins the ranks of the enlightened.

Next, one repents for the karmic retribution of suffering from hunger and thirst within the realm of hungry ghosts for hundreds of thousands of myriads of years, never even hearing the names of water or grain.
One repents for the karmic retribution of hungry ghosts who devour pus, blood, excrement, and filth. One repents for the hungry ghosts.
When moving the body, all limbs and joints burn with fire as a retribution for past sins; I repent for the retribution of having a vast belly and a narrow throat as a hungry ghost.
Thus, regarding the immeasurable sufferings within the realm of hungry ghosts, I today bow my head in prostration and seek compassion, repenting for them all.
The confession for the realm of animals is concluded. Next is the confession for the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*).

Regarding the realm of hungry ghosts, as stated in the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*: "The karmic retribution of the perilous and evil realm of hungry ghosts arises from a mind of greed, envy, and deception toward others;
from hoarding and accumulation out of a desire for long-lasting wealth; and from the extensive accumulation of various evils by failing to practice giving to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas."

Furthermore, those who suffer from various illnesses, emaciation, blindness, or poverty, and when others come to beg from them, give rise to stinginess and envy, refusing to give, failing to perform meritorious deeds, and failing to observe the precepts—by these causes and conditions, they fall among the hungry ghosts.
Furthermore, if there are sentient beings who receive deposits from others but refuse to return them, they will be born in that place. First:
They dwell among human beings; if people travel at night, some may see them.
Second, five hundred yojanas beneath Jambudvīpa, there are those who dwell within the ocean and those who dwell on ocean islands. Their evil-path retinues are immeasurable in number.
Briefly stated, there are thirty-six types; here, seven or eight are cited. First, the Torch-Mouthed: from their mouths issue fierce flames, and smoke issues from their limbs and joints.
Second, the Needle-Throated: their bellies are as large as drums, while their necks are like needles;
their form is emaciated by suffering. Third, the Foul-Mouthed: the breath from their mouths is foul and evil, its stench unbearable to hear. Fourth, the Great Goitered: their necks...
1. They develop goiters and tumors, which they consume along with pus and blood. 2. Fifth are those with needle-hairs; their hair emerges like needles and pierces their bodies.
3. Sixth are those with stinking hair; the hair on their bodies is so foul and filthy that it is unbearable even to hear of its odor. 4. Seventh are those who obtain discarded food;
they fill their hunger with what people have cast away. 5. Eighth are those who obtain lost items; they can only eat things after they have been lost and are no longer of use. This lasts for one day.
One night [in the hells] is equivalent to ten years in the human realm; five hundred such years constitute one lifetime.
Those with "large bellies and narrow throats" refer to those like the "needle-throated drum-bellied" and the "flame-mouthed scorched-bodied"—they are of this very class.
Next, one further repents of the retributive offenses of flattery, arrogance, and deceit committed within the realms of all ghosts, spirits, and asuras.
One repents of the retributive offenses of carrying sand and bearing stones to fill rivers and dam up seas committed within the realm of ghosts and spirits.

One repents of the retributive offenses of devouring flesh and blood raw and undergoing such ugliness, committed by ghosts, spirits, rākṣasas, kumbhāṇḍas, and all other evil spirits. Thus, [the ghosts...]
Regarding all immeasurable and boundless retributions for sins within the Way of the Gods, today I prostrate myself before the Buddhas of the ten directions and the Bodhisattvas of the great earth,
seeking their compassion to repent so that they may all be completely extinguished.

Next, repent for the path of the asuras. Asura means "non-deva. Because in their previous causes, although they wished to obtain a celestial body, they did not believe in the power of right action and the field of merit.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Among the sentient beings of the desire realm, there are three grades of roots of goodness:
the superior grade results in the fruit of rebirth in the heavens; the middling grade results in the fruit of rebirth among humans; and the inferior grade..."

As for the retribution of the asuras: their fetters and latent tendencies are rooted in their very hearts, and their minds are largely crooked and devious; thus, it is extremely difficult for them to attain the Way.
Although the devas also follow after these fetters and latent tendencies, they possess a straightforward mind and believe in the Way.

Although the asuras resemble the devas, because they are close to the Way yet find it difficult to attain, they rank below humans. They are the enemies of the devas and are called *asura*. They rule over the realm of desire.
Within the realms, they can manifest transformation bodies of various sizes according to their will. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:

"There are four types of asuras. If they belong to the realm of ghosts and, through the power of protecting the Dharma, attain supernatural powers and enter into space, these asuras are born from eggs and are categorized within the ghost realm (*preta-gati*).
If they belong to the realm of devas but have fallen due to a decline in virtue, the places where they dwell..."
Adjacent to the sun and moon, these asuras emerge from wombs and are categorized within the human realm (*manuṣya-gati*).
There are asura kings who uphold the world, whose power penetrates all things and leaves them fearless, able to contend for authority with Śakra, Brahmā, and the four heavenly kings.
These asuras exist through transformation and are categorized within the celestial realm (*deva-gati*). Inferior asuras are born in the heart of the great ocean. At dawn—
They roam through the void and return to dwell in the waters at nightfall. These asuras arise from moisture and are categorized within the realm of animals (*tiryagyoni*).
The aforementioned asura kings reside at the base of the great ocean, by the side of Mount Sumeru;

the city where they dwell is named Prabhāvatī, measuring eight thousand *yojanas* in length and breadth. Their lifespan is five thousand years, where one day and night is equivalent to that of the human world.
In the fifth hundred-year period, there will be flattery and sycophancy. To speak with fawning words is called *yú* (flattery); to speak with insinuating words is called *chǎn* (sycophancy).

*Jiāo* means arrogance, indulgence, and unrestrained license. *Zhuà* means falsehood, hypocrisy, and guile. As for *rākṣasas*, they are ghosts that eat humans; they are also ghosts that devour vital essence (*jingqi*).
Within the human heart, there are seven drops of sweet water that nourish and sustain the spirit. If a ghost devours even one drop, [the person’s life is lost].
It causes people to suffer from headaches; at three drops, they faint; at seven, they die. One who maintains the mantra with a single-minded focus will immediately escape this calamity.
The Kumbhāṇḍa is a fearsome ghost.
I vow that by virtue of this confession of the retributions for [the karma of] animals and other such states, and the merit thereby produced, may I, in birth after birth and life after life,
extinguish the defilement of ignorance, recognize my own karmic conditions, possess the clear illumination of wisdom, and sever the body of the evil realms.
The confession of the three retributions above is completed. This is the merit of making vows to accomplish the Three Paths;
in extinguishing evil and generating goodness, one must necessarily enter through the method of confession. Because of ignorance and lack of wisdom, one receives the retribution of an animal body.
Now that wisdom has been attained, awakening in a single thought-moment, one can immediately sever the animal body of the evil paths and be reborn [in a higher realm].
In the good realms of humans and devas, once the defilements of folly have been removed and the retribution of the animal realm exhausted, one is either reborn in the heavens or among humans.
With the nature of wisdom opened and clarified, one personally recognizes the karmic conditions and the fruits of retribution, and will certainly not undergo the state of an animal again;
this is surely due to the merit of repentance, as one knows for oneself.

I vow that by the merit produced through this repentance for the retributions of hungry ghosts and the like, in birth after birth and life after life, may I forever be free from stinginess, greed, and the suffering of hunger and thirst,
and always partake of the nectar-like flavor of liberation. I vow that by the merit produced through this repentance for the retributions of spirits,
demons, asuras, and the like, in birth after birth and life after life, may I be upright and sincere without guile, remain free from the causes of wrong livelihood, and eliminate all ugliness.
A lowly fruit. It brings benefit and merit to humans and devas.
In Sanskrit it is called *asura*; here it is translated as "non-deva" (*fei-tian*), because while they possess the fortune of devas, they lack the conduct of devas.

It is also said to mean "those without wine," etc. Their forms are extremely ugly, and they constantly engage in battle with the various devas; however, because their strength does not prevail, they [only...]
Because of being bound. Furthermore, it is said that there are four types of those fully bound, as explained above.

[To act] for the sake of gain and offerings, manifesting extraordinary signs, or raising one's voice to display authority so as to cause others to feel awe and reverence—this is a state where the mind is largely crooked and deviant;

all such things are causes of wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*). Now, since one is straightforward and without guile, this constitutes the departure from the causes of wrong livelihood and the cultivation of right conditions.
Naturally, the fruit of ugliness is eliminated, and one obtains the retribution of physical excellence;
even regarding self-benefit and the benefit of others, one likewise attains such results through the power of the repentance method.
From this moment forth, until I reach the site of enlightenment, may I never again receive retribution in the four evil realms;
yet, for the sake of sentient beings, through the power of my vow, may I dwell therein with great compassion and without weariness.
The realms of hungry ghosts, animals, and asuras, together with the aforementioned hells, constitute the retributions of the four evil paths.

Below this, we repent for the residual karmic fruits remaining from the human and celestial realms after having already repented for the retributions of the three miserable states. Now, once again, we shall prostrate ourselves in earnest supplication to repent for the residual karmic fruits of the human and celestial realms; let us do so together.
Having received this lifespan in Jambudvīpa, though it is said to last a hundred years, those who complete it are few indeed.

Within that interval, those who meet with untimely death in their prime are immeasurable in number; there are only manifold sufferings that oppress both mind and body, such that sorrow, anxiety, fear, and dread never depart for even a moment.

Regarding the phrase "having already repented, etc.": this serves to introduce what follows from what precedes. We have collectively received these instructions, "etc.," concerning the division of repentance for past and present transgressions that shorten one’s life.
*Jambudvīpa*—more fully called *Dakṣiṇa-jambudvīpa*—is translated here as "Foul Tree. Those who meet with premature death in the prime of their years [are addressed herein].
This refers, for instance, to those who die prematurely in their youth. All such cases are the retribution for having committed karmic deeds without yet having had the opportunity to repent.
In these instances, one's roots of goodness are weak while evil karma has proliferated, causing whatever one does in the present life to be thus affected.
None of these accord with one's wishes; one should know that all are caused by the residual retribution of evil karma from the past.
Therefore, one must now perform repentance.
This section concerns the repentance for past and present [faults]. Because one’s roots of goodness were weak, there are sufferings such as premature death during the prime of life.
[End of section] ○ From here below, all karmic retributions for transgressions clearly demonstrate that whatever one does, it never accords with one's wishes;
among the evil retributions of the human realm, there is none that does not involve the mind and body being tormented and oppressed by manifold sufferings.
From beginningless time until this day, among all those in the realms of humans and devas— both present and future—
there are immeasurable remaining retributions (*avaśeṣa-vipāka*).

Having first explained the causes of these remaining retributions above, I shall now specifically enumerate the immeasurable karmic offenses of these remaining retributions to provide a general exposition.
I repent for the karmic retributions of calamities from past lives, inherited afflictions, chronic illnesses, and the impairment of the six sense faculties that plague human beings.

I repent for the karmic retributions of being born in borderlands, holding false views, and falling into the three evil paths or the eight difficult conditions that plague human beings. I repent for the karmic retributions of frequent illness and emaciation that plague human beings.

I repent for the retribution of the crime of shortening lives through untimely death; I repent for the retribution of the crime whereby human beings and their six classes of kinsmen and relatives are unable to maintain their stability and protection;
I repent for the retribution of the crime of the suffering of separation from loved ones due to the loss and demise of human friends and kin.

This is a detailed confession regarding the present and future manifestations of retribution. "Flowing" (*liu*) means to drift away or be cast adrift; "calamity" (*yang*) refers to misfortune. This is due to karmic causes from beginningless time:
even if one cultivates wholesome dharmas and attains a human body, if evil karma has not been exhausted, there will still remain the calamities of drifting and being cast adrift.
Therefore, it is said, "the drifting calamities of past karmic retributions," and so forth. The six sense organs (*ṣaḍāyatana*): eye, ear, nose... [and so on].
Regarding the tongue, body, and mind, one cannot be fully complete. As for the three types of evil: there is evil, great evil, and the evil among evils.
"Evil" refers to when others treat one with malice and one responds by returning that malice. "Great evil" refers to when others do not encroach upon oneself, yet one harms them without cause.
"The evil among evils" refers to when people come to show respect and provide offerings, yet one does not think of repaying their kindness.
On the contrary, it harms them. ○ Regarding the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*): being born in a remote borderland or a family of wrong views, one does not know the Three Jewels.
First, hell; second, hungry ghosts; third, animals—these are also called the three evil realms (*trividha-durgati*) and are included among the eight difficulties.
Fourth, being blind, deaf, or mute; fifth, possessing worldly wisdom and eloquence; sixth, being before or after a Buddha; seventh...
Uttarakuru. These four are among the human realms. The eight heavens of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñisattva*).
As for these eight, if one is situated within any of them, one cannot see the Buddha or hear the Dharma; collectively, they are termed the "eight difficulties" (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*).

[From the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-ṭīkā*]. Regarding the inability to maintain constancy: it refers to when, among one's parents, siblings, or wife and children, there occurs a death or a separation by birth.
This is the withering and decay of the *o* [heart/mind]. It is parched and withered.
One repents for the retribution of offenses involving the gathering of human enemies, sorrow, grief, fear, and dread.

One repents for the retribution of offenses involving the dangers and terrors of water, fire, bandits, thieves, and weapons, as well as weakness and cowardice. One repents for the retribution of offenses involving human solitude and suffering.
I repent for the retribution of being dispersed, scattered, and driven from one's kingdom;

I repent for the retribution of being imprisoned, confined, shackled, flogged, and tortured in human jails; I repent for the retribution of engaging in public and private disputes, mutually ensnaring one another, and mutually slandering one another.
One who is young and without a father is called an orphan; one who is old and without a son is called a solitary.

Wandering and scattered like drifting waves, having lost their kingdom and land, they have no home to which to return, suffering hardships beyond measure. Imprisoned in seclusion, they stand huddled within the confines of the jail.
One may not wield the whip or scourge without self-restraint.
Because they mutually embellish their rhetoric and even address one another with malicious words and slander, it is said that they are "equal in mutual aggravation."
I repent for the retribution of human ailments—malignant diseases that persist for years and months without remission, leaving one bedridden on mats and unable to rise or move.
I repent for the retribution of human pestilences—the winter plagues, summer epidemics, toxic miasmas, and contagious fevers.

I repent for the retribution of human afflictions caused by malevolent winds, swellings, distensions, and obstructions. I repent for the retribution of being pursued by various evil spirits who watch for and seek out my vulnerabilities.

If one wishes to eliminate the retribution for the sins of causing calamities and misfortunes; the retribution for the false manifestation of strange anomalies by human beings, bird calls, the hundred monsters, flying corpses, and malevolent ghosts;
then these shall be rectified.
Illnesses shall be healed. This refers to the four seasons: toxic epidemics in the autumn, malaria in the autumn, and *shanghan* (febrile cold) in the spring.

Among these, those who have experienced the suffering of illness are as described in the *Lotus Sūtra*: "Those with dropsy, consumption, scabies, leprosy, carbuncles, and abscesses—those whose diseases serve as their clothing.
This refers to such conditions. "Phlegm" (*pi*) refers to the obstruction of the vital energies (*qi*).

Diseases such as the swelling and fullness caused by pathogenic winds, or chronic obstructions and entanglements, continue through the various karmic retributions described below; there is nothing that is not [included therein].
This is the lingering calamity of the past. ○ *Sì* (伺): To spy, to wait in ambush; to scout. ○ *Chóng* (崇): Divine calamity. ○ *Shī* (屍):
One who is dead upon their bed is called a corpse (*shī*). A "flying corpse" (*fēishī*) is a type of怪异 (*guàiyì*, strange anomaly).
As for the various "hundred anomalies" (*bǎiguài*), they are likely the same as the *vettāla* (起屍, *qǐshī*) and similar classes of beings.
I repent for the karmic retribution of having been harmed in human life by tigers, leopards, jackals, wolves, and all manner of evil beasts of air, land, and water.
I repent for the karmic retribution of committing suicide in human life by hanging oneself, stabbing oneself, or other forms of self-destruction.

I repent for the karmic retribution of casting oneself into pits, leaping into fire, drowning oneself, or falling from heights. I repent for the karmic retribution of lacking majesty, virtue, and renown in human life.
I repent for the karmic retribution of my human life’s food, clothing, and means of subsistence failing to accord with my heart's desires;
I repent for the karmic retribution of obstacles created by evil associates whenever I traveled, entered or exited, or engaged in any activity during my human life.
Likewise, I repent for the karmic retribution of immeasurable calamities, crosswise misfortunes, pestilence, afflictions, and distress within the realms of humans and devas, both present and future.
The tiger is a fierce beast. The leopard resembles a tiger but has circular markings. The *chái* (jaguar) belongs to the wolf family; the wolf resembles a dog. All are malevolent beasts.

This is that which torments and oppresses the heart and body with grief, anxiety, fear, and dread, never for a moment leaving them.
That there are so many such disagreeable things in the human world is precisely because one's roots of goodness are feeble while evil karma has proliferated;
thus, these various bitter retributions arise. How can one not give rise to great shame and remorse, and with great terror, seek relief through lamentation and repentance?
We, [names], today with utmost sincerity, turn toward the Buddhas of the ten directions, the Honored Dharma, and the Assembly of Sages, seeking their compassion to repent.
May all [obstacles] be extinguished.
The preceding repentance for the three obstacles is now complete. In the following text, we collectively present our vows to seek the accomplishment of merit and virtue.

Previously, I have already repented all afflictive hindrances of the three karmas and six sense faculties, all karmic hindrances, and all retributive hindrances of the four modes of birth and the six realms of existence.
Now, I shall successively make vows and dedicate the merit.
Continuing from what precedes to initiate what follows: the section below correctly names the dedication of merit.

We, [Name] and others, vow that by means of the merit produced through this repentance of the three obstructions, it shall be entirely dedicated and bestowed upon all sentient beings, so that we may all together perform repentance.
We vow that within our present lives, the bodies and minds of all sentient beings shall be at peace.
May all misfortunes—the three calamities, the eight difficulties, and inauspicious events—be entirely eliminated. May food and clothing be abundant.
May this [merit] reach all sentient beings so that they experience the fruits of happiness in their present lives. (The three minor calamities are famine, pestilence, and warfare;
the three major calamities are the fire, water, and wind kalpas. Here, it specifically refers to the three minor calamities.)
...and so forth. The eight difficulties (*aṣṭāv akṣaṇāḥ*) are as previously mentioned. The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

"If a person can observe the precept against killing for even one day and one night, they will certainly not encounter the calamity of weapons in future lives. If one uses even a single *harītakī* fruit..."
If one gives food to a sick monk with a profound and pure mind, one will certainly not encounter the calamity of pestilence in future lives.
If one gives even a single morsel of food to the Sangha with a profound and pure mind, one will certainly not encounter the calamity of famine in future lives.
With right faith in the Triple Gem, they shall all, upon casting off this retribution body, attain rebirth in the World of Ultimate Bliss (Sukhāvatī).

There, they will personally behold Amitābha and receive the prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa). In a future age, they will see Maitreya Buddha, hear the True Dharma, and advance in their practice according to the teachings.
The phrase "Right Faith in the Triple Gem" also universally reaches all sentient beings so that they may plant the causes of goodness in their present lives.

To have faith in this unsurpassed Dharma of the One Vehicle is what constitutes right faith. Setting this aside, the following refers to the universal reaching of all sentient beings so that they may draw near to the Buddha in the future.
"Setting this aside" means the evil karma and good karma performed in previous lives; in this present life...

The body is precisely that which receives the retribution of suffering and pleasure in the future; therefore, it is called the "retribution body" (*vipākakāya*). Upon death, one abandons this physical life and departs;
hence, it is said that one "leaves behind this retribution body. [In] the Land of Amitābha Buddha, the pure people and their manifold joys are all *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive);
they are not like those in the five turbidities of the evil world. This is what is meant by "seeing the small Amitābha."

Regarding the term *vyākaraṇa* (prediction): it refers to the seedlings of rice and grain. Etymologically, the character is composed of "grass" (*艸*) and "distinguish" (*別*). Since rice seedlings are a distinguished variety among grasses, they are called *bīja* (seedlings).
This serves as a metaphor for the prediction of Buddhahood, which is like planting the seedling of a Buddha; thus, one is said to "receive the prediction of seedlings.
In the land of Maitreya Buddha, the ground is level and even, with no mountains, hills, valleys, or gullies. The people...
The populace is largely free from greed, anger, and delusion; their lifespan is eighty-four thousand years, and their faces have the color of peach blossoms.
Maitreya shall preach the Dharma at three assemblies under the Dragon-Flower Tree:
at the first assembly, he will deliver ninety-six hundred million people; at the second assembly, ninety-four hundred million people; and at the third assembly, ninety-two hundred million people.
Maitreya Buddha shall remain in the world for sixty thousand years; the True Dharma shall endure for this long, and the Semblance Dharma likewise.

May I, in birth after birth and in every place, always encounter kings who cause the Three Jewels to flourish and descend, and may I never be born into the families of non-Buddhists or those with false views.
May this reach all sentient beings. In the future, may Māras, externalists, and false views be unable to flourish.

Furthermore, I vow that in birth after birth and in every place, I shall be born by transformation within a lotus flower, belonging to a noble and eminent lineage, dwelling in peace and happiness, with food, clothing, and necessities provided spontaneously.
This shall be universally bestowed upon sentient beings so that they may experience supreme [attainments] in the future through the merit of this method of repentance.
Furthermore, by adding single-minded mindfulness of the Buddha to purify their minds, the Buddha-lands in all places will become entirely pure;

thus, they shall not receive birth from a parent’s womb, but shall always take up residence within lotus flowers. If one must indeed be born by transformation within a lotus flower, it is due to the planting of [seeds].
The clans do not consist solely of the wealthy and noble of high standing.

According to these two lines, even those who are inferior remain in the palaces of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, while those who are superior will surely be reborn in the pure lands of the ten directions; this can be further verified by examining the subsequent text.
Furthermore, I vow that in every birth and throughout all lifetimes, in whatever place I may be, I shall be compassionate, benevolent, loyal, and filial;
I shall treat all beings with an impartial mind to rescue and aid them, never giving rise to even a single thought of hostility or harm.
May this be universally extended to all sentient beings; may it remain virtuous even in the future.
Furthermore, I vow that in every birth and in every place throughout all lifetimes, I shall always be protected and remembered by all Buddhas;

may I be able to subdue the enmity of Māras and all non-Buddhist paths, and may I assemble together with all Bodhisattvas in one place, maintaining the continuity of the mind set on the path to Bodhi.
It is uninterrupted. This also applies to meeting the Sages in the future. The *Jingyin Famen Jing* (Sūtra of the Pure Seal Dharma Gate) says:

"By means of a mind that acts with no purposeful striving, one is able to subdue all Māras. One should know there are four ways to subdue them: knowing suffering can subdue the *skandha-māra*; severing the origin [of suffering] can..."

It subdues the demon of afflictions (*kleśamāra*). By realizing cessation (*nirodha*), one can subdue the demon of death (*mṛtyumāra*); by cultivating the path (*mārga*), one can subdue the celestial demon (*devaputramāra*).

The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Because it severs the life-force of wisdom, it is called a *māra*. Furthermore, because it constantly practices negligence and harms oneself, it is called a *māra*. *Māra* means 'to kill'.
[He was] the twenty-first spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) in the assembly of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*. Throughout...
Practicing as an outsider, he said to Sudhana: "Within Jambudvīpa, there are ninety-six kinds of outsiders, each giving rise to divergent views and developing attachments.
I have skillfully disciplined them all therein, causing them to abandon all such views;
this extends even throughout the worlds of the ten directions, where it is likewise so. (Lengyan Zhu)

It is said: A person who has awakened to the Way remains in harmony with the Way throughout their life amidst the multitudes; they do not engage in the three karmas of body, speech, and mind, and therefore do not undergo birth and death within the triple world.
Furthermore, a person of the One Vehicle constantly enters into birth and death to deliver sentient beings;
this is truly sustained by the power of the Way, such that they are untainted by the fundamental afflictions of the triple world and move freely back and forth.
Furthermore, I vow that in birth after birth and in every place throughout all lifetimes, I shall cause the Buddha-dharma to flourish and manifest;
I shall practice the Mahāyāna, manifesting infinite emanations to rescue and deliver sentient beings, proceeding directly to the site of enlightenment without ever regressing.
This applies universally to those of the future. Regarding self-benefit and benefiting others, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:

"Although one manifests a body within the world, the mind has no attachment to worldly dharmas. This is not the same as ordinary beings who are forever submerged in the three realms, nor is it the same as those of the two vehicles who seek only to escape the three realms.
Only then does one know that for a student of the Buddha to be able to evade birth and death, the meaning lies therein.
In this regard, there is no birth-and-death from which one may escape, nor a triple world from which one may emerge;

for one contemplates the four modes of birth as if they were an only child, and regards the three realms with impartial benevolence. Regarding the manifestation of infinite bodies, as stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*:
"As for my manifested bodies—that is, the Buddhas—who are currently preaching the Dharma in the worlds of the ten directions, they should now all assemble," and so forth.
Just as all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have made their vows, cultivated merit and wisdom, and performed dedications, so too do I make these vows,
cultivate and accumulate [merit], and perform dedication.
Above this, it is the same as the various sages who have made vows. As with the Four Great Vows and so forth, one cultivates merit and wisdom;
this is the simultaneous cultivation of both merit and wisdom. There are ten types of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*):

First is the dedication to rescue and protect all sentient beings while remaining free from the mark of a "sentient being," for there is nothing to be delivered. Second is the indestructible dedication, which destroys that which is destructible. Far...
1. Because it is free from all [notions of] detachment. 2. The dedication equal to that of all Buddhas: awakening is identical to the awakening of the Buddhas.

3. The dedication reaching all places: illuminating the groundless. 4. The dedication of the inexhaustible treasury of merit: the mutual interpenetration of body and land. 5. The dedication of impartial roots of goodness:
being identical to the causes of the Buddhas. 6. The dedication of the equal contemplation of all things.

1. Dedication identical with sentient beings; its nature is the same as that of sentient beings. 2. Dedication of the characteristics of the eightfold true suchness (*tathatā*); neither identical nor separate. 3. Dedication of unbound liberation;
unhindered throughout the ten directions. 4. Dedication equal to the infinite dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*);
its nature attains perfect fulfillment.
Even if the realm of empty space were to end, the realm of sentient beings were to end, the karma of sentient beings were to end, and the afflictions of sentient beings were to end—
this dedication of merit collectively returns to clarify that these four dharmas are subject to exhaustion.
This dedication of my practice shall never come to an end;
this clearly explains that the practice is inexhaustible.
Having made this vow of dedication, I reverently pay homage with a sincere heart to the eternally abiding Triple Gem.
Summary: Paying Homage to the Triple Gem. The above ten kinds of dedication have been extensively explained in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*;

they will not be cited here at length. However, when a person practices dedication, they turn causes toward the fruit, turn the small toward the great, and even dedicate toward the true suchness (*tathatā*) and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), adorning the unsurpassed Bodhi of the Buddha-fruit. As the Sūtra says: "Dedicating oneself..."
"To bestow [merit] upon all sentient beings so that they may together attain the Buddha-way"—this is precisely the meaning intended here.
Regarding the phrase "dedicating merit in this manner" (*evam pariṇāmayati*) and the expression "until the realm of empty space is exhausted," it is as stated in the *Text for Repentance*:

"Until the world of empty space is exhausted, and until sentient beings, karma, and afflictions are exhausted—since these four phenomena are vast and boundless, I vow that this dedication shall likewise be so."
This is why it is said that this dedication of merit of mine shall never come to an end. Having made this vow, one further takes refuge in and pays homage to the eternally abiding Triple Gem.

One should know that regarding all the immeasurable and boundless karmic offenses described in the preceding section of this repentance text, those who wish to seek their purification through repentance must ultimately rely entirely upon the eternally abiding Triple Gem of the ten directions.

Through the power of vast majesty and supernormal faculties, and by the power of one’s own single-minded sincerity, the karmic obstacles of transgressions begin to dissolve, merit and wisdom increase, and one proceeds until the attainment of unsurpassed Bodhi; for there is nothing that transcends this.
We, the multitude, desiring to seek the methods of repentance, should exert ourselves fully before the Three Jewels and our own persons.
Take this to heart. Be careful not to treat it with negligence; be careful not to treat it with negligence.
Should there be even the slightest thought of levity, it will merely be the fabrication of flowery language. Not only will it fail to benefit principle, I fear it will also fail to benefit practice.
Reflect upon this.
